During the investigation, officers also found evidence on the device of him discussing sexually assaulting children. Detective Constable Helen Keighley, who led the investigation, said: "William Floyd subjected his victims to horrific sexual assaults and the severity of his crimes are reflected in the sentence handed down. "I would like to pay tribute to the victims: their immense bravery and courage in coming forward to tell police about these abhorrent crimes has led to Floyd being removed from society for a long time." Floyd, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty to six counts of rape, five counts of sexual assault of a child, three counts of assault by penetration of a child, two counts of possessing indecent photographs of a child, and one count each of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, engaging in sexual activity in the presence of a child, and possession of an extreme pornographic image. He was sentenced on November 12 at Peterborough Magistrates’ Court, which was sitting as a crown court. Floyd was also ordered to sign the Sex Offenders Register indefinitely and was given an indefinite sexual harm prevention order, along with an indefinite restraining order against the victims. He will serve eight years and six months in custody, with the total sentence of 17 years coming from concurrent sentences and a licence period.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Lifts can create some of the most memorable moments on Strictly Come Dancing, however, they are not allowed in every routine. The rules around lifts are often a source of confusion for viewers, contestants, and even the judges themselves. Here is a guide to what makes a lift illegal on Strictly, which dances allow them, and how the judges handle rule-breakers. A lift is defined as any movement where a dancer has both feet off the floor with assistance or support from their partner. Strictly judge Craig Revel Horwood highlighted the rule in 2024 after Pete Wicks and professional partner Jowita Przystał included two lifts in their Rumba. He said one foot should have remained on the floor and described both moves as "totally illegal", adding that couples could lose marks for doing so. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK motorists urged not to ignore this common night-time driving problem
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers who see blurred headlights or halos around lights are being urged to get their eyesight checked. Adam Aslam, director at Nevies Opticians, said changes in vision can be particularly noticeable when motorists are driving after dark. He said streaks, glare and blurred lights can have different causes and advised people whose sight is affected to ask an optometrist for advice. One possible cause is astigmatism, a common condition that can make headlights, streetlights and road signs appear blurred or distorted, particularly at night. The NHS says astigmatism can cause blurred vision, headaches and eye strain, and recommends visiting an optician if someone has symptoms. It explains that astigmatism means the eye is shaped more like a rugby ball than a football, causing light to focus in more than one place in the eye. It says the condition does not always need treatment, but glasses or contact lenses are among the options. The NHS also advises going to an optician if you have not had an eye test for two years, and says regular tests are important. Mr Aslam said: “Many people assume everyone sees headlights the same way they do, so they may not realise there could be an issue with their vision. “If lights appear unusually bright, blurry or surrounded by halos, it’s worth booking an eye examination to have your vision checked.” Even motorists with healthy vision can find driving after dark more challenging during the winter months, according to the optician. He also shared five ways motorists can prepare for journeys in low light, including cleaning the inside as well as the outside of their windscreen. Dust, residue and condensation on the glass can scatter light and make glare from oncoming headlights worse, he said. His advice is to clean both sides regularly and clear condensation before setting off. Mr Aslam also recommends avoiding a bright phone screen just before a journey and giving your eyes a moment to adjust to the dark. He advises drivers not to use their phones while driving. Changes in driving habits can be worth noticing, too. According to Mr Aslam, of Nevies Opticians, avoiding unfamiliar routes or driving after dark, slowing down more than usual and relying heavily on road markings can be signs that vision has changed. Anyone who has adapted their behaviour in these ways should consider an eye test, he said. Repeated star-shaped lights, streaks or halos should not simply be assumed to be normal, particularly if they affect how clearly someone can see. Motorists should also check that they have the right lights on, as daytime running lights often do not illuminate the rear of a car, according to Mr Aslam. He recommends switching headlights on in poor visibility and using dipped beam when other road users are nearby. The Highway Code advises drivers dazzled by oncoming headlights to slow down and, if necessary, stop. Mr Aslam added: “People routinely service their cars, check their tyres and replace worn wipers, yet many overlook their eyesight. “Your vision plays a huge role in how safely you drive, particularly during the darker months. “If you’ve noticed changes in your sight, booking an eye test is a sensible step.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WhatsApp users warned this group chat mistake could lead to criminal charges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A simple mistake in a WhatsApp group chat could leave people facing criminal charges under new laws, a legal expert has warned. Ruth Peters from Olliers Solicitors said an image automatically saved from a group chat can lead to serious charges, even if the recipient did not ask for it. New offences covering possession and publication of specified pornographic images came into force in England and Wales on November 6 under the Crime and Policing Act 2026. They do not apply to every explicit image, and receiving an unsolicited image does not automatically mean someone has committed an offence. But those found in breach of the new laws could find themselves facing criminal charges and time in jail. The new rules cover pornography that explicitly and realistically depicts strangulation or suffocation, certain incest-themed penetrative sexual activity, or sexual activity involving someone who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. The people depicted must appear to a reasonable person to be real, according to government guidance. Whether someone possesses an image is a question of fact for a court, but the guidance says it could include material stored on a device, in a personal account or in cloud storage. The maximum sentence for possession is two years for material depicting strangulation or suffocation or certain relatives, and three years for material depicting someone who is, or is pretending to be, under 16. Publication carries a maximum sentence of five years for all three offences. Ms Peters said Olliers Solicitors had encountered around 10 current or ongoing cases in which people faced serious consequences after images from group chats were found on their phones. She recalled a case involving an image of bestiality found during a phone examination in an unrelated investigation that resulted in no further action. The Disclosure and Barring Service dealt with the image offence with a caution, but was subsequently considering whether to place the person on a barred list, potentially affecting their employment, she said. Ms Peters said: “The important thing is to understand that possession can be a continuing act. “It is not necessarily about whether you actively went looking for something or whether you downloaded it yourself. “People need to be aware of what is on their devices and understand that images shared in group chats can have serious consequences.” WhatsApp users found breaking the new laws could find themselves facing criminal charges and time in jail. (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire) The Ministry of Justice says possession can be a continuing act and advises people to permanently delete or otherwise get rid of images covered by the offences. WhatsApp users may have a defence if they were sent an image without asking for it and did not keep it for an unreasonable length of time. There may also be a defence if they had not seen the image before and did not know or have cause to suspect that it was covered by the offences. Ms Peters said: “People arrested for offences where the police need to examine their phones will often have their devices checked by officers. “An image automatically saved from a group chat can lead to very serious charges. “While receiving an image you have not asked for is not necessarily an offence, if that image stays on your device for a period of time, you could potentially face prosecution. “Even if you didn't specifically opt to save that image, it may still remain on your device.” Were you aware of the new pornographic image laws introduced earlier this month? Brand began his career as a TV presenter and comedian and became a Hollywood star, appearing in films such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall, Hop and the Despicable Me franchise. A post shared by Centrepoint (@centrepointuk) Now, as Christmas approaches, Newsquest and Centrepoint are building on that work with a dedicated national Christmas campaign focused on both immediate support for young people facing homelessness and the need for longer-term change. At the heart of the campaign is a simple appeal to readers. A £20 gift could provide vital food and toiletries for a young person facing homelessness this Christmas, in the form of an emergency hardship voucher. Alongside the fundraising appeal, the campaign will encourage people to support Centrepoint's wider campaigning work to help create lasting change for young people. The Christmas campaign has deliberately been developed around the principle that homelessness does not end when Christmas does, connecting immediate winter support with Centrepoint's longer-term work to help young people move towards stable housing. Newsquest titles across the country will support the campaign through print, digital and social content, with central campaign material complemented by local stories and opportunities in selected communities to bring the issue of youth homelessness closer to readers. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned easy £10 fix could help avoid £2,500 fine and 3 points on licence
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers are being warned about a £2,500 fine which they could receive if they don't make an easy £10 fix. While you won't use your windscreen wipers on every outing, they certainly come in handy on wet days and when you need to improve your vision by clearing the windscreen. If you have damaged or broken windscreen wipers, it's important they're replaced because, as John Hood, the general manager at Auction4Cars.com explains, they can result in a £2,500 fine and three points on your licence. The vehicle company surveyed 2,000 UK drivers and found that almost a fifth of them (19%) have admitted to driving with broken or damaged windscreen wipers. Did you know how to spot when your wiper blades need replacing? (Image: Getty) Auction4Cars.com said that many drivers get behind the wheel despite their vehicles having common defects. Mr Hood said: "Autumn is one of the worst times of year for visibility on the road. "Rainy weather and spray from other vehicles puts more demand on your wipers, so it's important that they work properly. "If your wipers don't clear your windscreen well, you're putting yourself and other road users at risk. "Getting caught with worn-out wipers could land you a £2,500 fine and three points on your licence." If you're not sure if your windscreen wipers need replacing, Mr Hood has shared some advice to help you notice when they aren't up to scratch. He said: "If your wipers leave smears, make a squeaking noise or miss patches on your windscreen, it's usually a sign the blades are worn out. "Look for fraying or cracks in the rubber – these can stop the blades from clearing water effectively." Mr Hood said that, while you'll need to take into account how often the vehicle is used and what the weather has been like, "as a general rule, drivers should replace them every six months to a year". He said they're usually around £10 to replace and "compared to the cost of an MOT retest or a fine, it's a small price to pay that can make a huge difference to visibility, especially in the autumn months." The RAC added: "When you lift the wiper off the glass and you see that the rubber looks cracked, split, or is beginning to peel away from the frame, this means that the blades won't make proper contact with the windscreen and need replacing. "Finally, if you are driving during heavy rain and you have reduced visibility even if the wipers are moving, then it is important not to ignore it. "This is because worn wipers can seriously compromise safety. "Regular car maintenance involves checking the blades and cleaning them can extend their life, but once they show visible wear, replacement is the safest option." The RAC also shared a step-by-step guide for anyone who needs to replace their windscreen wipers. Lift the wiper arm away from the windscreen so that it locks and is upright, then find the release clip and either press or slide it to take the old wiper blade away. The RAC warns: "Carefully remove it, making sure the bare metal arm doesn't snap back onto the glass as this could cause several issues." Recommended reading: Then you'll need to "align the new blade with the hook or connector and push it into place until you hear a click." Once this is done, you need to "gently" return the wiper arm to the windscreen and then do the same again with the other blade if you're replacing both. When you have finished adding new blades, test them by using washer fluid so you can see if the wiper blades move over the windscreen correctly. Did you know windscreen wiper blades should be replaced every six to 12 months? Let us know in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Help us fight youth homelessness this Christmas with Centrepoint
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: This Christmas, too many young people will find themselves facing homelessness and the uncertainty that comes with it. When a young person is in crisis, practical support can make all the difference. Having access to everyday items that we often take for granted, such as food and toiletries, can provide comfort, dignity and a sense of stability at an incredibly difficult time. To help combat this growing issue, Newsquest has joined forces with youth homelessness charity Centrepoint calling on communities across the country to support young people facing homelessness this winter. A gift of £20 could provide vital food and toiletries for a young person facing homelessness this Christmas through an emergency hardship voucher. (Image: Steve Franck) That support can be a lifeline, helping a young person access the essentials they need while they take their first steps towards a secure future. Newsquest readers can donate here and help provide vital support to a young person this Christmas. You can also sign up to be a campaigner here. As a campaigner, you'll be the first to hear about opportunities to take action, from signing petitions and contacting decision-makers to sharing campaign messages with your community and helping raise awareness of the issues affecting young people facing homelessness. Centrepoint’s CEO Seyi Obakin explains why now is such a crucial time to share your support for the charity below: Newsquest CEO, Henry Faure Walker, and Centrepoint CEO, Seyi Obakin. (Image: Jeff Moore) This Christmas, national attention is rightly focused on ending rough sleeping. On his first day as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham stood outside Number 10 and made it his "moral mission" that nobody should be left without shelter by Christmas. At Centrepoint, we share that ambition. For 57 years, we've worked alongside young people facing homelessness, providing safe accommodation and specialist support to help them rebuild their lives. It is hugely encouraging to see the government backing this mission with significant investment. Winter can be especially dangerous for those without a safe place to stay, and every person helped off the streets is another person protected from harm. But homelessness doesn't end when Christmas does. Getting someone off the street is a vital first step, but lasting change means giving them the stability and opportunities they need to move forward. Because a home is more than a roof over your head. It's the foundation from which people can study, work, maintain relationships and build a future. Many readers will recognise how difficult life can feel for young people today. Perhaps you have a son, daughter, niece, nephew or grandchild taking their first steps into adulthood. Even with the support of family, finding an affordable place to live, securing a job and becoming independent can feel daunting. Now imagine trying to do all of that with nowhere safe to call home. When many people think about homelessness, they picture rough sleeping. But for most young people, homelessness is hidden. It's sleeping on a friend's sofa because there's nowhere else to go. It's riding buses through the night to stay warm. It's spending hours in a fast-food restaurant because it feels safer than being outside. These young people are often still going to college, turning up for work and trying to carry on as normal, all while worrying about where they'll sleep that night. No young person should have to live that way. And yet too many do. They have been let down by the very systems that should protect them and denied the security most of us take for granted. Homeless young people need more than emergency help. They need long-term support to rebuild their confidence, continue their education, find employment and develop the skills that will help them thrive. This matters to all of us, but it matters most to young people like Vicky. In the letter below, she shares what it was like to experience homelessness as a young person and the difference that support made when she needed it most. Her story is deeply personal, but it is far from unique. Behind every homelessness statistic is a young person with hopes, ambitions and potential. This Christmas, let's not only help them find safety today, but ensure they have the opportunity to build a brighter future tomorrow. One person who Centrepoint has helped is Vicky. After sofa-surfing with family members, sleeping rough, and seeking shelter in a McDonald’s, Vicky is now living in Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme, providing her safe, affordable housing. (Image: Rebekah Kennington) Vicky has written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham to emphasise how important the Centrepoint’s work is. These are her words: Dear Prime Minister, As a young adult with lived experience of homelessness, I really appreciate your commitment to end rough sleeping. Things haven’t always been easy for me. When my mum became seriously ill, my life changed almost overnight. My brother and I were still young, but suddenly we were trying to keep our home going without the support we needed. Eventually, it became impossible and I lost my home. Shouldn’t there have been systems in place to support my family when we were plunged into crisis? At first I couch-surfed with a family member, but they could only help me for so long. I didn’t want to be a burden, so I ended up sleeping rough. I was staying awake all night, and turning up to work exhausted the next day. The only place I could stay safe and warm was in McDonalds because it was lit and there were lots of people there. One night an older person sat down opposite me and asked if I was okay. That interaction really stuck with me. Homelessness so often gets ignored, but I know you agree, Prime Minister, we all have a responsibility to notice and act on it. That person told me about Centrepoint, and I eventually called their Helpline and was able to access their services. The first thing the support worker I met did was give me a Pot Noodle as I hadn’t eaten for a few days – it felt so good. That emergency support was a lifeline. But what helped me move forward was what came next. Centrepoint helped me navigate the complicated housing system, and always guided me through difficult moments. When I got a call to say I had somewhere to live I was shaking. I kept thinking they’d made a mistake. Then I cried, because I finally had a bed I could sleep on. A safe place I could go to. Today, I live in Centrepoint’s Independent Living Programme, where rents are capped at a third of income. Having affordable and stable housing means I can work, save money and plan for my future with confidence. So many more of these homes are needed around the country, so all young people can have the same foundation. Prime Minister, I hope you achieve your goal of ending rough sleeping this Christmas. But I also urge you to remember that homelessness doesn’t end when the festive season does. Young people need urgent support when they're in crisis, but they also need long-term solutions that let them look ahead with hope. Vicky Centrepoint is on a mission to end youth homelessness by 2037. But to get there, they need a growing movement of people willing to stand up for homeless young people and help change the systems holding them back. As well as donating to the Christmas campaign here, where a gift of £20 could provide vital food and toiletries for a young person facing homelessness, you can also sign up to be a campaigner here. As a campaigner, you'll be the first to hear about opportunities to take action, from signing petitions and contacting decision-makers to sharing campaign messages with your community and helping raise awareness of the issues affecting young people facing homelessness. Together, we can build the public and political support needed to ensure every young person has a safe place to call home and the foundation to build their future. When a young person is in crisis, practical support can make all the difference. Having access to everyday items that we often take for granted, such as food and toiletries, can provide comfort, dignity and a sense of stability at an incredibly difficult time. That support can be a lifeline, helping a young person access the essentials they need while they take their first steps towards a secure future.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Newsquest and Centrepoint launch Christmas campaign to support homeless young people
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Newsquest, the UK's largest local media group, and Centrepoint, the UK's leading youth homelessness charity, have launched a major Christmas campaign calling on communities across the country to support young people facing homelessness this winter. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP cuts warning as major benefits shake-up could leave claimants with less cash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Some young people could see their benefits cut under a major DWP shake-up, with those who refuse offers of work, training or employment support potentially losing financial help. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has confirmed that some young people will receive less financial support in future under recommendations expected in a major review of youth unemployment. Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is due to publish his independent report on Tuesday, November 17, setting out proposals to tackle the growing number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets), which topped one million this year. One of the biggest proposals is reported to be to move some young people currently receiving health-related benefits onto a new 'youth allowance', paid at the standard rate of Universal Credit. Mr Milburn has acknowledged that some young people would receive less financial support under his plans. Those who refuse a proposed legal guarantee of work, training or employment support could also risk losing their benefits. Mr Milburn is also expected to recommend gradually cutting the employer National Insurance contributions paid on workers aged 21 to 24 over five years, initially focusing on retail and hospitality. According to the BBC, the plans would double the threshold at which businesses start paying employer National Insurance on earnings from this age group, from £5,000 to £10,000. However, the changes would only be introduced "when economic conditions allow". Mr Milburn is expected to argue that a blanket cut would not be the best use of the several billion pounds of public money it could cost, particularly if young people cannot find jobs after gaining new skills. Mr McFadden has backed the proposed legal guarantee, arguing that employment support needs a stronger legal foundation and would give young people "more certainty about what they're entitled to". Speaking to Sky News' Sunday Morning programme, he said the Government needed to make changes not "in spite of being Labour people", but "because we're Labour people". "It's a different proposition from last year, and I hope that Parliament views it in that light," he said. The Government will be hoping to avoid another Labour rebellion after ministers were forced to water down proposed welfare cuts last year. Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the legal entitlement "might sound a nice thing to do" but "doesn't make sense". However, she described the move away from "handing out cash for relatively mild conditions" and towards employment support as "the right direction of travel". Reform UK's Danny Kruger said he was "encouraged" by "the suggestion that we need to be much stricter about benefits for young people who should be supported into work or should be working". Recommended reading: The review is also expected to call for the proportion of children considered school-ready at the start of reception to rise from 75% to 90%. Mr Milburn is expected to warn that too many five-year-olds struggle with everyday tasks such as using cutlery or going to the toilet. He has previously warned that tackling youth unemployment could take a decade and billions of pounds, arguing that "crude cuts" would simply result in young people appearing elsewhere in Government spending figures.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Environmental disaster fears after 14,000 litres of oil dumped in ditch off A14
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Calls for urgent action to avert an environmental disaster have been made after an estimated 14,000 litres of waste engine oil was dumped into a Huntingdonshire ditch. Robert Neilson has raised concerns after being alerted to the illegal 'fly-tipping' by a family member who farms the area off the A14 between the Leighton Bromswold and Catworth junctions. Mr Neilson, who lives in Ramsey, said his relative found the oil while working on the farm earlier this week. “He told me he contacted the Environment Agency straight away because he was so concerned about the amount of oil and the environmental disaster it could cause,” said Mr Neilson. Read more Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections Hunts man accused of distributing indecent images of children named New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed He said Environment Agency officers had visited the site, but no action had yet been taken to clear the mess. “I have been told the Environment Agency estimates that it's between six or seven tanker loads of the used engine oil that's been dumped – around 14,000 litres. This is not an accident. You don't accidentally dump that much oil into a ditch,” said Mr Neilson. He is worried that without action, the oil will make its way into the River Ouse at Huntingdon. Mr Neilson said the ditch currently contains little water, so the oil is not moving much, although some has reached a nearby brook. But heavy rain could send water from the A14 into the ditch, giving the oil enough water to reach the River Ouse. “This is an environmental disaster waiting to happen. That amount of oil is going to have a massive impact on the wildlife; it will kill fish and affect birds and other animals,” said Mr Neilson. He said the Environment Agency needed to act quickly before rain, adding that a digger could scoop most of the oil from the ditch. "Obviously someone has come along into the layby with their tanker full of oil and simply opened the tap. It was probably done after dark so no one would probably take much notice, and think it was someone parked up for a nap," said Mr Neilson, who added: "This is absolutely disgusting. It is vandalism, and the worst kind of fly-tipping and action is needed pronto." An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We've installed barriers to help protect Ellington Brook from the appalling dumping of oil on the A14 and are advising National Highways on clean-up measures to limit the environmental impacts." The spokesperson added that National Highways is leading the clean-up and, where appropriate, can take enforcement action where its drainage network has been misused. The police are responsible for investigating any suspected criminal activity and can support Environment Agency investigations through measures such as CCTV and ANPR enquiries.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Russell Brand shares message after he was reportedly moved to Cambridgeshire prison
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Laura Gallacher has shared a message from her husband Russell Brand, who has served the first week of his 10-and-a-half-year prison sentence for rape and sexual assault. The disgraced comedian was jailed this week after being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during his career. He was reportedly moved from HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey, near Huntingdon, last week, according to The Sun on Sunday. The prison offers a large variety of extra-curricular activities for its inmates, including yoga, choir and indoor bowls. Earlier this year Brand and Gallacher began releasing a weekly YouTube podcast called Sunday Service, which they carried on recording throughout his trial. On Sunday, Gallacher released another episode which began with her reading a passage from Brand’s bible. The 39-year-old, who is the daughter of Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher, said during the episode: “Russell has asked me to read something to you.” Reading the message from a notebook, she went on: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. “As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening. “The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. “I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. “The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. “And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone. “I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.” Gallacher choked up as she said: “Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell.” She began the episode by saying she is here to “continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday service community, something very, very close to mine and Russell’s heart”. “It may look different, but the ambitions are very much the same, and we trust God, and we trust his plan, and we trust everything he’s doing right now,” she added. “Even though it’s painful, and obviously, will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me, but I want to continue, and I’m grateful for the support.” Gallacher said she is speaking to her husband, adding: “He’s okay, and he’s praying.” Brand was sentenced to a 10-and-a-half-year prison term on Monday afternoon. He is expected to serve two-thirds of his prison sentence before being released on licence. He will be on the sex offenders’ register for life.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ready Steady Roll: award-winning café offers screen-free fun from £2
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Kath Sansom recently visited Ready Steady Roll, which has two sites - one near Kimbolton, and another in Peterborough - here's what she thought In an age when so much socialising revolves around screens, there's something really refreshing about gathering around a table, picking up some board games and spending a few hours laughing with friends. Ready Steady Roll is the sort of place you could easily drive past without ever knowing it exists. Yet this award-winning board game café was exactly what we were looking for when we stumbled on it during a Google search while looking for a halfway meeting place that offered more than the usual coffee shop or pub catch-up. As life gets busier, maintaining friendships when living in different towns many miles apart can become surprisingly difficult – so finding somewhere worth travelling to is a challenge. Thankfully, Ready Steady Roll offered the perfect solution, with an afternoon packed with laughter, nostalgia and friendly competition. The venue boasts an extensive games library with options ranging from light-hearted family favourites to deeper strategy games. Our afternoon began in unfamiliar territory with Shoot for the Stars, a “general knowledge” game with questions like how many beans in a can of Heinz. We then opted for a healthy dose of nostalgia, transporting back to childhood with the classics Frustration and Operation, before picking up Doodle Rush, a quick-fire drawing game. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or someone whose experience begins and ends with Ludo and Monopoly, there's something to tempt everyone of all ages with every genre imaginable neatly packed on well organised shelves – most of which we'd never heard of before. Board games are only half the story. The café serves a great selection of food and drinks, and we happily worked our way through impressive coffee, chips, sausage rolls and cakes during our four-hour visit. The table service meant we could stay immersed in the games while the food and drinks arrived at our table, helping create an unhurried atmosphere. Perhaps what stood out most was the welcome. The venue feels warm, cosy and genuinely inviting, somewhere that encourages you to settle in and stay awhile. It was a joy to escape to. There is also a strong community feel. Alongside regular daytime gaming, the venue hosts board-game evenings where people can come along, meet fellow enthusiasts and join games with others. For anyone looking to expand their social circle or simply find opponents for a favourite game, it's a lovely idea. What makes Ready Steady Roll special is that it offers something increasingly rare: a chance to slow down. No notifications, no scrolling, no rush. Just good company, good food, plenty of laughter and hundreds of games waiting to be explored. For three friends from across the region, Ready Steady Roll turned an ordinary catch-up into a memorable day out, leaving us already planning our next visit. Need to Know Where: Studio 5, Ivy Lodge, Rushden Road, Sharnbrook, MK44 1ND. Cost: £4 for adults and £3 for children for a two-hour session. Weekday term-time sessions are £2. Opening times: check the Ready Steady Roll website and social media channels for current opening hours.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Microsoft issues important update for all users following global outage
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Microsoft has fully restored services following a major global IT outage. The disruption affected police forces, the NHS, businesses, courts, and schools. The US-based company confirmed this morning (November 14) that services were fully restored for all remaining affected customers. In a statement on its Microsoft 365 status page, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions. Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration. We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete. — Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026 "Further updates can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center." The outage, which began around 6pm GMT on Thursday, November 12, disrupted email, messaging, and other Microsoft 365 services. The UK Government and others worldwide were forced to activate contingency plans. Microsoft said on Friday the disruption was due to a "technical issue not related to cyber or AI agents." Baroness Lloyd of Effra, the UK Government’s cyber minister, said the problem mainly affected back-office functions. Baroness Lloyd said there had been "limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery" and the incident had been "inconvenient and disruptive". She confirmed she had spoken with Microsoft UK chief executive Darren Hardman about the outage. Monitoring website Downdetector first showed a spike in users reporting problems with Microsoft Teams in the UK at about 6.15pm on Thursday. It recorded a surge in complaints, with more than 130,000 users in the US reporting problems with Outlook at its peak on Thursday evening. Millions of its customers were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook, while Microsoft’s Copilot AI assistant, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were also affected for many. Other AI chat platforms, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, were disrupted. Police forces in England and Wales said on Friday that they could not receive crime reports online. NHS England said staff had switched to "long-standing measures" to manage the outage, including the use of paper records. Rail passengers were unable to access e-tickets for their journeys as they couldn't open the emails in their Outlook inboxes. National Rail warned travellers to use alternative methods to access their tickets. A spokesman said: "We’re aware of the ongoing Microsoft global outage, which may be affecting customers’ ability to access their train tickets via their email inbox. "If you’re unable to locate or access your tickets through your email due to this issue, you may still be able to access your tickets by visiting the website or app where you purchased your tickets from and logging into your account. ‼️We’re aware of the ongoing Microsoft global outage, which may be affecting customers’ ability to access their train tickets via their email inbox. 🔗Latest Information and advice can be found here: https://t.co/pYa714hR8k — National Rail (@nationalrailenq) November 13, 2026 "We recommend doing this before you travel to ensure you have your tickets readily available for your journey. "This may not be possible if you checked out as a guest – please contact your ticket retailer directly if you are unable to access your tickets. "If you are still unable to access your ticket, please contact a member of onboard staff or station staff for advice." Other rail operators, including Southeastern, Chiltern Railways and London North Eastern Railway (LNER), reported similar problems with emailed tickets. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Airline used by Jet2 and TUI ceases operations after 16 years in sudden closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A European airline that operated flights for UK carriers, including Jet2 and TUI, has ceased operations after 16 years. AirExplore, based in Slovakia, was founded in 2008 and began ACMI (wet leasing) operations in 2010. It provided aircraft and crew to UK carriers, including Jet2 and TUI, through ACMI  arrangements, helping support services across the UK and Europe. AirExplore aircraft have been seen at major UK airports, including Manchester, Bristol, Newcastle International, and London Stansted. The airline was acquired by Avia Solutions Group in June 2023. AirExplore officially ceased operations on Tuesday (November 10) and submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC). In a statement posted on its website, the airline said: "The Slovakian ACMI and charter airline AirExplore has ceased operations on 10 November 2026 and has submitted a request to surrender its Air Operator Certificate (AOC). "We thank all our employees, customers, partners, and team for their support over the years." No reason has been given for the closure. Meanwhile, UK-based Global Airlines has been ordered into compulsory liquidation. The UK startup, which planned to use a fleet of Airbus A380 planes, was formally ordered to wind up by the Insolvency and Companies Court on Wednesday (November 4), according to The Gazette. The winding-up petition was originally filed in May, with several hearings taking place in the following months, including the most recent in October. With the order now in place, an officer of the court, known as the official receiver, has taken control of winding up the company. A post shared by Global Airlines ® (@globalairlines) Government guidelines state that once a winding-up order is issued, the company’s bank accounts are typically frozen and its assets sold off to repay creditors. Companies have the right to apply for cancellation of a winding-up order within five working days if they believe the action is unwarranted. Global Airlines is still listed as "active" on Companies House, though its most recent accounts are overdue. Global Airlines has been contacted for comment. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £200,000 funding secures Trusted Adult Scheme for young people until 2028
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A youth scheme is helping young people in Cambridge and Peterborough find their path and reach their potential. The Trusted Adult Scheme (TAS), funded by Police and Crime Commissioner, Darryl Preston, with support from Anglia Ruskin University (ARU), offers a safe space for 13 to 18-year-olds to explore new opportunities, build confidence, and develop life skills through weekly sessions. Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner, said: "Funding projects like the Trusted Adult Scheme (TAS) delivers on many levels offering the group new and different experiences in supported environments. Young people can access mentoring, activities and safe spaces through the scheme. (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) "Often young people need someone to talk to, to confide in and this trust is something which only grows when they feel safe, seen and heard within an inclusive environment." The programme, led by criminology lecturer Dr Paul Nelson, includes young people who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), who may be exhibiting risky behaviours. Since its inception, the commissioner has committed more than £200,000 of Home Office grant funding to the scheme, securing its future until March 2028. Dr Nelson said: "By receiving further funding for two years we can provide art sessions, music studios to record in, gaming and street art sessions alongside outdoor activities like laser tag. The Trusted Adult Scheme supports young people across Cambridge and Peterborough (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) "The 13 to 18-year-olds come to us needing support, guidance and encouragement – seeing them leave as matured individuals just can't be measured." Each week, the scheme offers activities such as street art, sports, gaming, creative arts and crafts, and one-to-one mentoring. Young people have shared positive feedback about their experiences. New funding will help the youth programme continue until 2028 (Image: Trusted Adult Scheme) One participant said: "TAS is the first place I’ve felt listened to. "It’s helped me stay out of trouble and focus on what I want to do next." Referrals to the scheme are made by partners in Education and Targeted Support at Cambridgeshire County Council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Mayor tours innovative AMFRESH and Encocam businesses in Alconbury Weald
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two businesses making waves in manufacturing and fresh produce recently welcomed a visit from the mayor. Paul Bristow, mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, toured AMFRESH and Encocam at Alconbury Weald in Huntingdonshire to see first-hand how these companies are contributing to the region’s economy through innovation and industry partnerships. AMFRESH, a family-owned Spanish company with a presence in Peterborough, operates a packhouse and laboratory focused on citrus fruits, grapes, juices and other fresh produce. Matvii Smirnov, innovation director at AMFRESH, said: "We were delighted to welcome Paul Bristow and his team to our OMEGA Innovation Centre and to see the strong interest from the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority in our efforts to deliver the highest quality and nutritional value to consumers." The company recently opened its OMEGA centre, which is dedicated to advancing fruit biochemistry and packing technology. Mr Bristow praised the company’s approach. He said: "It's great to see such innovation happening in our agri-tech sector. "AMFRESH is working with local schools, training skilled young people and contributing towards our regional economy." Encocam, a globally recognised advanced manufacturing business, focusing on automotive safety technologies and advanced engineering, was the mayor’s second stop. During his visit, Mr Bristow toured Encocam’s crash test dummy facility and discussed opportunities and challenges facing the automotive sector. Mayor Paul Bristow with James French at Encocam (Image: Combined Authority) Chris Hartley, HR manager at Encocam and a former apprentice, highlighted the company’s commitment to skills development. He said: "I continued my development with the support of some amazing workplace mentors and module tutors at Cambridge Regional College. "We see great potential in all our young people and recognise their importance to the future of our business. "That’s why we strive to give them the best support and training opportunities." Encocam has delivered more than 20 apprenticeship schemes over the past decade.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs libraries not removing David Walliams books, council confirms
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire libraries will not be actively removing David Walliams’ books from their shelves, the council has confirmed. Cambridgeshire County Council said its libraries will not be taking action to withdraw the author’s titles after an ITV News and The Guardian investigation saw him accused of sexual misconduct this week. Mr Walliams, 55, known for titles such as The Boy in the Dress and Gangsta Granny, wrote more than 40 books, which generated a revenue of £100 million by 2019. He has been accused of inappropriate sexual behaviour with girls allegedly as young as 15. He has also been accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Mr Walliams has denied all allegations of misconduct. Cambridgeshire County Council confirmed that Cambridgeshire Libraries "will not be actively removing" his books. A council spokesperson said: “Cambridgeshire Libraries is part of Libraries Connected, the body which represents all Public Library Services in England. "Libraries Connected has issued the below statement, which is consistent with our own Stock Policy, and specifically addresses the writings of David Walliams." Libraries Connected, which represents public library services across England, said that while all books should be available unless illegal, stock is routinely refreshed based on demand. Libraries Connected said: "In this case, we understand that demand for Walliams’s books has fallen significantly in recent years. "We would therefore expect the number of copies in circulation to decline naturally as they are replaced by newer and more popular titles, particularly as he is now without a publisher." Decisions about whether to keep Mr Walliams' books in Cambridgeshire schools will be made by governing bodies or trustee boards, the council confirmed. The council added that should the Department for Education issue any guidance, this would be shared with schools.

Residents fear an historic market town is “losing its heart” as updated plans to revitalise the area are being discussed. The St Ives Town Team published an updated document suggesting new riverside moorings, pedestrianised streets and an enhanced market area to boost business in the town. A meeting will be held with businesses, organisations and other interested parties next month to share their views. Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, posted to Facebook that he had met with the St Ives Town Team to discuss how best to “regenerate the heart” of the town. The Conservative MP said pedestrianising Market Hill and Bridge Street could give an “opportunity for businesses to thrive in St Ives”. He said this could create a “community space that would encourage more cafes and restaurants, a bigger market, the filling of empty shop units and making the town centre a destination”. Mr Obese-Jecty said: “Speaking with the Town Team this matches their vision for the town and they were even able to show me existing plans for pedestrianising the centre from some 25 years ago. “The plans look contemporary enough to still work today without really being changed. “I think St Ives has a huge amount of potential, as demonstrated by the recent additions of businesses from Cambridge.” Robert Stevens, who has lived in St Ives for nearly 30 years, said he feels the town needs “more businesses” as he spoke in front of the Townrow department store, advertising a closing down sale. The 70-year-old said: “It’s a shame – I remember 20 years ago when it was still Eaden Lilley. Apart from the loss of shops, it was starting to look a lot better with a lot more eateries and restaurants around. Making it a bit of a foodie place would be a good idea.” Richard Ibbott, area manager for West End DIY, said he had written to Mr Obese-Jecty to object to the pedestrianisation of Bridge Street. The 59-year-old said: “How am I supposed to get deliveries in? They said use your back door – but I don’t have a back door. “They need to improve the town centre, but not by stopping people from getting into the town. Townrow is gone – Poundland is up the creek – even the hairdressers are going.” A 67-year-old man, who did not want to be named, said reading about the controversial plans proposed by Capital and Centric to build homes on car parks, while free car parking was promoted by the combined authority makes you think “you were in an asylum”. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Royal Mint Beatrix Potter 50p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Royal Mint Peter Rabbit 50p coin has sold on eBay for more than £200. The Royal Mint's Beatrix Potter collection began in 2016, marking 150 years since the author's birth. The first Peter Rabbit design showed a close-up of the character facing forward, complete with whiskers. Other 2016 designs featured Squirrel Nutkin, Mrs Tiggy-Winkle and Jemima Puddle-Duck. Four more designs arrived in 2017, featuring Tom Kitten, Benjamin Bunny, Jeremy Fisher and another Peter Rabbit. The 2018 Peter Rabbit and Flopsy Bunny designs each had a circulating mintage of 1.4 million. The Peter Rabbit editions from 2019 and 2020 were not put into general circulation. The seller described the coin as a 2016 Royal Mint Peter Rabbit 50p in silver proof, with a fineness of 0.925. The listing eventually sold for a total of £219.20, including a £9.03 buyer-protection fee. The Royal Mint lists the 2023 Atlantic Salmon 50p as the rarest circulating 50p, with a mintage of 200,000. Next on its list is the 2009 Kew Gardens 50p, with 210,000, followed by the 2011 Olympic football design, with 1,125,500. The date matters: the Royal Mint's table also records two million Atlantic Salmon 50p coins dated 2025. Other low-mintage circulating designs include the 2011 Olympic wrestling, judo and triathlon coins, alongside the 2018 Peter Rabbit and Flopsy Bunny 50ps. Mintage is the number of coins made, and a lower figure can make a design harder for collectors to find. A coin's condition, design, material and demand from collectors can also affect what someone is willing to pay. A genuine error can be of interest to collectors, but a seller's description alone is not independent verification. The Royal Mint advises buyers of second-hand coins to check for original packaging and, for proof editions, a certificate of authenticity. A specialist valuation can help an owner establish a coin's history and likely value.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: PM gives flat owners new powers to challenge 'unfair' service charges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of leaseholders are set to gain new powers to challenge unfair service charges. The government says more than three million leaseholders in England will benefit from the reforms, with the first changes planned for April 1, 2027. The measures are due to be introduced in stages through to November 2028, subject to parliamentary approval. From April 2027, leaseholders will be able to request information about their service charges, including details from previous years. Landlords will need a good reason to refuse to provide the information, according to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Service charges are fees paid by leaseholders or tenants to cover the maintenance, repair and management of shared areas of a building. The ministry says the changes will give leaseholders a clearer picture of how their building is managed, maintained, repaired and insured. The first stage also includes stronger protection against having to pay a landlord's legal costs when challenging a charge. Landlords will need court or tribunal approval to pass on legal costs, while leaseholders will gain a right to recover their own legal expenses, the government says. Further measures are planned for November 1, 2027, when leaseholders will receive clearer information about charges, including details of building insurance and administration fees. There will also be stronger protections against excessive or unreasonable fees for arranging and managing insurance. Private landlords will have to use standardised service charge demand forms and provide financial accounts and annual reports from November 2027. Councils and housing associations will have until November 1, 2028 to introduce those forms, accounts and reports for their leaseholders. Kion Ahadi, chief executive of the Leasehold Advisory Service, said: "Service charges are the most common issue leaseholders contact us about. "We welcome these changes as an important step forward in helping people understand what they are paying for and challenge costs they believe are unfair. "Leaseholders need clear information about how their money is being spent and a fair opportunity to raise concerns. "Better access to that information and stronger protection from landlords’ legal bills will give them more confidence to hold their landlord to account."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP Universal Credit claimants face new payment rates - check what you could get
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of people claiming Universal Credit are set to receive a higher monthly payment next year, after the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) confirmed the new benefit rates. The Government has published its annual review of benefit payments, setting out how much claimants will receive from April 2027. Working-age and disability benefits will rise by 3.5%, with the new rates mainly coming into effect from April 12, 2027. Inflation-linked benefits and tax credits will rise by 3.5% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rate of inflation for September 2026. Universal Credit standard allowances will receive an additional uplift as specified in the Universal Credit Act 2025. The basic and new State Pensions will be uprated by 3.9% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in the Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) index for May–July 2026. Universal Credit is currently paid to more than 8.4 million people across the UK. Due to the increase in line with CPI, and the additional uprating factor, in 2027/28 Universal Credit standard allowances will increase: Universal Credit is a means-tested benefit designed to help with living costs for people on a low income, out of work or unable to work. The number of people claiming it has increased as the DWP continues its managed migration programme, which is moving people from older benefits onto the newer system. Around 2.2 million Universal Credit claimants are in employment, while a significant number of others are not expected to work because of health conditions or caring responsibilities. Recommended reading: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden confirmed the increases in a statement to Parliament following the Budget. He said: “The new rates will apply in the tax year 2027-28 and will mainly come into effect from April 12 2027. “The other state pension and benefit rates covered by my statutory review will be increased by 3.5%, in line with the increase in the consumer prices index in the year to September 2026. “This includes most working-age benefits and other benefits for people below state pension age; benefits to help with additional needs arising from disability; statutory payments including statutory sick pay and statutory maternity pay; and additional state pension. The pension credit savings credit maximum amount will also increase by 3.5%.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A prolific thief who targeted cash machines across England and Wales, including Cambridgeshire, has been jailed. Bogdan Gasparov, 40, used cash-trapping devices to steal more than £16,000 from at least 180 ATMs between May and October 2026. Police found him hiding in a loft crawl space during a raid on his Hardie Road home in Dagenham. Detective Sergeant Mike Simpson from ERSOU's Proactive Economic Crime Team (PECT) said: "This was not opportunistic offending. "Gasparov carried out a calculated campaign of theft, targeting cash machines across the country and repeatedly returning to steal money that belonged to unsuspecting customers. "What makes this case even more brazen is that Gasparov had previously been convicted for similar offences and deported from the UK, only to return illegally and resume the same criminal behaviour. "He clearly believed he could stay one step ahead of investigators. He couldn't. "Thanks to the determination of our officers and the strength of the evidence gathered, he has now been brought to justice once again." Read more Sawtry school celebrates double award success for careers and outdoor learning Hinchingbrooke Hospital plans revised as fresh environmental assessment begins Huntingdonshire council seeks consent to fly three flags at Pathfinder House 'Attempted rape' arrest after woman sexually assaulted in Hunts village Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure Gasparov targeted ATMs in Bury St Edmunds, Lowestoft and Sudbury in Suffolk, Great Yarmouth in Norfolk, Huntingdon and Peterborough in Cambridgeshire, and Harlow in Essex. He also struck near Nottingham, Oxford, Somerset, Bristol, Derby, Gloucester, Lincoln and the West Midlands, as well as in parts of Scotland and Wales. The scheme involved Gasparov posing as a legitimate customer, fitting homemade cash-trapping devices to ATMs, and leaving the area. When genuine customers attempted to withdraw money, the cash would become trapped in the device. Gasparov would then return later to retrieve the device and the stolen funds. CCTV from several locations repeatedly placed Gasparov at the scenes. A search of his vehicle uncovered clothing worn during the offences, homemade cash-trapping devices and tools to make them. Moldovan national Gasparov used several aliases and had previous convictions for similar crimes. He had re-entered the UK illegally after being deported. Within 24 hours of his arrest, he pleaded guilty at Chelmsford Magistrates’ Court to two counts of theft from an ATM, covering all the offences. He also admitted entering the UK in breach of a deportation order and possessing items for use in fraud. On November 9, Gasparov was jailed for three years and six months at Chelmsford Crown Court. He is expected to face another deportation hearing after his release.

The support is in response to concerns arising from the Early Release Scheme, which is seeing some offenders released from prison before their full sentence is served. Police and Crime Commissioner Darryl Preston has increased the capacity of the Victim and Witness Hub to ensure timely and comprehensive support for those affected. Darryl said: "I understand the anxiety such news could cause especially for victims of domestic violence. "That's why I am keen to raise awareness of the local offer of support available here in our county to ensure victims feel safe, informed and supported." The Victim and Witness Hub offers emotional and practical support, including referrals to home security services and enhanced emotional support programmes. Victim and Witness Care Co-ordinators can also reconnect individuals with specialist services they have previously used. Victims whose offenders are being released early will be notified and directed to support services in their area. For those worried about personal safety, the Bobby Scheme is available to provide home security assessments and install devices such as locks and video doorbells. Additional funding of £195,000 over two years has been allocated to increase support services. A national Offender Release Helpline, set up by Victim Support, is also available on 0808 168 9280. The helpline operates Monday to Friday from 9am to 5pm, excluding bank holidays. The Early Release Scheme, known as the Progression Model, applies to offenders with fixed-term sentences. It allows part of the sentence to be served in the community under supervision. All individuals released under the scheme are subject to licence conditions and a period of intensive supervision. Victims in Cambridgeshire seeking support can contact the Victim and Witness Hub on 0800 781 6818 or by emailing victimandwitnesshub@cambs.police.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners are set to receive a higher weekly State Pension from April 2027 after the Government announced the new payment rates for the next financial year. The full new State Pension will increase to £250.70 a week, up from £241.30, while the full basic State Pension will rise to £192.10 a week from £184.90. The increases amount to an extra £9.40 and £7.20 a week respectively, giving eligible pensioners hundreds of pounds more over the course of a year. The new figures have been set out in a House of Commons Library briefing published on Wednesday, November 11, covering the benefit and pension rates announced for the 2027/28 financial year. Both the basic and new State Pension will rise by 3.9% from April 2027, in line with the annual increase in average weekly earnings between May and July 2026. The increase is part of the Government's commitment to the State Pension triple lock, which means payments rise each year by the highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The full weekly rates will be: Over a full year, the increase works out at around £488.80 for someone receiving the full new State Pension and £374.40 for someone receiving the full basic State Pension. The new State Pension applies to people who reached State Pension age on or after April 6, 2016. The basic State Pension is the core payment under the old State Pension system, for people who reached State Pension age before that date. The figures are the full weekly rates. The amount an individual receives will depend on their National Insurance record and whether they qualify for the full entitlement. The Department for Work and Pensions updated their website on Wednesday, November 11, to outline proposed benefits rates for the 2027-28 tax year. Benefits caps are used by the government to limit the total amount of money claimants can receive and it applies to most people over 16 and below State Pensions age. -Widowed Parent’s Allowance (or Widowed Mother’s Allowance or Widow’s Pension if you started getting it before 9 April 2001) The current annual maximum for couples (with or without children) or single claimants with a child of qualifying age is £22,020 or £25,323 for those in Greater London. The annual maximum for single adults households this tax year, which ends in April, is £14,753 or £16,967 in Greater London. This is proposed to be frozen for the 2027-28 tax year, meaning Brits won't be able to claim more than this amount between April 2027 and 2028. The monthly equivalent is also planned to be frozen at £1,835 and £2,110.25 (Greater London) for couples, with or without children, or single claimants with a child of qualifying age. Single households without children face the same freeze, with the maximum remaining at £1,229.42 and £1,413.92 in Greater London. Weekly equivalents are planned to remain at £423.46 and £486.98 (Greater London) for couples, with or without children, or single claimants with a qualifying-age. The weekly maximum for single households is planned to remain at £283.71 or £326.29 (Greater London). This is despite the Office for National Statistics' most recent inflation rate being recorded at 3.6% in September and many economists forecasting that this is expected to rise next year. The government explains that the cap may not start for nine months if someone is claiming Universal Credit but this depends on their earnings. Recommended reading: Brits are not affected by the benefits cap if they or their partner get Universal Credit because of a disability that 'stops them from working' or get it because they care for someone with a disability. The UK startup, which planned to use a fleet of Airbus A380 planes, was formally ordered to wind up by the Insolvency and Companies Court on Wednesday, November 4. The winding-up petition was originally filed in May, with several hearings held in the following months, including the most recent in October. The Gazette published the notice on Thursday, November 12, confirming the order. A post shared by Global Airlines ® (@globalairlines) Former company directors Tom Stokely and Prashant Uttamchandani joined the case as supporting creditors and were represented by the law firm Katten Muchin Rosenman. With the order now in place, an officer of the court—known as the official receiver—has taken control of winding up the company. Government guidelines state that once a winding-up order is issued, the company’s bank accounts are typically frozen and its assets sold off to repay creditors. Companies have the right to apply for cancellation of a winding-up order within five working days if they believe the action is unwarranted. A post shared by Global Airlines ® (@globalairlines) As of the latest update, Global Airlines is still listed as active on Companies House, though its most recent accounts are overdue. Global Airlines has been contacted by Newsquest for comment. Global Airlines Limited operated as a virtual airline with ambitions to operate a fleet of four Airbus A380 aircraft. The company, which was founded in 2019, acquired its only aircraft in May 2023, and claimed to be the first new A380 owner in eight years. Its maiden flight, operated under a damp lease from Hi Fly Malta, flew from Glasgow to New York-JFK on May 15, 2025. After completing just four transatlantic flights, the aircraft was placed into long-term storage in Tarbes, France, on July 16, 2025, with no known return-to-service date. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Support for pubs only ‘lip service’ after budget says landlady
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridge pub landlady has accused the government of only paying “lip service” to supporting hospitality following the latest budget. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey delivered the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government last month, with a number of changes for pubs. This includes raising the threshold for Small Business Rates Relief in England from £12k to £18k – meaning businesses with a rateable value below this will pay no business rates. But pub operators will also face higher wage bills with the national living wage for workers aged 21 and over increasing from £12.71 an hour to £13.21. Both changes will come into effect from April 2027 and alcohol duty will also increase in line with inflation from February 1. Hayley Pellegrini, who runs five pubs in the city with her husband Steve including The Portland Arms and The Alex, said she does not feel small businesses are getting the support they need. The 56-year-old said: “We work ridiculous hours and what we pay ourselves we worked out is probably below minimum wage. “But it’s a case of we just have to suck it up and get on with it. “I don’t feel like we are getting the support we need – they aren’t doing anything, they want to be seen as being pub goers and that but they aren’t doing anything. “It’s not just pubs, it’s small businesses in general – we have friends who have small businesses and they are struggling as well.” She said small businesses are discouraged from expanding as they will lose relief and face higher wage bills from increased national insurance contributions and the rise in wages. Ms Pellegrini said it was harder for them as a living-wage employer, but that they’re “fortunate” to be based in Cambridge with a steady stream of business from students and tourists. She said: “Why am I going to employ someone with no experience, when I could be paying someone with ten years of experience the same? I think we are losing the next generation of hospitality managers, in 10 or 15 years we might find we haven’t brought up the next generation of managers.” She said the government was being “narrowminded” by not considering a reduction in VAT – with more than 400,000 signing the VAT’s the Problem petition to cut it from 20 per cent to 10 per cent, in line with other countries in Europe like France, Spain and Italy. Ms Pellegrini said: “We were hoping that Andy Burnham was actually going to be the one who will do something, but now we think – ‘ah, here we go again’. “What worries me is our retirement – we’re so busy trying to keep the business afloat we aren’t actually able to put anything away for our retirement and we’re going to be a burden on the government. “I work long, unsociable, hours often seven days a week to keep this industry going – who am I doing this for? “The slice of the pie being taken off us is just getting bigger and bigger and bigger. “It seems to be targeted at small businesses while companies like Amazon pay a tiny proportion of tax. “Something needs to be redistributed – the rich are getting richer and the rest of us are working our butts off to try and make a living.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare fish 'considered locally extinct' found in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare fish thought to be extinct locally has been discovered in Cambridgeshire. The sturgeon, weighing 15lb, was found on the banks of the Twenty Foot Drain last week, the Environment Agency said. According to the Zoological Society of London, the UK is home to two native species of the fish. The Atlantic and European sturgeon can both reach up to five metres long and can live for more than 60 years. They are among the most critically endangered group of animals on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List. The Environment Agency said it hadn't been made aware of any catch reports in the drains or surrounding rivers. "We have absolutely no idea what the story with this one is," a spokesperson said. They added: "Native sturgeon are considered locally extinct in our patch, although historically there have been reports from the River Great Ouse. "Reports exist of a 130lb sturgeon being caught in Huntingdon way back in 1754. "There have been introductions of the species in France in recent years with some of these fish migrating across the channel and being caught in UK waters." It is illegal to keep sturgeon in fisheries in England due to the risk of hybridisation with the few remaining native European sturgeon in the UK's waterways. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families of adults with learning disabilities have raised concerns over plans to move a Huntingdonshire day service from St Ives to Huntingdon with just five weeks' notice. Cambridgeshire County Council has told users of the CATS centre in Bull Lane, St Ives, their families, carers and advocates that the service is due to move to Huntingdon Community Centre on December 7. In a November 2 letter, Cambridgeshire head of provider services Mandy Langley told the Singh family that activities and support would move to the Huntingdon centre, around six miles away. The family says the letter was the first it knew about the plans and questions why relatives were not consulted before the announcement. Surj Singh said his brother has Down syndrome, is non-verbal and relies heavily on familiar people and surroundings. He said the family feared moving the service could seriously affect his brother and others who rely on familiar routines. The family has questioned whether the new centre is suitable, citing noise, summer heat, staffing, supervision, privacy, facilities and personal care. The Singh family complained to the council on November 5 and asked it to pause the move until families had been consulted and individual needs and transition plans addressed. The family wants to know when the decision was made, what assessment and consultation took place, and how staffing, personal care and individual suitability will be assured. Mr Singh said his brother had been away from the service because of ill health, and the family had spent weeks planning his return with social services and the provider without hearing about the move. The family has also questioned the move’s timing, just weeks before Christmas. The council said the move was planned because fewer people were using CATS St Ives. It said Huntingdon Community Centre already provides day services and has room for St Ives users, allowing it to "make better use of our buildings and resources". The council said familiar staff would continue supporting users and similar activities would be available in Huntingdon. But Mr Singh said the family feared the Huntingdon centre was much larger and noisier than the St Ives site. The council said users would still have access to the St Ives community while being offered opportunities in Huntingdon. The council said users would be offered extra visits to the Huntingdon centre in November to prepare for the move. It said there would be no break in service and that the St Ives centre would operate until the move. The council said it would discuss any changes to care arrangements or transport with those affected. The letter said: "We are committed to supporting everyone through this change and making it as smooth as possible." The family says the council has acknowledged its complaint but has yet to answer its concerns. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: "From Monday, December 7, the council will be bringing together the CATS day service in St Ives with services provided at Huntingdon Community Centre for adults with learning disabilities. "Huntingdon Community Centre already provides a wide range of activities and opportunities, including the Blossom and Bloom Café and TAG Bikes. "Bringing the services together will give people attending CATS access to a broader choice of activities, opportunities to build confidence and independence, and the chance to meet and develop relationships with new people. "Our priority is to ensure a smooth transition for everyone affected, and we will continue to work with individuals and their families throughout the process, including reviewing any transport arrangements required. "The move will also bring services together on one site, providing greater operational resilience and making the best use of council resources. “We can confirm this complaint is being investigated and we have contacted the family to explain the complaints process."
