summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Face of controlling partner who strangled victim amid decade of abuse
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A controlling partner who subjected his victim to a decade of abuse and even strangled her has been jailed for more than two years. Anthony Bernard, 49, of Croyland Road, Walton, Peterborough, pleaded guilty to engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship and intentional strangulation. His abuse came to light after an incident on August 11, when he emptied his partner’s wardrobe, took her belongings, and threatened to burn them in a car. Police uncovered more than a decade of coercive and controlling behaviour during their investigation. Bernard had installed cameras around the home to monitor the victim, restricted her contact with friends, and tried to prevent her from having hobbies. He regularly questioned her about her whereabouts, went through her phone while she slept, and checked her smartwatch to track how far she had travelled. If she was out longer than expected, he would accuse her of cheating. When the victim challenged his behaviour, Bernard became aggressive and verbally abusive, often punching walls in anger, leaving her frightened. In June last year, he pinned the victim against a wall and strangled her during an argument. Anthony Bernard admitted engaging in controlling or coercive behaviour (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Bernard was jailed for two years and three months and given a restraining order at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, November 4. Detective Constable Isabelle Wilding said: "Bernard subjected his victim to years of controlling behaviour, monitoring her movements, restricting her contact with friends and invading her privacy. "His behaviour left her frightened and was designed to strip away her independence and control different aspects of her life. "I hope this sentence gives her some reassurance and sends a clear message that coercive and controlling behaviour is domestic abuse and we will take reports seriously." To report concerns or for more advice and support on domestic abuse, including coercive control, visit Cambridgeshire Police's dedicated web pages.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Reform councillor complains to Parliament over MP’s response to 199-home plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A Reform UK councillor has complained to Parliament about MP Sam Carling over a 199-home development between Ramsey and Bury. Cllr Karan Maheshwari, who represents Ramsey on Huntingdonshire District Council, has submitted a complaint to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. It concerns North West Cambridgeshire MP Mr Carling’s response to Cllr Maheshwari’s request for him to intervene in planning application 25/01382/OUT, for 199 homes between Ramsey and Bury. A copy seen by this publication is dated November 2 and marked “DRAFT – NOT SUBMITTED”, but Cllr Maheshwari later confirmed he submitted it on November 3 and received confirmation on November 4. The dispute began after Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee said it was minded to reject the scheme. Cllr Maheshwari says he asked Mr Carling to urge the Secretary of State not to “call in” the application. A planning application being called in means the Government takes responsibility for deciding it instead of leaving the final decision with the local authority. Mr Carling replied in social media posts included with the complaint: “Karan, this is misinformation. MPs have no power over planning.” Mr Carling also said intervention with the Secretary of State could trigger a judicial review and give the council another route to overturn its refusal. Cllr Maheshwari disputes the suggestion that his request amounted to misinformation. He argues that, although an MP cannot decide a planning application, an MP can make representations about a planning case. The row continued the next day when Cllr Maheshwari posted a further criticism of Mr Carling and urged him to stand up for residents. The councillor accepts in his complaint that the post contained “direct political criticism”, including a call for Mr Carling to stand down if he would not represent residents’ concerns. Mr Carling replied that there was “absolutely no need for full-on personal nastiness” and said voters wanted politicians to work together. He added: “I am not going to engage. Particularly when most of what you're doing is AI-generated anyway.” The AI reference forms another part of Cllr Maheshwari’s complaint. The Reform councillor argues that using AI to research or draft material should not by itself discredit someone’s arguments. He stresses that he is not accusing Mr Carling of unlawful discrimination and accepts that the comments do not prove a wider policy of refusing to engage with AI users. Instead, Cllr Maheshwari asks whether residents’ or elected representatives’ concerns could be dismissed because they used AI to prepare their arguments. The complaint asks the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to consider whether the exchanges breached Rule 11 of the House of Commons Code of Conduct. Rule 11 covers conduct serious enough to damage the reputation and integrity of the House of Commons or MPs generally. Cllr Maheshwari accepts that the rule sets a high bar and that an ordinary political disagreement would not normally be enough. The complaint acknowledges that the Commissioner may decide the matter is not serious enough to investigate. If that happens, Cllr Maheshwari has asked the Commissioner to consider whether the concerns should instead be raised with Mr Carling under a separate parliamentary procedure, without a formal investigation. He says the complaint is not intended to stop robust political debate or force Mr Carling to support a particular planning position. Instead, it asks for scrutiny of how elected representatives handle public concerns. The document includes screenshots of the exchanges and copies of Cllr Maheshwari’s posts as evidence. A Facebook post at the centre of the dispute has since been removed, but Cllr Maheshwari says he does not know who deleted it or why and makes no allegation about its removal. Mr Carling has been approached for comment. The application was submitted by David Wilson Homes South Midlands.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: David Walliams tried to block publication of sexual misconduct allegations
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: David Walliams has been named as the celebrity who tried to block publication of his identity amid allegations of “inappropriate sexual activities” with girls and young women. Multiple women have accused David Walliams of sexually inappropriate behaviour and grooming including when they were teenagers, according to an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Walliams denies all allegations against him. A joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian alleges Walliams preyed on teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. Multiple women accuse Walliams of “grooming” them as teenagers, while another described her alleged encounter with Walliams as “sexual assault”. Walliams is also accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Responding to the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams denied all allegations against him. He said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with... I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. “And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did... “I am not a sexual predator... I have not broken the law... I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Gavin Millar KC said that reporters from the media organisations had spoken to more than 100 people, including more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts as well as Walliams’ friends and colleagues. Walliams’ lawyers said that he had initially attempted suicide after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his reply to the allegations, because of “long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media”. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. Walliams’ book publisher HarperCollins dropped him in December 2025, after an investigation into allegations he had “harassed” young women, which Walliams strongly denied. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 film and television locations you can visit in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Famous film and TV locations are closer than you might think. Cambridgeshire has quietly become a star of the screen, with its historic streets, rural villages, and grand buildings providing the backdrop to some of cinema and television’s most memorable moments. From Netflix’s The Crown to ITV’s Grantchester, the county has featured in a growing list of productions, attracting fans keen to follow in their favourite characters’ footsteps. Here are some of Cambridgeshire’s best-known filming locations. Wansford Station and the Nene Valley Railway near Peterborough has been used for not one, but two James Bond films. (Image: Nene Valley Railway) Ely Cathedral is one of Cambridgeshire’s most spectacular filming locations. The cathedral stood in for Westminster Abbey in Netflix’s The Crown, including during wedding and coronation scenes. More recently, Bradley Cooper filmed one of Maestro’s most memorable scenes inside the cathedral. Cooper played legendary American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, and directed and co-wrote the film. For one of the film's major scenes, Cooper recreated Bernstein's celebrated 1973 performance of Gustav Mahler's Resurrection Symphony at Ely Cathedral. The sequence was filmed inside the cathedral with a live orchestra, choir and extras, and much of it unfolds in a single six-minute take. Visitors to Ely can walk through the cathedral used for one of the Oscar-nominated film’s major musical sequences. The Green Man n Grantchester is used by ITV for its detective drama Granchester starring Robson Green. (Image: Google Street View) Few places in Cambridgeshire are as closely linked to a television programme as Grantchester is to Grantchester. The picturesque village provides the setting for ITV’s detective drama of the same name, which uses several real locations. Fans can explore the village’s buildings and landscapes, which regularly appear on screen alongside Robson Green, Tessa Peake-Jones, Kacey Ainsworth and Al Weaver. One particularly recognisable location is the Church of St Andrew and St Mary, which has appeared in Grantchester as the village church and churchyard. Grantchester Meadows is another location visitors can enjoy for free. The meadows beside the River Cam feature in Grantchester and offer fans a taste of the countryside behind the programme. The meadows are also worth visiting in their own right, especially for fans who want to combine screen tourism with a riverside walk. Fans can stop for a drink at The Green Man pub, frequented by Geordie and his colleagues in the show. It lets visitors step inside a genuine screen location instead of viewing it from the road. Wisbech offers a very different look, with the Fenland town’s historic streets appearing in films and television productions. Peckover House in Wisbech has been used for films including Dean Spanley starring Peter O'Toole. (Image: Image: National Trust Images Jemma Finch) The town is known for its Georgian architecture, particularly North Brink, which overlooks the River Nene and has an impressive row of period properties. The National Trust’s Peckover House, a Georgian merchant’s home dating from 1722, also stands on North Brink. Productions filmed in Wisbech include the 1994 television adaptation of Martin Chuzzlewit, David Copperfield from 1999 to 2000 and the 2008 film Dean Spanley. The 2022 independent film Wild Bones was also filmed in Wisbech. Peter O’Toole filmed Dean Spanley in Wisbech in 2007 alongside Sam Neill, Bryan Brown and Jeremy Northam, with Peckover House and Wisbech Castle among the locations used. Visitors can explore much of the town’s Georgian heritage on foot, especially around North Brink, South Brink and the River Nene. James Bond fans have good reason to visit Peterborough: the area provided locations for two 007 films. The Nene Valley Railway featured in 1983’s Octopussy, starring Roger Moore as James Bond. Wansford Station became the fictional Karl Marx Stadt station, while filming also took place around Orton Mere and Ferry Meadows. The Bond franchise returned to Peterborough for 1995’s GoldenEye, Pierce Brosnan’s first 007 film. The Nene Valley Railway hosted action scenes involving the film’s imposing Russian armoured train. The former British Sugar factory at Woodston also featured in GoldenEye. Part of the site became a Russian rail depot, and Peterborough provided the backdrop for the tank chase’s finale. The former industrial site has been redeveloped, but the Nene Valley Railway remains open, so Bond fans can still visit a location featured in two 007 films. Just outside Cambridgeshire’s modern boundary, Burghley House is one of the wider region’s most impressive filming locations. Burghley House, just over the border near Stamford was used for the 2005 series of Pride and Prejudice among other films and TV series. (Image: Burghley House) Read more 5 Christmas markets and fairs to visit in Cambridgeshire this winter 'A sad loss': Hunts residents react to beloved department store closing 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support Tom Littler appointed to lead Arts Theatre Cambridge ahead of 90th anniversary Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax The Elizabethan mansion is best known for appearing as Rosings Park, Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s imposing home, in the 2005 adaptation of Pride & Prejudice. The house and grounds are open to visitors during the visitor season, giving film fans a chance to see the grand setting for themselves. From Bradley Cooper conducting inside Ely Cathedral to James Bond racing through Peterborough, Cambridgeshire has made a striking mark on the big and small screens. And with many of the locations open to the public, film and television fans do not have to settle for watching them from the sofa.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare Royal Mint 50p coin sells for more than 420 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 400 times its face value after an online auction. The 2009 Kew Gardens piece drew 19 bids on eBay on November 4. A winning bid of £221.36 landed the coin, with an extra £9.55 buyer protection fee included. Released by the Royal Mint in 2009, the Kew Gardens 50p had a circulating mintage of 210,000. It marks the 250th anniversary of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. Its reverse shows the Great Pagoda encircled by a climbing vine, while the obverse carries a portrait of Queen Elizabeth II. The Royal Mint ranks the 2009 Kew Gardens coin as the second-rarest 50p to enter circulation by mintage, behind the 2023 Atlantic Salmon. It says demand for the 50p denomination was low in 2009, accounting for the unusually small number struck that year. The 50p piece has a seven-sided shape and provides space for commemorative designs. The Kew Gardens 50p measures 27.30mm across. A coin's mintage, design and condition can all influence its value, according to the Royal Mint. An unusually low mintage may mean a coin sells for more than face value on the secondary market. Condition can also matter, with coins closer to mint condition potentially worth more. The Royal Mint advises collectors to research secondary-market listings and consult a coin expert if in doubt. The price paid for this graded Kew Gardens coin does not guarantee the same return for another example. Royal Mint figures list these 50p coins among the rarest to enter circulation, ranked by mintage: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin has the lowest mintage of any 50p issued for circulation, according to the Royal Mint. Collectors can check the Royal Mint's published mintage figures to find out how many examples of a circulating design were issued.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands of Vauxhall owners warned 'stop driving' over safety issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of Vauxhall drivers have been told to stop driving over an airbag safety risk. Stellantis UK, Vauxhall's parent company, issued the stop-drive instruction for certain vehicles fitted with Takata airbags, which were already part of a recall. Vauxhall says the airbag inflator can degrade over time in high heat and humidity and may explode with excessive force in a crash, causing serious injury or death. Law firm Bond Turner estimates the recall affects 320,000 vehicles and is investigating potential claims over motorists' losses. The firm's estimate is not a confirmed count of vehicles currently subject to the stop-drive instruction. Vauxhall says drivers who receive a stop-drive warning should stop using the vehicle as soon as it is safe to do so. Its recall page lists the following models under the stop-drive action: Astra Hatch (2005 to 2015), Astra Van (2006 to 2013), Astra Twin Top (2006 to 2015), Vectra (2005 to 2008) and Signum (2005 to 2008). Not every vehicle in those model ranges is necessarily affected, and owners should check their vehicle identification number (VIN) to see whether their car is included and what action is advised. Vauxhall says the only exception to the stop-drive instruction is a direct journey, without stops, to a pre-booked recall repair appointment, provided the vehicle can be driven there lawfully. Other models are subject to the recall but not the stop-drive instruction, and their owners should still take action as soon as possible. These are the Astra J and Astra GTC (2010 to 2018), Meriva B (2010 to 2017), Mokka and Mokka X (2013 to 2018), Cascada (2013 to 2018) and Zafira C (2012 to 2016). Drivers can use Vauxhall's vehicle recall checker to check their VIN and register for a free repair. The 17-character VIN can be found on a V5C registration certificate or in the vehicle. Owners who cannot register online can call Vauxhall's recall helpline on 0800 917 9285. Vauxhall says registered keepers of affected vehicles will be sent a letter and should make sure their contact details are up to date with the DVLA. Bond Turner is looking into whether motorists may be able to recover expenses linked to the recall, including alternative transport, replacement vehicle hire and loss of earnings. Malcolm Lewis, head of group litigation at Bond Turner, said: "For many people, their car is essential to everyday life, whether that is getting to work, taking children to school or fulfilling family and personal commitments." Mr Lewis said: "Our investigations will look at who may be legally responsible for the losses experienced by affected motorists, including the cost of alternative transport and replacement vehicle hire, loss of earnings and other associated expenses." Vauxhall says it has made mobility solutions available for customers affected by the stop-drive action and asks them to discuss any specific needs with their retailer when booking.

The savings announcement comes as figures from the Current Account Switch Service (Cass) reveal that 411,384 current account switches were completed between July and September 2026. September was the busiest month, with 152,299 switches completed. The latest figures take the total number of completed switches in 2026 to 1,019,912. Nationwide was among the biggest beneficiaries in the second quarter, recording a net gain of 23,636 customers switching to it. It was followed by Barclays, with a net gain of 21,169, NatWest with 20,287 and Monzo with 17,544. Do you understand ISAs? All in the new Martin Lewis podcast... https://t.co/O7b14FLwb2 https://t.co/RCrSyznDx9 And elsewhere... — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 5, 2026 Other providers saw more customers leave than join. Halifax recorded a net loss of 20,728 switches, while TSB lost 17,008 and Santander lost 14,124. The figures are based on information voluntarily provided by banks and building societies and cover switches made through Cass, rather than every account move. Fred Powell, head of current accounts at Nationwide, highlighted the society's “fairer share” payments to members, its promise to keep branches open until at least the start of 2030 and services including dementia clinics. Abigail Foster, a personal finance expert at Compare the Market, said: “With over one million switches completed so far in 2026, it’s encouraging to see so many people exploring their options. “With continued pressure on household budgets, ensuring that your money is working as hard as possible is essential. “Switching accounts could potentially provide better interest rates, lower fees, and enhanced benefits.” John Dentry, product manager at Pay.UK, which owns and operates Cass, said: “The huge range of providers underscores the competitiveness of the market.” The Current Account Switch Service is designed to make moving banks or building societies easier. Customers can also move their current account outside the scheme if they prefer. Small businesses with a turnover of up to £6.5million, small charities with an annual income below £6.5million and small trusts with net assets below £6.5million can also use the service. Smaller banks are also trying to tempt customers to switch by offering perks and rewards on their current accounts. Zopa, for example, has revamped its Biscuit current account to let customers choose the benefits that best suit their spending habits. The free account pays 1% AER variable interest on all balances and offers fee-free card spending abroad, while customers can select one additional benefit: 2.75% AER variable interest on their balance, 3% cashback on up to £150 of eating-out spending each month, or 3% cashback on up to £150 of Direct Debit payments each month. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP confirms State Pension age change - people with these birthdays face longer wait
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People approaching State Pension age are being warned they could have to wait several months longer before receiving their first payment as the Government continues its phased increase from 66 to 67. The change is being introduced gradually over two years, with the State Pension age rising by one month at a time for people reaching 66 during the transition. The next stage begins on November 6 and affects people born between November 6 and December 5, 1960. Rather than receiving their State Pension when they turn 66, this group will have to wait until they are 66 years and eight months old before becoming eligible. For someone born on November 6, 1960, that means they will reach State Pension age on July 6, 2027. The delay increases by another month for each subsequent group of birthdays. Those born between December 6, 1960 and January 5, 1961 will have to wait until they are 66 years and nine months old, while the next group will reach State Pension age at 66 years and 10 months. The phased increase will eventually mean people born from March 6, 1961 onwards have to wait until their 67th birthday to claim their State Pension. The State Pension age is currently 66 for men and women, but is rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028. The increase began on April 6, 2026, and affects people born between April 6, 1960 and April 5, 1961. The exact age at which someone can claim depends on their date of birth, with the delay increasing by one month for each successive group. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) timetable is: The latest increase comes amid calls for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone. A public petition calling for the change has attracted thousands of signatures, with campaigners arguing that people in their mid-to-late 60s can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited options to remain in work. Tim Grimsditch, Managing Director of Unbiased, said: “A public petition calling for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone has gathered more than 80,000 signatures and is approaching the 100,000 needed for Parliament to consider debating it. Its argument is that many people aged 65 to 67 face poor health, caring pressures, and limited options to keep working - and the evidence that healthy life expectancy varies considerably by income and occupation gives that weight. “The Government has consistently rejected calls to lower the State Pension age, and the Third State Pension Age Review is currently underway to determine what the age should be in future decades. There’s a difficult balance here: the State Pension is one of the largest items of public spending, and allowing people to claim it earlier would mean paying it to more people for longer. Both sides of this are serious arguments. “Either way, the timing matters for planning. The State Pension age is currently rising from 66 to 67, a change that began in April 2026 and completes in March 2028, affecting people born between March 1961 and August 1977. Legislation already exists to take it to 68 after that. “The practical issue for most people isn’t the State Pension age itself - it’s the gap before it. "Private pensions can generally be accessed from 55, rising to 57 in April 2028, while the State Pension now arrives at 67. Someone who stops working at 63 through ill health or caring responsibilities is funding four years entirely from their own provision. That’s the question the petition is really about, and it’s worth planning for regardless of what happens to it." Recommended reading: The increase from 66 to 67 was brought forward under the Pensions Act 2014. The legislation changed the timetable so that the State Pension age for men and women would rise to 67 between 2026 and 2028, rather than over the longer period previously planned. The DWP said: “The Pensions Act 2014 brought the increase in the State Pension age from 66 to 67 forward by eight years. The State Pension age for men and women will now increase to 67 between 2026 and 2028. “The Government also changed the way in which the increase in State Pension age is phased so that rather than reaching State Pension age on a specific date, people born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach their State Pension age at 66 years and the specified number of months. “For people born after 5 April 1969 but before 6 April 1977, under the Pensions Act 2007, State Pension age was already 67.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers crisps and Rubicon drink recalled from UK supermarket shelves
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drink and a snack box feature in this week's round-up of product recalls. AG Barr is recalling Rubicon Yuzu & Pink Grapefruit cartons, while PepsiCo is recalling its Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has published allergy alerts for both products, including details of which batches are affected and what customers should do. The FSA says the 1L cartons may contain sulphites not mentioned on the label, posing a possible health risk to people sensitive to sulphur dioxide or sulphites. Four batches are affected: Anyone with a sensitivity to sulphur dioxide or sulphites who has bought an affected carton should not consume it, the FSA advises. They can return it to the shop where it was bought for a full refund, or contact consumercare@agbarr.co.uk for further information. The FSA says notices explaining the recall will be displayed in retail stores selling the product. PepsiCo is recalling the 655g box of six packs because wheat is not declared on the outer packaging, according to the FSA. The problem concerns an 85g pack of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten. The affected batch code is 107543, with best-before dates of 21 November 2026 or 16 January 2027. The FSA says the product poses a possible health risk to people with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease. Those customers are advised not to eat the affected product and can contact the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800274777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers for a full refund. The alert applies to England, Scotland and Wales. The FSA explains that a food may be withdrawn from sale when there is a problem that means it should not be sold. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. Food can be withdrawn or recalled because allergy information is missing or incorrect, or because there is another food allergy risk. When there is a food allergy risk, the agency issues an allergy alert.

The offences took place between 2004 and 2009, during the height of Brand’s fame. Today, November 9, at Southwark Court, Mr Justice Bennathan, sentenced Brand to 10 years and six months. Russell Brand with his wife Laura Gallacher (Image: Maja Smiejkowska/PA) On Monday, Mr Justice Bennathan slammed Brand’s “staggering arrogance” as he sentenced him to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and three counts of sexual assault. Beginning his sentencing remarks, he told the defendant: “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. “You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. “You had also become a sexual predator.” Mr Justice Bennathan told the court: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent.” The judge told Brand “imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father, that sad loss to them however is caused by your serious offending.” The judge said factors in mitigation for Brand included his lack of previous convictions and that “17 years had passed” since his final offence, and how Brand had lived his life subsequently including helping those “wrestling with addictions”. Brand showed no emotion as he was jailed for 10 years and six months, but told his wife “we’ll be OK” as he was taken downstairs by the dock officers. Ahead of the sentencing, victim statements were shared in the courtroom, with Brand's rape victim sharing: "When I eventually reported what had happened, it was not simply because of the media documentary. She later visited Brand’s Hampstead home for sex, but said the encounter turned violent when he forcibly raped her. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman at a Nordic bar in Soho in 2004, groping her breasts just seconds after being introduced to her. Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher outside Southwark Crown Court. (Image: PA) Brand was cleared of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families in Cambridgeshire are being encouraged to apply for the NHS Healthy Start scheme through a new outreach campaign. Cambridgeshire County Council, in partnership with district and city councils, is targeting around 1,700 low-income households identified via its Low-Income Family Tracker (LIFT) platform. The campaign will run throughout November and aims to raise awareness of unclaimed financial support for healthy food and milk. Councillor Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee, said: "We know that many families across Cambridgeshire continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures, and Healthy Start can provide valuable support at a time when every pound counts. "Through this targeted campaign, we're helping families access money that they are entitled to, putting additional income into household budgets while supporting healthy eating and giving children the best possible start in life." Healthy Start is a national scheme offering pregnant women and families with young children weekly payments of £4.65 per child under the age of four, rising to £9.30 for infants under one. The funds are loaded onto a payment card and can be used in most supermarkets to buy items such as cow’s milk, fresh fruit, and vegetables. The campaign is part of the council’s wider anti-poverty programme, which includes income maximisation services, targeted outreach, and crisis payments. Just 62 per cent of eligible Cambridgeshire families currently claim Healthy Start, meaning more than £431,000 could be going unclaimed each year. Households that have been identified will be contacted by letter, email, phone call, or text message. Those who do not receive a notification are still encouraged to check their eligibility through the NHS Healthy Start website. Residents are reminded that if they are ever in doubt about the authenticity of a letter, email, text message or phone call, they can contact their district or city council directly for verification. Information on scam awareness is available on the Cambridgeshire County Council website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Romesh Ranganathan tackles online outrage and family life in sharp Cambs comedy show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge welcomed Romesh Ranganathan as part of his sell-out 'Romesh Will Change Your Life' tour, with the evening proving to be anything but a conventional comedy show. A live DJ, a sell-out audience and a comedian with absolutely no intention of playing it safe, the TV star delivered an evening of sharp wit, awkward truths and wonderfully self-deprecating humour. Before the, a live DJ set was accompanied by various clips from Romesh's television appearances, including Rob & Romesh and his recent winning moment on Celebrity Traitors. It was an unconventional opening, but one that immediately established the atmosphere of the evening. From family life and relationships to racism, immigration and wider social issues, no subject was entirely off limits. Romesh moved effortlessly between everyday observations and contentious topics, delivering his trademark dry humour with a healthy dose of self-deprecation. Romesh Ranganathan on the Cambridge Corn Exchange stage (Image: Angela Smith) He also addressed the recent controversy surrounding his BBC TV advert "What has the BBC ever done for me", which attracted online criticism and abuse directed at both him and his wife. Rather than shy away from the subject, he used it as another opportunity to expose the absurdities of online outrage and the world of keyboard warriors. However, some of the evening's biggest laughs came when Romesh turned his attention closer to home. Joking about being fed up with seeing himself on television, he launched into imagined stand-up performances by his wife and son. His ability to impersonate his own family, while simultaneously making himself the butt of the joke, proved a particular highlight, generating some of the most raucous laughter of the night. He weaved jokes about his childhood trauma and his womanising dad into a therapy-themed narrative, which made it feel as though he was baring his soul on stage under the guise of comedy. It is this willingness to ridicule himself, alongside his sharp observations and unapologetic approach to difficult subjects, that makes Romesh such an engaging performer. 'Will Change Your Life' may be a bold promise, but if the measure is an evening of laughter, uncomfortable truths and refreshingly honest humour, Cambridge certainly got its money's worth.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From a medieval bridge with its own chapel to a 55-arch causeway, Huntingdonshire is packed with unusual crossings. The district’s rivers, floodplains and Fenland waterways have shaped travel for centuries, leaving medieval crossings and Fen drainage bridges behind. Here are some of Huntingdonshire’s most striking bridges and where to find them. St Ives Bridge One of the county’s most extraordinary bridges spans the River Great Ouse at St Ives. The town’s first bridge was built of wood in 1107, before work began on a stone replacement in the early 15th century. The stone crossing was completed in 1425, and a chapel was added the following year. It is one of only three bridges in England with a chapel. The bridge also still bears the scars of the English Civil War. Parliamentary troops destroyed part of it to hinder Royalist forces, so a temporary drawbridge was installed. When the damaged section was rebuilt in 1716, it was given rounded arches instead of matching the pointed medieval ones, leaving a visible difference today. The chapel has also served as a toll house, inn and private home. The bridge is also a scheduled monument. Huntingdon Old Bridge Another remarkable medieval bridge links Huntingdon and Godmanchester across the River Great Ouse. Grade I-listed Huntingdon Bridge dates from around 1330 and has six pointed stone arches. Historic England says a band of trefoil decoration above two arches probably marks the bridge’s oldest surviving section. Its third arch was replaced by a drawbridge during the English Civil War. The bridge also has a slight kink. Historical accounts say builders started on both riverbanks, but the two sections failed to meet in a straight line. Historic England calls it a "fine and famous example of a medieval bridge". The Nuns' Bridge, Huntingdon The lesser-known Nuns’ Bridge stands on Brampton Road in Huntingdon. Grade II-listed Nuns’ Bridge dates from the 15th or 16th century, was repaired in the 17th and largely rebuilt in the 18th. The stone-and-brick bridge has five arches and brick parapet walls. Unlike many historic bridges, it has avoided modern traffic because the main road now bypasses it. It is both a Grade II-listed building and a scheduled monument. The New Bridges, St Ives Despite their name, St Ives’s New Bridges are more than 200 years old. The extraordinary brick causeway runs about 220 yards across the Great Ouse flood plain and opened in 1822 after being built by the Bury to Stratton Turnpike Trust. Its astonishing number of arches makes the causeway stand out. It has 55 arches, keeping the route across the flood meadows open when the surrounding land flooded. About 1.2 million bricks were reportedly used to build it. One brick carries its own piece of history. One brick bears the date 1822 and the signature of John Turner, who oversaw the work and apparently signed the wet clay before it was fired. The New Bridges are Grade II* listed. Bridge over the River Great Ouse, Godmanchester Godmanchester has another historic crossing a short distance from the famous medieval Huntingdon Bridge. The bridge over the River Great Ouse at The Avenue is separately Grade II listed. It makes a useful stop on a riverside walk, where visitors can see several generations of crossings around Huntingdon and Godmanchester. Forty Foot Bridge, Ramsey Forty Foot For a bridge in a very different landscape, head into the Fens around Ramsey Forty Foot. Forty Foot Bridge carries the road over the Forty Foot River, part of the Middle Level Navigations. The unusual name refers to the waterway, not the bridge’s length. The Forty Foot Drain, also known as Vermuyden’s Drain, is part of the historic network built to drain the Fens. The name traditionally refers to the width of the original drainage channel between the bank tops. The surrounding settlement also took its name from the waterway and bridge, making them defining features of the Huntingdonshire Fen landscape.

Nearly 4,000 of the most financially vulnerable homes in Huntingdonshire currently receive up to 100 per cent support through the district council’s council tax scheme, which is now under review for 2027/28. The scheme cleared its first approval stage after the Overview and Scrutiny (Environment, Communities and Partnerships) Panel met on November 5. Councillor Nathan Hunt, executive councillor for resident services and corporate performance, said: "HDC's up-to 100% Council Tax Support Scheme is one of the most important things we do to keep people out of crisis and build a fairer Huntingdonshire. "It puts money back in the pockets of those who need it most, takes a fair and compassionate approach, and helps make processing the scheme much more efficient." Some 3,997 households currently receive the maximum support, accounting for 4.69 per cent of all households in the district. That is 56 more households than in August 2025 and 104 more than in August 2024. By August 2026, 5,035 households were receiving council tax support, about 5.92 per cent of households in the district. Read more Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them Paralympic champion Lauren Steadman to open inclusive community gym in Hunts Cambridgeshire PC praised after cutting deliberate fires at landfill by 81 per cent Beloved African lion Ghana dies aged 16 after declining health at Cambs zoo Four EV charging bays approved at Hunts shopping centre despite parking concerns The scheme, which is means-tested, is designed to reduce council tax bills for working-age residents on low incomes. Central government sets support for pension-age claimants. For 2024/25, Huntingdonshire District Council raised the maximum support under the scheme from 80 per cent to 100 per cent for many claimants. The council also introduced income bands linked to Universal Credit allowances and scrapped the need for claimants to submit a separate application. The council says the change has helped more residents claim support they might otherwise have missed. Under the banded scheme, the highest category gets a full discount, while lower bands offer 75, 50 or 25 per cent support. Eligibility thresholds are updated each year to reflect changes to Universal Credit. The scheme also encourages people to work by ignoring up to £50 a week of their earnings in assessments. The assessment excludes some benefits, including disability payments, Carer's Allowance, child benefit, child maintenance and parts of Universal Credit. The council says the revised scheme has made administration more efficient. Between April and August 2026, 71.44 per cent of changes in circumstances were processed automatically, up from 69.84 per cent in 2025 and 62.52 per cent in 2024. The number of processed changes also rose by 5,400. The average processing time for changes rose slightly to 3.02 days, from 2.86 days in 2025, but remained below 3.42 days in 2024. New claims took an average of 20.79 days to process—up from 18.8 days the previous year but down from 22.7 days in 2024. The council says scheme changes meant 452 fewer council tax bills were issued despite more updates being processed. The council also reported further falls in non-payment reminders and summonses. The scheme reduces the council’s tax base because it is classed as a discount, not a benefit. All authorities that collect council tax in the district share the cost. Officers recommend keeping the scheme’s core principles for 2027/28, while raising income thresholds in line with Universal Credit. The proposals go to the council’s cabinet on November 17, with full council expected to make the final decision on December 16.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six historic churches have been named on Historic England’s 2025 Heritage at Risk Register. Located across Huntingdonshire, the churches are among nearly 1,000 places of worship in England on the register. Historic England’s annual register highlights buildings and sites most at risk from neglect, decay and other threats. All six Huntingdonshire entries are churches, including Grade I-listed buildings in Huntingdon, Abbots Ripton and Bythorn and Keyston. Four of the six currently have no agreed plan in place to address their condition. Here is a closer look at each site on the register. PARISH CHURCH OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, BYTHORN AND KEYSTON The Grade I-listed church is in “poor” condition and has medium vulnerability. The building is in slow decline, and no solution has yet been agreed to address the issues. It faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of fabric, with no agreed solution. CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, OFFORD CLUNY The Grade II*-listed church on High Street faces the same threat. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of B, meaning it faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration. A solution had been agreed but was not in place when the site was assessed. CHURCH OF ST MARY, HUNTINGDON The Grade I-listed Church of St Mary on Huntingdon High Street is one of the district’s most prominent buildings at risk. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of C, indicating slow decay. No solution had been agreed at the time of the assessment. CHURCH OF ST ANDREW, ABBOTS RIPTON The Grade I-listed church on the High Street is in poor condition and has medium vulnerability. Like St Mary’s, it has a priority rating of C, and no repair solution had been agreed. PARISH CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, BROUGHTON The final entry is Broughton’s Grade II-listed Parish Church of All Saints on Causeway Road. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of historic fabric. No solution had been agreed when it was assessed. A place on the Heritage at Risk Register does not mean a building will be lost, but it signals that urgent action is needed. The register helps Historic England direct support and resources to the most vulnerable heritage sites. Sites can leave the register after repairs or once a sustainable plan is in place. The 2025 register includes 1,460 buildings and structures across England, along with 986 places of worship, 1,864 archaeological sites, 105 parks and gardens, three battlefields, four protected wreck sites, and 469 conservation areas. This year, 138 sites were added to the register and 129 removed after conservation work. The register underlines the need for investment, community support and long-term planning to protect the region’s heritage.

Nigel Hugill, chair of the Arts Theatre, said: "In Tom Littler, we have found exactly that calibre of visionary leader able to advocate and demonstrate the value of humanities in a tech-driven environment. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: BBC licence fee could change as Government makes major announcement on future plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the BBC licence fee not to be extended to subscribers of rival streaming services has received a Government response, amid growing questions over how the broadcaster will be funded in future. The petition, which has attracted 18,418 signatures, warns that households could face extra costs if ministers decide to extend the licence fee to people who subscribe to streaming platforms not owned or operated by the BBC. Campaigner Alec Burns, who created the petition, argues the move would be "wholly unacceptable", particularly during the cost-of-living crisis. The petition, which can still be signed, states: "Amid a cost-of-living crisis, we believe the Government should be finding ways to save the public money, not expanding their means of taxation." It also claims the BBC already has a "tarnished reputation" and warns that extending the charge could further damage public confidence in the broadcaster. The Government has now responded, confirming it is considering a range of options for the BBC's future funding but stressing that no final decisions have been taken. In its response, published on November 2, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said ministers were considering feedback from a public consultation on the BBC Charter Review Green Paper. It said: "The Government is keeping an open mind on the future funding of the BBC and no decisions have been taken at this stage." The response added that ongoing policy development was looking at the potential impact of different funding arrangements on households, consumers, investment and the wider creative economy. Ministers said the BBC remained a "vital national institution" which informs, educates and entertains audiences across the UK. The Government also highlighted the broadcaster's contribution to the UK's creative industries, saying it supports jobs and growth across the nations and regions. It pointed to research from the Reuters Institute, which found that 59% of UK respondents trusted BBC News in 2026, making it one of the country's most trusted news brands. However, ministers acknowledged that viewing habits have changed significantly as more people turn to streaming services and other ways of watching television. The Government said: "The changing media market and audience viewing habits mean the Charter Review needs to consider whether the current funding model remains suitable for the future." It also revealed that the total number of TV licences in force has fallen by three million since 2017/18. The Government confirmed it is looking at several options to ensure the BBC has sustainable funding in the years ahead. These include making the broadcaster operate more efficiently, generating more commercial revenue and potentially reforming the licence fee itself. Ministers also acknowledged concerns about the cost of the charge for households already struggling with their finances. The response said: "We understand that ensuring the licence fee is affordable is important." It added that the Government wanted to keep costs as low as possible for households while ensuring the BBC had the resources it needed to continue providing its services. The response did not confirm whether people subscribing to non-BBC streaming platforms could eventually be required to pay the licence fee. Instead, ministers stressed that they were still considering consultation responses and engaging with stakeholders. A White Paper setting out the Government's plans for the BBC's future is expected before the end of 2026. Recommended reading: The Government also highlighted existing support for households struggling to pay the annual licence fee. Since February 2025, more households have been eligible for the Simple Payment Plan, allowing them to spread the cost through weekly, fortnightly or monthly instalments. Other support includes: Ministers said the Charter Review was also considering whether further concessions or alternative payment schedules could better reflect different household circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Shoppers at Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Lidl and more risking £100 parking fines
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers could face a £100 charge for parking outside a supermarket's opening hours. Some supermarket car parks restrict when vehicles can be left there, even if the car park is empty. Select Car Leasing highlighted the issue. Graham Conway, managing director of Select Car Leasing, urged drivers to read signs before deciding whether to park. He said: “Check the signage as you enter the car park carefully before making a decision about whether to stay or not. “Not all store car parks punish after or before-hours parking, but many do, and it’s an issue that’s causing real confusion among motorists.” Mr Conway said the company had seen cases where people were charged after leaving a vehicle for a matter of minutes. Supermarket car parks can be managed by private operators, which issue Parking Charge Notices when they believe conditions have been broken. Some use automatic number plate recognition cameras, with notices sent by post. Other conditions can include limits on the length of a stay, parking within marked bays and restrictions on who can use disabled or parent and child spaces. A private Parking Charge Notice is different from a penalty charge notice issued by a council. In England and Wales, Citizens Advice says drivers should check whether the parking company belongs to an accredited trade association when considering an appeal. It advises that if a non-member puts a ticket on a vehicle, the driver should not contact the company unless it writes to them first. In Scotland, Citizens Advice says someone who wants to challenge a private ticket should first contact the operator, explain their reasons and ask for it to be withdrawn. It says they could also approach the landowner, such as the supermarket, and provide the operator with evidence including photographs of unclear signs. In Northern Ireland, the Consumer Council says a driver who believes a private notice was issued incorrectly may be able to appeal, using evidence such as photographs of damaged signs. It says registered keepers in Northern Ireland cannot automatically be held liable for private parking charges, unlike in England and Wales, and that the driver is liable. An independent appeal may be possible if an operator rejects a challenge, depending on the company and the relevant appeal service.

The proposals will see four rapid EV charging bays and associated equipment installed at the King James Retail Centre in Ermine Street. Huntingdonshire District Council planning officers recommended approval despite strong objections from Godmanchester Town Council. Application 26/01647/FUL revised an earlier scheme, cutting the proposed charging spaces from six to four. Plans to install four electric vehicle charging stations at a Godmanchester shopping centre have been approved despite concerns over parking and safety near a school. (Image: Google Maps / Street View) Six existing parking bays will be replaced by four EV charging spaces. Planning officers said the scheme would improve access to rapid EV charging and encourage greener transport. They concluded that it would provide sufficient parking and vehicle movement and would not cause significant harm to neighbours, highway safety or biodiversity. However, Godmanchester Town Council strongly recommended the plans be refused, arguing that dedicating four spaces to EV charging had not been adequately justified given demand for parking at the site. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Officers seize huge stash of illegal fireworks from Peterborough shop
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A large stash of illegal fireworks has been seized from a shop in Peterborough. Officers found unlicensed fireworks at a Lincoln Road shop on November 6 during a joint operation involving Peterborough City Council’s trading standards team, Cambridgeshire Constabulary and Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. The inspection followed intelligence that fireworks were being sold there without a licence. Councillor Zameer Ali, cabinet member for communities and public safety, said: "In the lead up to Bonfire Night, the community in this area has been disturbed by several firework-related incidents, which have been widely reported on. "While we don't know if these are linked, I am relieved that this sizeable quantity of fireworks has been removed from this address, as it was clearly presenting a hazard to those who lived nearby. "There are obvious serious safety risks in buying, storing, and selling fireworks in an unlicensed premises. "Fireworks are explosives and those sold by unlicensed sellers may not meet safety standards. "They could be improperly stored, incorrectly labelled, damaged and unsafe to use, increasing the risk of injury, property damage and fire." During the visit, officers found more than 21kg of fireworks with net explosive content (NEC). NEC is the total mass of explosive substances, excluding packaging, outer casings, containers, or inert components. These fireworks were subsequently seized. Sam Tucker, Peterborough neighbourhoods inspector, said: "Our officers joined partners in visiting this premises as part of our ongoing efforts to tackle issues involving inappropriate use of fireworks in the city. "Additional patrols will take place in the area tonight and this weekend, and we would strongly urge anyone with any concerns to report this to us, so we can build an accurate picture of anti-social behaviour in the area and work to combat this." Anyone who believes fireworks are being sold illegally can contact the Citizens Advice Consumer Service on 0808 223 1133. If someone is in immediate danger always call 999.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wetherspoon set to open up to 25 more pubs as sales jump higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Up to 25 more Wetherspoon pubs could open this financial year. JD Wetherspoon estimates it could open a further five to 10 managed pubs and 10 to 15 franchised sites in the year ending August 1, 2027. That would be in addition to the six managed pubs and two franchises it has already opened this financial year. The expansion plans came as the pub group reported an 8.2 per cent rise in like-for-like sales in the 14 weeks to November 1, covering its first quarter and a further week. Chairman Tim Martin said: “The company has had a good start to the financial year. “There are still three quarters to go and profit forecasts are very dependent on the level of sales growth.” The six managed pubs opened so far are at Manchester Airport and Heathrow Airport, and in Crewe in Cheshire, Ferndown in Dorset, Dibden Purlieu in Hampshire and Kempston in Bedfordshire. Wetherspoon said it had sold one pub during the period and now had 797 trading managed pubs, alongside 25 franchises. Bar sales rose by 9.4 per cent over the 14 weeks, while food sales increased by 6.8 per cent. Like-for-like growth slowed to 7.5 per cent in the most recent five weeks, compared with 8.6 per cent in the first nine weeks of the quarter. Martin said the company was “comfortable” with market expectations once adjusted for the 53-week financial year. The company put the consensus profit estimate, compiled from seven analysts, at £76.4 million. In the previous 52-week financial year, pre-tax profit fell 28 per cent to £58.6 million as staff and other costs offset higher sales. The company also argued that labour cost increases affect pubs more heavily than supermarkets, estimating the labour cost of a pub pint at £1.68 compared with about 15p for a supermarket pint. Its calculation used an AI-derived estimate of the price of a supermarket pint and wage costs as a percentage of sales. The group argued that the effect had widened the price gap between pub and supermarket pints and reduced employment. Its next trading update is expected on January 20, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands could unlock £2,600 savings after major government rule change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of young people who lack the mental capacity to manage their finances could find it easier to access money held in their Child Trust Funds under new Government plans. The proposed changes aim to remove a complicated legal hurdle that has left many disabled young adults and their families facing lengthy and costly court processes to release savings that belong to them. Under the reforms, parents and carers will be able to approach Child Trust Fund providers directly to access the money on behalf of young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions. The Government said the changes could help between 63,000 and 126,000 young adults who have so far faced difficulties accessing their accounts. Child Trust Funds are long-term, tax-free savings accounts introduced for children born between September 1, 2002 and January 2, 2011. The accounts were designed to give young people a financial asset when they reached adulthood, with money becoming accessible at the age of 18. Justice minister Jake Richards said: “Young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions should be able to access their savings as easily as possible – especially when this money was put aside by loved ones to help them take their first steps into adulthood. “This is simply an injustice that we’re finally putting right and as campaigners have argued for years, change is long overdue. “This legislation will ensure this group of young adults no longer face difficulty from accessing money that is rightfully theirs.” Economic secretary to the Treasury Lucy Rigby said the reforms would help tens of thousands more young people access their accounts. She said: “The changes that we’re introducing will help tens of thousands more young people to connect with their child trust funds - worth on average £2,600 each.” Recommended reading: The Government said it would work with others to develop the new process, including deciding who will be able to access the money, what evidence will be needed and what safeguards should be put in place to protect young people who lack mental capacity. Speaking in the Commons, Ms Rigby said: “The last Labour government introduced child trust funds with the intention that every child in this country could access a financial asset as they enter adulthood, and almost three million young people have already accessed their funds, currently containing an average of £2,600 each.” She added: “I am going to be bringing forward an amendment to the Financial Services Bill. The second reading of which is next week, which will enable the Ministry of Justice to make regulations to put this in action.” Anna Bird, chief executive of Contact, said families had faced unnecessary difficulties when trying to access the money. She said: “For too long, tens of thousands of young disabled people and their families have faced a complicated and costly process to access money that rightfully belongs to them.” The Court of Protection will remain available as an alternative route for protecting the financial interests of adults who cannot make financial decisions for themselves.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Channel 4 has cancelled Married At First Sight UK. The decision follows an external review prompted by "serious allegations of wrongdoing" involving the show. Earlier this year, two female participants alleged rape and a third claimed sexual misconduct by their on-screen husbands in a BBC Panorama documentary aired in May. In June, a cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape. All three men have denied the allegations. Chief executive of Channel 4, Priya Dogra, said: "Welfare across all our programmes is a primary concern. "Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that Channel 4 breached the Ofcom Code or that the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format. "The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years." She also addressed the women who made the allegations. Ms Dogra said: "I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt. "I hope our actions – in swiftly commissioning the review and taking clear, decisive steps – demonstrate our commitment to the wellbeing of all contributors and our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards." The sixth season of Married at First Sight UK, filmed earlier this year, will not be aired. A planned spin-off series, featuring contestants from the UK and Australian versions, was also halted during the review. The external review was commissioned by Ms Dogra after the allegations surfaced. It was split into two parts: Channel 4 said the reviews did not attempt to judge the allegations, which remain a matter for the relevant authorities. Clyde & Co reviewed more than 31,000 documents and 20 hours of footage. Their findings concluded that Channel 4 and production company CPL had complied with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code and had not breached any regulations in handling the issues raised. However, the review identified isolated incidents where the welfare framework was not fully followed. One example involved participants breaking the code of conduct regarding "prohibited substances." They received a first and final warning instead of being removed from the show. Ms Heggessey’s review also found that some aspects of the programme could "implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate" and that participants could "become dependent on production and lose touch with reality," impacting their ability to make decisions. A post shared by Shona Manderson 🪐✨🌸 (@shoniemandy) The review recommended improvements, including reducing the frequency of questions about couples’ physical relationships and discontinuing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week. It also suggested changing the show’s "leave or stay" mechanism. Currently, if one person in a couple chooses to leave but the other wants to stay, both must remain for another week. The review proposed allowing a participant to leave if they wish. Despite these concerns, the review described the welfare protocols as "extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard." Ms Dogra said implementing the recommendations would require a "materially greater level of intervention, monitoring and supervision that would fundamentally alter the format and editorial proposition of the programme." She concluded that, given the maturity of the show and the required changes, ending the series was the right decision. Channel 4 said the budget for Married At First Sight UK will be redirected toward "bold, innovative new programmes from the UK independent production community." A spokesperson said: "CPL has always put contributor welfare at the heart of its programme making and will continue to do so. "CPL have worked closely with Channel 4 for many years and throughout the review process, and we look forward to working with them again in the future." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Minister responds to claims smoky bacon crisps could be banned in UK in new EU deal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cabinet minister told an interviewer to “get a life” over a question about smoky bacon crisps. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle was asked whether closer alignment with the European Union could lead to restrictions on the crisps' labels. Speaking to Times Radio host Stig Abell, she compared the issue to the debate about EU rules on bananas during the Brexit referendum. She said: “Oh, Stig. I mean, really, we’ve had EU straight bananas, and now we’re talking about banning smoky bacon crisps, I think you should get a life.” (Image: Peter Byrne/PA) Dame Angela added: “If you want to obsess about smoky bacon crisps, I suppose that’s your choice.” The concerns relate to whether rules on the use of meat names for products without meat could affect flavour descriptions, rather than ban the crisps themselves. FoodNavigator reported that the European Snacks Association had raised the possibility that flavours such as smoky bacon could be caught by the rules. It also reported that an amendment had been proposed to exempt products including snacks from restrictions on flavour descriptions. The question comes ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on November 20, where Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to seek agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility. The proposed food deal is expected to align the UK with EU plant, animal and food trade standards to remove post-Brexit checks on exports. Dame Angela argued that reducing barriers would make it easier for farmers and food producers to trade with Europe. She said: “We’ve got huge potential growth in our economy if we allow our farmers and food producers to be able to export into Europe again without all the huge uncertainty and the costs and frictions that Brexit brought us.” “This will be a deal that improves that situation and it will enable this economy to grow and for us to have higher levels of prosperity than we’ve had before.” The minister declined to commit to giving farmers more time to adapt to the new trading arrangements, saying that removing barriers quickly would bring “huge economic benefits”. Asked on BBC Radio 4's Today programme about the Government's rejection of farmers' calls for a 24-month transition, she said ministers were listening to their concerns. She said: “The transition is a balance between getting and accessing those benefits as quickly as possible, but dealing with some of the transitional issues that you have to deal with whenever you’re moving from one system to another.” Mr Burnham has said the deals could raise GDP by 0.4%, compared with a previous estimate of 0.3%. Meanwhile, former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier suggested the UK could negotiate to rejoin the bloc without being obliged to adopt the euro, but would have to accept freedom of movement and single market membership. He told Sky News: “If it is the choice of the UK to ask for a new negotiation to rejoin, it’s perfectly possible to begin such a negotiation without any kind of obligation to take part in the euro.” On the single market, Mr Barnier said: “There is no … possible negotiation on any kind of cherry-picking or the single market ‘a la carte’.” Mr Burnham has said the Government will “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with the EU after the summit. He has insisted voters would be “the boss” of any changes, amid questions about EU membership and freedom of movement.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Which? warning over common mistake that is making homes colder and bills higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drying clothes on radiators could leave homes colder and bills higher, Which? has warned. In a TikTok video, the consumer organisation advises households to stop putting wet washing directly on radiators and suggests using an airer instead. It says damp clothes can act as a barrier to heat, potentially leaving a room taking longer to warm up and increasing energy use. Which? also raises the risk of mould when moisture from drying clothes ends up in the air inside a home. Which? suggests putting washing on an airer near a radiator rather than covering it, allowing air to circulate around the room. For people who need another option, it suggests a heated airer for smaller loads or a tumble dryer. However, a heated airer does not make the moisture disappear, so the room still needs ventilation. In separate tests of indoor drying methods, Which? found that the cheapest option depends partly on the amount of washing. It says an unheated airer uses no electricity, while its tested heated airers took around four to five hours to dry a small cotton load. The organisation found a heated airer could save money compared with vented or condenser tumble dryers when a small load fits on it in one go. For larger loads that need several rounds on an airer, Which? says a tumble dryer is likely to be cheaper to run. Heat pump dryers have lower running costs than vented and condenser models, according to its comparison, although they can cost more to buy. Ventilation matters whichever indoor drying method is used: South Kesteven District Council advises drying washing outside if possible. If that is not possible, it recommends a heated, well-ventilated room, such as a bathroom with the door closed, and says not to put clothes on radiators. The council advises opening windows wider or using extractor fans where fitted when drying clothes, and keeping permanent vents clear. Energy Saving Trust says condensation forms when moisture in the air meets a cold surface, such as a window. Its advice notes that damp can have other causes too, including leaks, damaged guttering and faults that allow groundwater into walls. Signs of a problem can include persistent condensation, a musty smell, peeling wallpaper or mould, according to the trust. It says the underlying cause needs to be addressed, and leaks or signs of rising damp should be dealt with quickly.

He is expected to be flown back to the UK for treatment following the diagnosis. A Government spokesperson said: "A British citizen currently in the DRC has tested positive for Ebola. "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated." The patient, identified by Reuters as a healthcare worker, is expected to be medically evacuated to the UK, though the timing of the flight remains unclear. Only four cases of Ebola have ever been confirmed in the UK, including three involving health workers who responded to the outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015. Dr Damien Tully, associate professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Uganda Research Unit, said: "This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. "However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased." Dr Tully described the infection as "deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected." He said: "Healthcare workers are on the front line of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. "Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur." Read More He stressed that the risk to the British public "from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low" because Ebola is "transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms." The UK has two high-level isolation units equipped to handle such cases – at the Royal Free Hospital in London and the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Dr Tully said: "These facilities are equipped with specialist isolation systems and staffed by highly trained infectious disease teams."

The venue, considered the largest performance venue in the East of England, would see upgrades to the main auditorium, improvements to foyers and bar areas, improved seating, acoustics, sound quality and lighting. The wider plans also include work on refurbishing the Guildhall, Market Square and public spaces in-between. A report to Cambridge City Council ’s performance, assets and strategy overview and scrutiny committee said a revived Corn Exchange would act “as the catalyst for a renewed arts and culture scene in Cambridge drawing on its roots which saw it at the forefront of the changing trends in the UK’s music scene.” Sam Scharf, the council’s director of communities, said: “It’s already failed – I mean, last year it rained a bit and we had to cancel Tim Peake. “We then put a short-term remedy in with a bit of leading on top and that is not going to hold up – it’s not got any longevity.” Council officers said income from the venue will help fund the rest of the Civic Quarter scheme and project it will increase by a large amount after the refurbishment. Performances are estimated to increase from 180 a year to 340 and average ticket prices for council-run events from £24 plus VAT currently to £50 plus VAT in year five of the new venue’s opening. Officers said this only applies for events they self-promote and a larger amount of their income comes from hiring the venue out, when they don’t have control of ticket prices. Cllr Beth Gardiner-Smith said: “The business case also notes that the projection of event income is high compared to the benchmark venues. “I think it’s projecting a 43 per cent increase in attendance in year five and similar increases in performances.
