summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: One million people warned to act before major UK landline change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: One million people risk losing landline phone access unless they upgrade to digital lines The warning comes as the UK prepares to retire its old analogue phone network and complete the switch to digital lines. BT-owned Openreach are phasing out the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), a system in place since the 1870s, with a full shutdown planned for January 31, 2027. James Lilley, director of customer migrations at Openreach, said: "It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something." Moving to digital lines is expected to provide a more reliable service, better-quality calls and improved blocking of unwanted calls. Despite these benefits, around one million residents and businesses remain on the old network. Those who do not upgrade in time could lose service or be transferred to a basic emergency phone system without features like voicemail. The UK government says the transition is necessary due to the declining reliability of the copper-based PSTN, and Ofcom has said most users are unlikely to experience significant disruption. The original switch-off date was set for December 31, 2025, but concerns about the impact on vulnerable and rural users, particularly those relying on telecare alarms, led to a revised timeline. Under the PSTN Charter, providers have agreed not to migrate customers using telecare devices unless their equipment is confirmed to be compatible with digital lines. Telecom companies, including BT, are supplying vulnerable customers with free back-up battery packs to ensure phones remain operational during power outages. Read More Unlike the digital system, the traditional PSTN does not depend on mains electricity and will continue to function during a power cut. Openreach has stated that there will not be a single day when all customers lose service. Tens of thousands of customers are reportedly switching to the new system each week, Lilley said a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change. Have you switched to a digital phone service yet? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knifeman had ‘eyes wide open like he was on something’, court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train was described by a boy he stabbed the day before as having ‘his eyes wide open like he was on something’, a court heard. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, where CCTV of the knife attack was shown in court. Anthony Williams, 33, denies ten counts of attempted murder relating to the incident. He also denies the attempted murders of three people in Peterborough on October 31, and of a 17-year-old boy at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1. His trial opened at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, October 28. Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. Cambridge Crown Court (Image: LDR) A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, told police in a video-recorded interview played in court on Friday that he was stabbed on Halloween last year. He said he was going to go trick or treating with friends and was walking over a bridge behind an Asda store in Peterborough when a man ‘just pulled out a knife and stabbed me’. He described the person as "this random guy" and said it happened shortly after 7pm as he was walking with a friend, along a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk. "We’ve pretty much got right up close to him as we’re walking past him and he’s pulled out a knife and just stabbed me," the boy said. He added: "I didn’t feel like he was mentally sane. "His eyes were wide open like he was on something." He said the man "shouted something, I don’t know what he said". "I jumped back a little when I saw he was reaching for something and I started running," the boy said. He continued: "He was screaming something. "My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'." He said he and his friend ran and hid in bushes and called the police. Asked what force the man had used, the boy said: "It was strong, like it pushed me back a little bit. "He was using his full force, his arm was fully stretched out." He said the man was dressed in black and he believed the knife was around 10 inches long. A group of police officers stand close to the emergency equipment left behind after an incident at Huntingdon train station (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) The boy’s friend, who also cannot be identified for legal reasons, said the man who he described as a black male had shouted "are you two involved?". In a statement read in court, he said the man "pulled out a large knife" from a rucksack, describing the knife as a "type of zombie knife or Rambo-style knife". Williams is accused of the attempted murders of two others in Peterborough on October 31, Dawid Taborski and William Ogelby. Mr Taborski said in a video interview that he had been on his way to a rave when a man he had never seen before "kept saying are you involved, are you involved?" He said he "didn’t know what he (Williams) was on about, I was really confused" and he initially thought it may have been "a Halloween thing". "As soon as he took that knife out I ran," he added. "It happened so quickly." The scene at Huntingdon train station after the incident last year (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) Detective Constable Ryan Burke said he was on high-visibility foot patrols when Mr Taborski approached him by Charters bar in Peterborough and told him "someone had attempted to stab him but they hadn’t been able to do so". The officer said in a statement that Mr Taborski told him the man had "brandished a long silver blade" and "lunged attempting to stab him". Mr Ogelby told police he had been walking to a cashpoint to get money out when a man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting. "I’ve said (it) back and he’s pulled a knife out and tried to stab me three times in my stomach and once in my chest," he said in a video interview played to jurors. He said he ran home "as fast as my legs would carry me" and "checked myself to see if I was bleeding – I wasn’t bleeding". "I thought he was going to kill me," he said. Jurors were shown a photo of Mr Ogelby wearing a jacket which had what prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC described as a "knife cut" to it. The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday, November 2.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Are you owed £8,000? HMRC is sending out 311,000 new letters to people due money
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of people - mostly mums - are due money back from historic State Pension errors, as HMRC has sent out 311,000 letters to people who could be missing out. The letters are aimed at parents and carers who may be missing Home Responsibilities Protection (HRP) from their National Insurance records, potentially leaving them with a lower State Pension than they should receive. HMRC says the latest mailout will run until the end of March 2027, with 215,000 letters going to people who have already reached State Pension age. The department says the letters will include a claim form for the first time, making it easier for people to apply for HRP without having to download or print the paperwork themselves. Official figures show that more than 25,000 people have had HRP added to their National Insurance records since HMRC began sending letters in September 2023. Nearly all were above State Pension age, and they have received a share of more than £100million in pension arrears. The average arrears payment has been around £8,000, although the amount an individual receives depends on their circumstances and whether they are eligible. Home Responsibilities Protection was introduced to help protect the State Pension entitlement of parents and carers who took time away from paid employment to raise children or care for others. People who claimed Child Benefit between 1978 and May 2000 may be affected if HRP is missing from their National Insurance records. During this period, people claiming Child Benefit were not always required to provide their National Insurance number. HMRC says that while HRP was automatically added to the records of people who supplied their NI number, some people who did not provide it may have missed out. HRP reduced the number of qualifying years a person needed on their National Insurance record to receive a full basic State Pension. The scheme was replaced by National Insurance credits in 2010, meaning people who started claiming Child Benefit after that date will not be affected by this particular issue. HMRC and the Department for Work and Pensions have been contacting people who may be missing HRP for the past three years. The department says it has already sent 340,000 letters inviting people to check whether they qualify. Following a successful trial of a revised letter, a further 311,000 are being sent out by next March. The latest letters will include the CF411 claim form, which recipients can complete with their personal details and return by post. HMRC says checking eligibility online remains the quickest option for people who can use the service. Claimants can use the GOV.UK eligibility tool to check whether they may be missing HRP and submit a claim online. Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer, said: “We're hopeful that by including the claim form in the letter, people are more likely to fill it in, send it back and find out quickly and easily whether their entitlement will increase on retirement or, if they've reached State Pension age, they're owed a payout.” Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 HMRC says people do not need to use a third-party company to check their eligibility or submit an application, meaning they can avoid paying a firm a share of any arrears they receive. Anyone who needs help can call the National Insurance Helpline on 0300 200 3500. Further support is also available online. Research published by the Department for Work and Pensions in May 2025, based on work carried out by Verian, examined why some people did not respond to the earlier campaign. The research identified several possible reasons, including fears that letters could be scams, confusion about the terminology used and uncertainty about whether the recipient was eligible for money. Some people struggled to understand how HRP related to their own circumstances. Others were concerned that making a claim could leave them worse off or lacked confidence in completing the process online. The findings highlight the challenge of reaching people who may be entitled to arrears but do not realise that the letters apply to them. Elaine Walker, director of AskRose, said: “The government's own research tells us exactly why so many people didn't respond last time. "Letters didn't arrive, people didn't think they applied to them, they couldn't see what they stood to gain, and many understandably feared the letter was a scam.” Recommended reading: HMRC is encouraging people who have retired or are approaching retirement to check their National Insurance records for gaps that could affect their State Pension entitlement. The main steps are: Not everyone who checks their record will be entitled to arrears. The amount, if any, will depend on their National Insurance history and individual circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wrong council tax band? What it could mean for your £100 bank energy payment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Around 20 million households will receive a £100 energy payment this winter under plans announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget. Households in council tax bands A to D in England are expected to receive the money through the council tax system from January 2027, most likely paid directly into their bank accounts, according to Martin Lewis. The scheme will cost £2.6 billion, with funding also being provided to devolved administrations so they can introduce similar support elsewhere in the UK. Mr Healey said the payment would help families cope with rising energy bills during the coldest months. He told the Commons: “This winter, for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I am announcing a £100 energy payment for households, paid directly into people’s bank accounts to deal with rising energy bills. “That’s a £2.6 billion scheme to take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people though to the spring.” Mr Healey urged devolved administrations to “do the same and give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter”. But how can you tell if you are eligible for the £100 payment, and what happens if you think you are in the wrong Council Tax band? It's not clear what the deadline will be for this yet, but Martin Lewis has previously shared his advice about what to do if you think your council tax bill is too high. The consumer champion explained how two simple checks can lower your Council Tax bill this year and forever - but it has to be done with care. He explained: "Up to 400,000 people in England and Scotland are in the wrong band, a higher band, and I've been looking at how you can challenge this since 2007. "Effectively, what you need to do is go onto voa.gov.uk to check your council tax band of an identical property, or if it's Scotland, saa.gov.uk. "If you're in a higher band, the name is in identical properties, then you need to work out what bad you would have been in 1991 if that shows you had a band. "Then you need to look at going forward to get your band lower." 'What can you do if your council tax is going up?' - @susannareid100@MartinSLewis explains what you can do, as he points out that many people could be missing out on discounts. pic.twitter.com/VkucbcAS2K — Good Morning Britain (@GMB) April 1, 2025 Council tax bands were drawn up in 1991 based on drive-by valuations of homes at that time. They are subsequently out of date and many people may actually be in the wrong council tax band. In 2007, financial expert and Money Saving Expert founder Martin Lewis started a campaign to show how you might be able to challenge it. The Check and Challenge approach made huge headlines that year and many people have been able to use it to save themselves money since then. Here’s how it works: You can find out more about Martin Lewis' method - read it carefully before making any challenge. The Check and Challenge method has two steps, and it is absolutely vital you do both before deciding whether to get your council tax banding assessed. Step one involves finding out if your band is higher than neighbours in similar or identical properties. Thankfully, this is public information, so you don’t need to go and ask them. England valuation bands are listed here, and the valuations are here. The band of every property in Scotland can be found on the Scottish Assessors Association website. All domestic properties in Wales are put into 9 tax bands (bands A to I). The tax bands are based on how much a home and the land it is on is worth. The Valuation Office Agency (VOA) values properties for Council Tax purposes. They are the government's property experts for Wales and England. When comparing your band with your neighbours’, make sure the properties are as close in size and value as possible, and would have been in 1991. If neighbours in similar properties are in a lower band than you, then you may have a claim. However, you could land yourself in bother if you don’t do the next step. If your band is different to your neighbours’ and you’re in similar properties, then it could be that their band is wrong and not yours, and you could actually end up landing them with a larger bill if you appeal - you risk becoming an unpopular neighbour. So here is an important next step before deciding to challenge… A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) A second crucial step is to estimate what your home was worth in 1991, as that's when and how the council tax bands were defined. If you bought your house after 1991, you can simply use its price and date of sale to do this. If you rent or bought earlier, you'll need to find an estimated price. It's also worth doing this with similar neighbouring properties. To find a price quickly, you can use a website which offers free historic sales price information such as Zoopla or Rightmove. Enter your street name and it'll tell you the prices of all properties sold there since 2000. Find the most recent sale price of a similar property to yours in your street. Now note down both the price and the date of sale. Once you have that information, you can use it to estimate what your property would've been worth back in 1991, and what band it's in. There is a calculator you can use here, which uses house price data from Nationwide. Recommended reading: This will only give a rough indication, but it gives an idea. You may be in a higher band than your neighbours because they’re in the wrong band, not you. In that case, if you appeal and stay in the same band, but their band is increased, you might not make many friends. Now you've worked out roughly what your property was worth in 1991, you can compare this to a table here to see what band you should have been put in, based on that home value. If you're convinced your property band is unfair after all the checks, you could challenge it. In Scotland, the SAA deals with council tax bands. Enter your postcode in the council tax bands search box on the homepage. Select your property from the list. If you want to challenge the banding, click on "Make a proposal". You can then fill in an online form which will be sent to your local assessor, who will contact you. But do remember, you can’t just ask for your band to be lowered, only for it to be reassessed, which means it could be moved up or down. This is why it’s important to do both checks and think about whether you’ve added an extension to your home or bought extra land or outbuildings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned over viral fuel-saving petrol pump trick that experts say won't work
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A motoring expert has debunked a viral fuel-saving tip making the rounds on social media. The so-called "slow squeeze" method, gaining traction on TikTok and Instagram, claims that gently squeezing the fuel pump trigger while filling up will get motorists more petrol or diesel for their money by reducing air bubbles and foam in the tank. The theory has gained attention online, with one TikTok post under the tag "Fuel Prices UK" reaching almost 250,000 views. However, Graham Conway, managing director at Select Car Leasing, said the advice is misguided and unlikely to deliver any real benefit. Mr Conway said: "The ‘slow squeeze’ hack is popular on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, but you’re highly unlikely to see any real benefit. "Modern fuel pumps have clever systems designed to prevent air or vapour from affecting the measurement of fuel that comes out of the nozzle. "You can’t somehow game the system with the trickle method. "The only thing that might happen is that you take ages to fill up, angering other drivers patiently waiting behind you." The creator of the trend argued that filling up too quickly creates bubbles in the tank, similar to pouring a fizzy drink too fast. Despite Mr Conway’s explanation, some social media users remain convinced the method works. One commenter said: "I always fill up holding the lever halfway and my petrol lasts way longer. "By holding the lever in all the way in we are paying for a lot of air too." Another claimed that it could "make a litre or two difference in a fill up." Mr Conway also used the opportunity to warn against another common mistake at the pump: topping off the tank after the nozzle clicks. He said: "Squeezing the fuel pump trigger after the nozzle has automatically clicked off, also known as ‘topping off,’ might seem like a sensible way to squeeze a little extra fuel into your tank. "But doing so repeatedly could actually end up damaging your car, potentially leaving you facing an expensive repair bill. "Most modern petrol cars are fitted with an evaporative emissions control system, which captures petrol vapours from the fuel tank and stores them in a charcoal canister, preventing them from escaping into the atmosphere. "However, if you continue forcing petrol into an already full tank, liquid fuel can enter parts of this system that are designed to handle vapour rather than liquid. "This can damage the charcoal canister and other components, potentially triggering an engine management warning light and even contributing to an MOT failure. "Although diesel vehicles generally don't use the same charcoal-canister system, overfilling can still cause fuel to spill or interfere with the tank's venting arrangements. Read More "Repairs to a damaged evaporative emissions system can run into hundreds of pounds, depending on the vehicle and the extent of the damage. "So, while an occasional extra squeeze isn't guaranteed to cause problems, it's best to stop filling when the nozzle automatically clicks off. "That way, you can avoid the risk of an unnecessary repair bill." The warnings come as UK motorists continue to look for ways to cut costs at the pump amid persistently high fuel prices. Have you ever tried this 'slow squeeze' method before? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Village’s only café scales back hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridge village’s only café has been warned it will ‘run out of money’ if it doesn’t make major changes. The Cherry Branch café in Cherry Hinton has faced major finanial issues in its first year. Cambridge City Council owns the building, which includes the library, with the kitchen, café and meeting rooms rented by the charity Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society (CHCBS). Kate Jones, one of the cafe’s trustees, said a business consultant told them, “there’s no two ways about it – you’re going to run out of money”. The 51-year-old said: “It’s difficult when something like this happens – which nobody wanted – and understandably people were upset.” The group said they were required to pay a facilities management charge of £32,000 per year as part of the lease agreement with the city council. This covered building maintenance such as cleaning, gardening and repairs but left the group unable to hire their own contractors meaning they had to do some tasks themselves. Ms Jones said: “That contract meant we were paying a lot of money as a small charity, bearing in mind this is our first year.” The CHCBS also hired a catering manager as a contractor instead of an employee – which would have been cheaper – as they said the council wanted their contract to be terminated more easily if the lease ended. They said the fees for this on top of the facilities management charge were too much as they could only make money from café sales and hiring out meeting rooms. The group took the decision to end the catering manager’s contract and the council has frozen the facilities management charge until March 2027. Ms Jones said: “What we were finding was trustees were doing day to day work in the hub – including the chair actually cleaning the toilets. That meant our ability to have that thinking time was taken away – every time there’s a regular booking someone needs to be here. Now we need to focus on making the hub sustainable – the council have been super helpful and have offered us a hub manager.” The cafe will now be able to stay open with scaled back hours after closing temporarily. A meeting was held this month to reassure Cherry Hinton residents that it is not closing. Ms Jones added: “I think the meeting was good because we were able to just address some of the things people had heard that weren’t right. “We wanted to reassure people the hub is still here, the café is still open, and the trustees are absolutely committed and working extremely hard to deliver this community facility to the people of Cherry Hinton.” Cllr Mike Todd-Jones, the council’s cabinet member for communities, said: “I’m determined to work in partnership with the Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society to help put the Hub on a sustainable financial footing for the future. “Through workshops with the CHCBS, and support from local councillors and the council team, we will work hard together to develop a plan that means the Hub will be in a strong position to serve the people of Cherry Hinton for many years to come.” Be sure to set CambridgeshireLive as your preferred news source to make sure you never miss a story. Simply click here and tick the box. A spokesperson for Cambridge City Council said they were helping to support the CHCBS “through this tricky period”. They said: “Cherry Hinton Hub and Library is a vital focus for the local community and Cambridge City Council is fully committed to its success having redeveloped the former library at a cost of over £1.5 million – funding from the City Council and S106 developer contributions. “The first year or two operating a community facility and establishing a café can be really tough. Maximising income from room hire and the café in this early period is difficult and, combined with the expenses associated with opening new premises, this has proved financially challenging. “The city council has already stepped in to support the CHCBS, suspending facilities management charges from June 2026 to March 2027 alongside other financial help that should save CHCBS around £30,000. The city council is also proposing to pay for an interim Hub manager.” The cafe will be open from 10am to 2pm on Wednesdays only.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Just a couple of miles from the centre of Cambridge, this picturesque village offers a rare combination of countryside tranquillity and city convenience. Frequently rated among the best places to live in Cambridgeshire, the village boasts beautiful surroundings and feels frozen in time. It has a strong community spirit and easy access to some of the county's most famous green spaces. Set on the banks of the River Cam, Grantchester feels a world away from the bustle of city life. The village is surrounded by open countryside, grazing land and the renowned Grantchester Meadows. The meadows have inspired poets and visitors for generations and remain one of the area's biggest attractions today. Despite its peaceful character, Grantchester boasts a selection of well-loved amenities. Among the most famous is The Orchard Tea Garden, which has been serving visitors since 1897 and remains a favourite spot for afternoon tea beneath fruit trees. The village is also home to traditional pubs including The Red Lion and The Green Man, both of which draw locals and tourists looking for classic food and drinks. Grantchester has long been associated with literary figures including Rupert Brooke, while its centuries-old Church of St Andrew & St Mary stands at the heart of the community. The village gained international recognition through the ITV drama Grantchester, which introduced its idyllic streets to television audiences around the world. For those seeking a quintessential English village experience, Grantchester delivers in abundance. With historic pubs, charming architecture and a setting that feels timeless, it is easy to see why so many people consider this riverside gem a must-visit location. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire scientist dies in high-speed Spanish train crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A university scientist living in Cambridgeshire has been named as one of 69 people killed in a deadly high-speed train crash in Spain. Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling on one of the trains involved in the collision near Urda, south of Madrid, on Wednesday (October 28). Her death was confirmed by the Centre for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS) three days after the disaster. In a statement posted online, the centre, based in Santiago de Compostela, paid tribute to the "brilliant young researcher". At least 69 people have been killed in the rail disaster (Image: Manu Fernandez/AP) It reads: "The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October. "Marta was a brilliant young researcher, Group Leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology and Affiliate Associate Professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, University of Cambridge. "At this difficult time, we extend our heartfelt condolences to María José and her family, as well as to Marta Shahbazi’s colleagues and collaborators. "Our thoughts are with them all, and we wish them strength and comfort as they come to terms with this profound loss." The 41-year-old had been travelling to receive the scientific excellence prize from the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology. She had been nominated for her research into stem cells and the early stages of human development. Born in Spain, the mum-of-two had been living with her living with her children, aged three and seven, in Cambridge. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. (Image: Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press via AP) Dr Shahbazi began her career at the Autonomous University of Madrid where she received an undergraduate degree in Biology. She also received an MSc in Molecular Biomedicine before obtaining her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre. In 2019, she received the 3Rs Prize for "providing an opportunity to replace and reduce the use of mice in developmental biology studies." The affiliate associate professor at the University of Cambridge led a group of researchers at the MCR Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB). The Laboratory had previously confirmed Dr Shahbazi was on one of the trains but said here whereabouts were "unknown". In a tribute on its website, the LMB said it is "deeply saddened" by the "tragic death" of the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist". "Her death is a profound shock and a huge loss. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time. "The LMB is offering support to members of its community as they navigate this tragic loss." The collision occurred when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company. It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. Sir David, president emeritus of The Wildlife Trusts, said: "The Wildlife Trusts called for your support and you answered in your thousands. "The appeal to secure the future of the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland has been successful and now the opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality. The scheme received around £1.9 million from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, as well as £5 million from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. Public donations totalled £17 million, with contributions from more than 25,000 people across 50 countries. Eilish McGuinness, chief executive at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: "By working with local communities to develop new approaches to land management, this transformational project has the potential to deliver nature recovery at a grand scale, helping to reconnect people to the unique natural and cultural heritage of this remarkable and nationally significant landscape." A post shared by A Life On Our Planet (@davidattenborough) Mike Pratt, chief executive of Northumberland Wildlife Trust, described it as a "remarkable achievement." Mr Pratt said: "The completion of the Rothbury Estate purchase is a defining moment for Northumberland and the North East. "Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare. "By securing this extraordinary landscape, we’ve the potential to create a flagship for nature recovery supported by sustainable farming, whilst delivering lasting benefits for wildlife, local people and the rural economy for generations to come." Portions of the estate have already been secured, and initial work is under way to survey wildlife, landscapes, and historical features. Sir David has previously praised the estate’s remote beauty, where visitors can explore crags and prehistoric rock art.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fake beauty products found to contain mercury, lead, nicotine and methanol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Counterfeit beauty products containing mercury, lead and methanol are putting consumers at risk, following testing of hauls seized by Trading Standards. The toxic chemicals were found in fake cosmetics, skincare and perfumes seized during recent investigations, with four in 10 seized cosmetics found to contain potentially harmful substances. Among the most alarming discoveries was a skincare product containing 13,200 parts per million of mercury, as well as high levels of lead in lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products. Nicotine was also found in some counterfeit perfumes, and one fake fragrance was made up of approximately 80 per cent methanol. The Intellectual Property Office has issued warnings. (Image: IPO/Press Association) Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: "When you hear that mercury has been found in face cream, lead in make-up or nicotine in perfume, it raises serious questions about what is going into these products and how they are being made. "Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. "But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. "Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally, and those effects may not be immediately obvious. "Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. "You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made, or what risk it might pose. "That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters." The Intellectual Property Office’s (IPO) latest Counterfeit Goods Tracker revealed that one in five 18 to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly bought counterfeits, up from six per cent in 2023. In July, the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products, including extensions, shampoos and conditioners, from a warehouse in Manchester. A separate raid in Bolton uncovered £2 million worth of fake goods. This included perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes. The IPO’s Face the Fakes campaign is working with content creators and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential harms of counterfeit beauty products. Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: "These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. "Products can look remarkably convincing, but behind the packaging they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions. Counterfeit manufacturing equipment. (Image: IPO/Press Association) "Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet. "With our latest research showing a sharp rise in counterfeit beauty buying among young adults, we want to make sure people understand the potential risks and know how to protect themselves. "Our Face the Fakes campaign is giving consumers practical advice to shop more safely, including checking who is actually selling a product and choosing trusted sources." Dr Emma Meredith, director-general of the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association, said: "There is a rigorous safety framework behind every legitimate cosmetic product sold in the UK. "Ingredients are carefully controlled, products have to be made in clean and hygienic conditions, and they must undergo a safety assessment. "Companies have clear legal responsibilities for the products they place on the market."

Mr Cook says the deteriorating floor has left the material inadequately protected and should have been sealed and covered before he moved in. Places for People tenant Michael Cook says flooring in his flat contains asbestos and is a health risk, however the landlords say surveys show it is 'low risk'. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts council leader slams latest 'deeply disappointing' LGR delay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council leader has slammed the latest government update on Local Government Reorganisation, calling the lack of action "deeply disappointing". Sarah Conboy, leader of Huntingdonshire District Council, criticised the update, which confirmed that no final decision had been made on Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. LGR would see the two tier system of county and district councils in Cambridgeshire replaced with a number of unitary authorities across the county. An announcement on the form this would take was expected in July, but the Secretary of State for Local Government at the time, Steve Reed, delayed the decision until October. On October 29, Jim McMahon MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth, announced in Parliament that only five of the 14 areas under review would be proceeding. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough was not included in the five. Cllr Conboy said: "Today's announcement is deeply disappointing for Huntingdonshire and the wider Cambridgeshire and Peterborough area. "After months of work developing and assessing proposals, we had hoped the Government would provide certainty about the future of local government in our area. "Instead, residents, businesses and councils are being asked to wait longer for a decision. "We will continue to work constructively with our partners while seeking greater clarity from Government on the next steps and timescales." The Government says it expects to make a final decision by early next year. In the meantime, HDC will continue to work with regional partners to assess the implications of the announcement and plan for the next phase of the LGR programme. The council confirmed there will be no immediate changes to council services, which will continue to be delivered as normal while councils await further details. The Government said all options would remain under consideration, with a further update due by Christmas and outcomes for every area expected early next year.

Plans have been submitted to create a new residential traveller site for a family near Ramsey. The application, reference 26/01646/FUL, seeks permission to change the use of land on the south side of Middle Drove, Ramsey Heights, to accommodate four static caravans for residential use. The proposals also include parking for vehicles, space for two touring caravans and the construction of a brick and tile utility and day room for residents. Existing hardstanding at the site would be retained. Applicant Christopher Reilly is seeking permission for the development to provide a permanent home for his family, who are members of the Gypsy and Traveller community. The supporting statement says there are already a number of similar developments in the area and claims the proposed design and layout would be in keeping with its surroundings. The application describes the 0.15-hectare site as currently vacant and "derelict ground". Documents submitted with the plans indicate that the proposed day room would be constructed using red facing brick with smooth grey concrete roof tiles. Post-and-rail timber fencing is proposed around the site, while the hardstanding would have a permeable surface. The applicant has stated that there are no trees or hedges on the development site or neighbouring land which could influence the scheme. The applicant argues that the usual Biodiversity Net Gain condition would not apply because the development involves an existing hard-surfaced area of less than 0.2 hectares. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited Cambs garden centre’s new pottery studio - here's what we thought
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nestled into Huntingdon Home & Garden’s spacious restaurant area is its newest attraction – The Potting Shed Studio. Immediately after walking through its doors, the sage green interior decor gives an instant feeling of calmness. It really is a place to unwind and let your imagination takeover. The staff – a small team led by studio manager Sophie – are equally as welcoming, leading us to the well-stocked display. It can be tricky deciding what to paint due to the vast selection, but don’t worry as they have every age covered. From cute little animals to small plates, platter plates, jugs and photo frames, the £1 booking fee per person is redeemable against the price of your pottery. Though it’s not quite as well equipped as some of the longer established pottery studios – for example Center Parcs – this can be forgiven as the studio only opened its doors in late March. Nonetheless, we as a family loved our experience; our two young children had great fun mixing the different squeeze paints together in their palette and getting creative. It’s worth noting, however, that they were not provided with or offered aprons, but we have been assured that the paint comes off very easily in the wash. Something else to bear in mind is that the turnaround is up to two weeks, so you will have to make a return visit for collection — though this isn’t really a problem as Blue Diamond has its customers covered. The Potting Shed Studio has been open for around two weeks (Image: Ben Jolley/Newsquest) Visitors can get topped up on your fresh fruit and veg, browse the clothing range, enjoy a cuppa and a slice of cake, and even refresh your fish tank by popping into Maidenhead Aquatics. Overall, The Potting Shed Studio is a great addition not only to the garden centre – which gave out a complimentary glass of bubbly upon entry to celebrate one year of being open – but for the wider Cambridgeshire area. Alongside being great for families, it would make for a quirky few hours out to get the girls together or even for part of a date day. And, with plans to run exciting events in the future, make sure to keep your eyes peeled on their socials. Visit https://events.bluediamond.gg/event-tickets/75710?branches.branchID=3618 to book.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Why Hamerton Zoo Park is one of Cambridgeshire’s best attractions
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: When it comes to a day out at the zoo, the UK’s biggest are likely the first ones that spring to mind. But, much closer to home, there’s a more local alternative that’s equally worth visiting: Hamerton, near Sawtry, between Huntingdonshire and Peterborough. What began its life as a private collection when it first opened its doors to the public in June 1990, has since grown into a park that is home to many rare and unusual animals. Fast forward 35 years, and not only has the number of distinct breeds massively increased, the entrance area has had a makeover and there’s a brilliant new park (Treetop Adventure Play) that has just as much to occupy children as it does adults. Tree Tops Adventure Play(Image: Newsquest) This includes an obstacle course in the sky that’s connected with ladders and ropes, a great zipwire, plenty of slides and a disorienting Rubix cube-like climbing puzzle that’s sure to challenge parents. Onto the zoo’s main attraction, and there are countless stunning animals to see and learn about: from cute common marmosets that would fit in the palm of your hand to swinging lemurs, to tiny dik-dik deers, hopping white wallabys and adorable lettuce-munching tortoises of all sizes. Read more Witnessing the Greater Flamingo stood on parade is a sight, too, as is being able to walk through the bird enclosure as a myriad of colours zoom past your eyes. Though acclimatised to living in dark, the sloths are equally mesmerising to watch, clinging to branches and ropes while somehow managing to eat upside down. It’s entrancing to witness them move along at such a slow pace, especially in such close proximity. The same can be said for the reptile and rodent house, which has all manner of rare lizards and snakes. It’s worth noting that all the enclosures are incredibly well kept and presented, especially in the bird area (a highlight of which is the strikingly colourful Scarlet Ibis). The flamingos(Image: Newsquest) The meerkat enclosure, meanwhile, has had an upgrade with two new bubble head viewing platforms that provide a great photo opportunity - little ones are sure to want to go through the tunnel on repeat, and they may even be able to snap a selfie with a meerkat. A word of warning, though: it might be a bit tiring for adults - especially those who are taller. As if all that isn’t enough, there are also swimming otters, miniature donkeys, zebra, massive camels, several tigers and, if you’re lucky like we were, one or more of the Syrian Brown Bear family might pop out to say hello. The animal-spotting doesn’t stop there, though, as even while enjoying a tasty panini and delicious cake, there are opportunities to spot some impressive aquatic species. The viewing platforms inside the meerkat enclosure(Image: Newsquest) With all this and more for an affordable price - £19.99 an adult, £15.99 a child, free for under threes and carers - it’s a great value experience. Undoubtedly one of Cambridgeshire’s best attractions, you can easily spend the whole day at Hamerton Zoo Park, and its annual pass option makes for a perfect family gift that’s guaranteed to create lots of special memories. To book, visit https://hamertonzoopark.com

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited bird sanctuary in Cambridgeshire and here’s what we thought
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ben Jolley reports back from a visit to The Raptor Foundation in Woodhurst, Cambridgeshire It’s more important than ever to support local attractions - especially ones that are making a real difference. A registered charity for over 30 years and situated at its current site for the same amount of time, visiting The Raptor Foundation is not only fun for all ages but you'll be supporting a crucial cause too. Having started its life in Ramsey St Mary, before moving to its current, bigger premises in the late 1990s, the sanctuary is home to around 170 birds of prey, including between 35 and 40 different species. The Buzzard Lawn (Image: Newsquest) As the majority of these have come from a rescue background, money spent (entry is very affordable at £8 for adults, £5 for children and free for under threes) goes towards rescuing, rehabilitating and then returning native birds of prey back to the wild. Open to the public all year round, and currently appealing for builders to help create new aviaries, time spent at the foundation is both exciting and educational. The bird of prey displays - which feature rare owls and falcons soaring overhead - are thrilling to watch. If you’re lucky, some may even decide to perch on the seat next to you, which takes the phrase up close and personal to a whole new level. Action from the bird of prey display (Image: Newsquest) Having trained the birds inside out, the keepers and handlers are incredibly knowledgeable, informative and able to answer any question posed to them. This extends to the talks and feeding sessions throughout the day which offer further meet and greet opportunities; a parrot might even land on your shoulders. It’s not just birds, however, as the reptile house is home to a gigantic tortoise (and many smaller ones), as well as lizards and snakes. Beyond animals, there is also a play area and pond that will amuse younger children and a tearoom serving food and drink. Read more The foundation also runs experience days which, ranging from one-to-one handling to junior keeper days, would make for a perfect Christmas present. It also hosts photography tours and is an ideal venue for birthday parties. As if that wasn't enough, there is also the option to stay overnight, at either the Falcons Nest guest accommodation or the caravan site. Whilst we didn’t spend the whole day at The Raptor Foundation (largely due to the weather), there's no question that it is one of Cambridgeshire's most treasured gems.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 ways you can recycle your Halloween pumpkin after October 31
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pumpkins are picked for carving every Halloween, becoming a staple decoration in homes and windows across the UK. However, once October 31 has been and gone, many people are left wondering what to do with their pumpkins. Around eight million are reportedly thrown away in the UK each year, despite there being several ways they can be reused or recycled instead. If you have a leftover pumpkin at home, there are plenty of ways to make the most of it before reaching for the bin. Millions of pumpkins usually end up being thrown away by Brits every year   (Image: PA) Pumpkins can be used for a variety of foods once they have been cleaned out. Dominique Delacour, dairy expert at CAMBOZOLA, shared: “The best way to recycle your pumpkin after Halloween is to cook with it - never throw it away! "Both the flesh, puplp and the seeds can be turned into something delicious. "Roasted pumpkin works beautifully with creamy cheeses in puff pastry parcels, pasta bakes or toasties, while the seeds can be washed, seasoned and baked until golden for a crunchy topping or snack. "It’s an easy way to cut down on waste and turn your Halloween leftovers into something comforting and indulgent for autumn.” Grating the pumpkin pulp you pull out when carving could also be ideal for use in a pumpkin loaf, pie or muffin. The fruit is high in vitamins A and C, as well as being a good source of fibre. Pumpkins don't just have to be used for food after Halloween, with several creative ways to give them a second life. One option is to turn your pumpkin into a seasonal candle. Clean out the inside before adding melted wax, spices such as cinnamon and ginger, and a wick to fill your home with autumnal scents. Leftover pumpkins can also be turned into planters. Remove the inside, add drainage holes and fill with potting soil and your choice of plants. Another option is to make a bird feeder by cleaning out the pumpkin, cutting openings into the sides and filling it with bird seed before hanging it outside. Pumpkins can be composted (PA)  (Image: PA) Using pumpkin in a DIY face mask can be beneficial. AHAs, or alpha hydroxy acids, are widely praised in the skincare world for their ability to help exfoliate and renew skin, and pumpkins are packed full of them. Josh Novell, Director of Polhill Garden Centre, has shared that pumpkins can be used in your garden once they have been cleaned out. He said: "Next, break the pumpkin up into small chunks. Large pieces take much longer to decompose. "Cutting them into fist-sized chunks or smaller helps them break down quickly and release nutrients evenly into the soil. “One of the biggest mistakes people make is scattering pumpkin pieces across the surface; that’s an open invitation for rats and slugs. "Always bury your pumpkin a few inches deep in the soil as this keeps pests away and helps the microbes get to work faster.” “If you’re digging pumpkins into borders or beds, mix in some dry garden materials like leaves, straw or old compost. "That stops the soil from getting too wet or slimy, and it balances out the carbon and nitrogen levels as the pumpkin breaks down.” If you do need to get rid of your pumpkin, then composting it would be the best option. Chris Taylor from Chris Taylor Gardening shared: "Pumpkins break down quickly and make great compost material. "Just remove any candle wax or decorations, chop it into smaller chunks, and add it to your compost heap. Recommended reading: "The high moisture content helps balance drier materials like leaves or cardboard." You could also offer it up to any gardeners or allotment owners who might be interested in taking it off your hands Aside from that, putting it in a food waste recycling bin also works. What do you do with your pumpkin once Halloween is over? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: I'm a personal finance writer - here are the 8 Budget changes I'm most pleased to see
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Budgets always have winners and losers, but this week there are some genuinely welcome bits of news for many people, and as a personal finance writer, I'm particularly pleased to see help for households facing rising energy bills, pensioners getting a boost, more money for workers and new support for people hoping to buy their first home. Chancellor John Healey has announced a package designed to give families, savers and businesses some breathing space during a challenging economic period. And while there's no magic wand to make the cost of living disappear overnight, I think there are some measures worth celebrating. From £100 landing in millions of bank accounts to a higher State Pension and a new scheme to help first-time buyers, here's what I'm taking away from the Budget – and what it could mean for your money. One of the biggest wins for families is the £100 energy support payment - and the fact that they have chosen to put it in people's banks and not give it directly to the energy companies. Around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will receive £100 from the Government this winter, with the money expected to arrive directly in bank accounts from January - a time when most people will need it most. I particularly like that families will be free to spend the money however they choose. Whether it's going towards an energy bill, the weekly food shop or another household essential, it gives people a little more flexibility. Some may say it'll get frittered away, but I like the idea that billpayers get to choose - if that's a day out with the kids or new school shoes or even a drink with mates, a cash boost could help the economy as tills ring with a tiny bit more optimism. There's more good news for energy customers, too. The Government plans to move some of the cost of standing charges on gas bills into the unit rate. Around 60% of households are expected to save an average of £45 a year. The removal of VAT from electricity bills is also being extended until July 2031. Of course, households using more energy could end up paying more under the standing charge changes, so it's worth keeping an eye on how your own bill is affected. But overall, I welcome the focus on making energy costs more manageable. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey delivering his Budget in the House of Commons, London. (Image: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA Wire) There's some particularly good news for pensioners, with the State Pension set to rise to £13,036 a year from next April under the triple lock. For millions of people who rely on their State Pension to cover everyday essentials, this increase will be an important boost. I also think the announcement of a new tax allowance for pensioners on lower incomes is worth highlighting. The measure is designed to protect pensioners from being dragged into paying income tax simply because their State Pension has increased above the £12,570 personal allowance. This is particularly welcome for those who rely largely on the State Pension and don't have significant additional retirement income - the people who really need some help. Did you spot some good news for savers, too? The planned reduction in the annual cash ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 has been scrapped. That's a big win for anyone who likes the flexibility and tax-free benefits of a cash ISA. It feels like trusting people to make the right choice with their own money rather than legislating where and how they can save. It means savers can continue to put away up to £20,000 a year across their ISAs, subject to the usual rules. I think this is particularly important at a time when people are trying to build emergency savings, put money aside for a deposit or simply earn a return on their hard-earned cash. However, there is a sting in the tail (when isn't there?). Tax on savings income is set to increase from April 2027. Basic-rate taxpayers will pay 24%, higher-rate taxpayers 44% and additional-rate taxpayers 49%. This makes making the most of tax-efficient savings options even more important. My advice is to review where your savings are held and check whether you're making full use of your available ISA allowance. A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) One of the most interesting announcements for aspiring homeowners is the new £4.7 billion Your First Home scheme. The aim is to help around 70,000 households in England take their first step onto the property ladder. The scheme will offer first-time buyers 20% equity loans, potentially reducing the deposit and mortgage they need to find themselves. There will be household income limits of £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in London. For anyone who has been saving for years but struggling to get together enough money to buy a home, this could be a welcome opportunity. There's also a new First-Time Buyer ISA coming in April 2029, which will replace the Lifetime ISA. For eligible buyers, it's certainly an announcement worth watching. This is another announcement I'd put firmly in the positive column. The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will rise by 3.9% in April 2027. For workers aged 21 and over, the hourly rate will increase from £12.71 to £13.21. For those aged 18 to 20, it will rise from £10.85 to £11.27. Around 2.3 million workers are expected to benefit. For people on lower incomes, even a modest increase can make a difference to the monthly budget. With food shopping, transport and household essentials continuing to put pressure on finances, having more money coming in is certainly welcome. However, income tax thresholds remain frozen, meaning some workers could find more of their earnings falling into a higher tax bracket as their pay increases. It's a reminder that it's not just your headline pay rise that matters, but how much you actually take home. There's good news for motorists too, and goodness knows, we need it. The fuel duty freeze has been extended, keeping the rate at 52p a litre and cancelling a planned increase in January. For anyone who relies on their car, this is another welcome measure. There's also good news for people who use their own vehicles for work, with the higher tax-free mileage allowance of 55p being made permanent. That should provide some reassurance for employees who use their cars for business journeys and claim mileage expenses. With motoring costs adding up quickly, keeping these allowances in place is a positive step. Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 I'm also encouraged by the business rates announcement. The threshold for small business rates relief for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses is increasing from £12,000 to £18,000. The Government estimates this will take around 70,000 additional businesses completely out of paying business rates. That's potentially a significant saving for independent shops, restaurants, cafés and other businesses that are the backbone of our local communities. For businesses trying to keep their prices competitive, invest in their premises or take on staff, reducing overheads could make a real difference. A thriving high street is good news for everyone, so I'm pleased to see measures aimed at supporting the businesses that keep our communities going. The global economic picture is undoubtedly challenging, particularly with the conflict in the Middle East putting pressure on energy prices. But there are some encouraging signs in the forecasts. The OBR has increased its growth forecast for 2026 from 1.1% to 1.2%. While growth for 2027 has been downgraded to 1%, the longer-term forecasts point towards growth of 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029 and 1.7% in 2030. There is still work to do, but I think it's important to look beyond the immediate economic headlines and recognise that there are opportunities for improvement. The big priority now must be making sure economic growth translates into better wages, more jobs and more money in people's pockets. Let's face facts - times are pretty tough. Most people are struggling - food and fuel cost far too much. But, for me, the biggest takeaway from this Budget is that there are some practical measures that could make a difference at different stages of our financial lives, and no big shocks to make matters worse. Whether you're a pensioner, a first-time buyer, a family with young kids, a saver or a small business owner, there is something in this Budget that could help. I'm particularly pleased to see the State Pension increase, the protection for lower-income pensioners, the decision to retain the £20,000 ISA allowance and the new support for first-time buyers. The £100 energy payment and minimum wage increases are also welcome measures for households feeling the squeeze. Recommended reading: Of course, there are still challenges ahead. Inflation, borrowing costs and weaker growth forecasts show that the economy isn't out of the woods yet. But I think it's important to recognise the positives too. My advice? Take a fresh look at your finances and make the most of any changes that could benefit you. Check your pension, review your savings arrangements, look at your ISA allowance and, if you're hoping to buy your first home, keep an eye on the new scheme. It's not a Budget that's going to change everyone's financial fortunes overnight, but there are some encouraging steps in the right direction. And with household budgets needing all the help they can get, that's certainly something worth celebrating.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Legal expert reveals your rights if trick-or-treaters disturb you on Halloween
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Halloween is an exciting time for many families who will be dressing up and trick-or-treating this weekend. Many houses will be decorated with pumpkins and will be handing out chocolates and sweets to children. However, some people are not a fan of this holiday and will be keeping their doors shut during the evening. A property law expert has revealed what homeowners can do if they want to avoid being disturbed on Halloween. If you do not decorate your house, it indicates to people that you do not want to be disturbed. (Image: Getty) Janet Lane, a property law expert from Rogers and Norton, has shared a few steps that homeowners can take to indicate to trick-or-treaters that they do not want to be disturbed. She said: “There is generally an implied permission for somebody to walk up the usual route to your front door and knock, which is why a delivery driver, neighbour or other caller does not normally need express permission first. “But homeowners can make it clear that they do not want Halloween callers. “A locked gate, or a simple and prominent ‘no trick-or-treaters’ notice on the door, gate or window is one of the clearest ways of communicating that visitors are not invited to approach.” Legal action or police involvement is only necessary if the situation escalates into criminal damage, harassment, or anti-social behaviour. Throwing things at a property like eggs, flour, rocks, and silly string or damaging walls, windows, and vehicles falls under criminal damage, according to the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The Public Order Act 1986 states that using abusive, threatening or insulting words or behaviour that causes alarm or distress is also an offence. Lane added: “There is an important difference between a child innocently knocking on the wrong door and behaviour which becomes intimidating or destructive.” “A single knock is one thing. “Repeatedly banging on somebody’s door after being asked to leave, damaging their property or throwing objects at their home is something very different and should never be dismissed as simply part of Halloween.” Janet says that using a clear sign that says ‘no trick-or-treaters please’ and not putting out pumpkins or decorations will signal to people that you do not want to be disturbed. You should also keep gates closed and make sure any signs are visible before people reach your front door. Do you love Halloween or will you be keeping your door closed this year? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Council-owned developer may not be able to pay back loans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council-owned developer has said they may face a multi-million pound cash shortfall as the housing market faces an “economic squeeze”. This Land, which is owned by Cambridgeshire County Council, could face a shortfall of as much as £7.7m in March 2029, against its loan obligations. A report said the company may not be able to pay back the loans and interest it took from the council under the current forecasts. Michael Hudson, the council’s executive director of finance, told a meeting of the shareholder sub-committee this was not an “immediate insolvency event”. He said that “national market factors” were increasing risks of cash shortages for housing developers and other businesses “as the economic squeeze hits harder and harder”. Set up by the county council in 2016 to build homes and sell land to other developers across Cambridgeshire, the company currently owes the council £58m and a further £22.5m in interest. The report said they expect losses of around £2.7m, around £400,000 worse than planned, by the end of the 2026/27 financial year partly driven by delayed sales at Eddeva Park. Approved in 2021, the development just south of Cambridge of up to 230 homes is a mix of detached, terraced and apartments, with 40 per cent marked as affordable. Rob Williams, chief executive officer of This Land, said that “sales are taking a bit longer at the moment” and “things are slow” in both house building and the wider economy. He said: “The planning system is getting slower if anything. “I think the raft of improvements that have come from central government, whilst they are positive, are taking time to embed and for planning authorities to get their heads around.” The report said council officers are working with This Land “to assess options to protect the council’s position and address the 2029 cashflow risk”. These include “close management of the principal receipts, potential rephasing of disposals, management of loan and interest timing and consideration of the company’s future operating model”.

A Cambridgeshire village has been given funding for a permanent Christmas tree – though concerns were raised over its ability to survive a heatwave. Bar Hill Community Association applied to plant the Christmas tree on land owned by the parish council ahead of the lights switch-on scheduled in November. They told South Cambridgeshire District Council that the scheme would be a “long-term community asset” and help “enhance community cohesion”. The report said it would cost a total of £2,807.20 with £1,000 funded by the parish council and asked the district council for a grant to cover the rest. This was broken down into £1,129.20 for the lighting and electricity, £1,278 for the tree and installation, £150 for a banner and £250 for Christmas presents. William Scantlebury, ward councillor for Bar Hill, wrote in support of the application and said it would be a “simple but meaningful addition, helping to bring residents together and add some festive spirit to the heart of Bar Hill”. Cllr Dr Richard Williams, vice chair of South Cambs Council’s grants advisory committee, said it’s “a lovely thing to have” but the costs “jump out a bit”. Cllr Eileen Wilson, of Cottenham, said: “The one thing that came to my mind when I was reading about this was the ongoing maintenance after the heatwaves that we had this summer. “Have they got provisions in place to maintain the tree, to keep it watered if we have a heatwave, because seeing the example of the trees along the A14 that have perished, it does take quite a lot to keep trees going when they have these very big heatwaves.” Emma Dyer, development officer with the communities team, said she’d check the tree management policy but assumes that would be covered. She said: “I think it’s something that they want to keep as an asset so I should imagine they would take a lot of care and look after it.” Cllr Farhan Hussain, of Shelford, said he grew up in Bar Hill and it is “quite an isolated village”. He said: “I think it’s quite a good, community spirit thing to have and I know a lot of villages are isolated at the moment. “Having that in place might actually help out a lot of low disposable income families. You know, things are quite tough at the moment. “I think this is a nice way to do it, but I think it would be very good to just clarify the detailed cost of how they’ve come to that price.” Councillors decided against delaying the application for more details about the pricing as it would mean it wouldn’t be decided until after Christmas. Cllr Williams said: “I think it’s a lovely idea, I really wouldn’t like to delay it and then miss Christmas”. The grant was approved unanimously.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The stunning Cambridgeshire walk with incredible views and riverside tea room
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: For those looking to escape the crowds and discover a quieter side of Cambridgeshire, the St Ives and Hemingfords Walk is one of the county's best-kept secrets. Beginning at Houghton Mill, this picturesque route follows the banks of the River Great Ouse through water meadows and historic villages. The five-mile circular walk is largely flat, making it accessible for most abilities, and offers a constantly changing landscape. Walkers pass through the peaceful Ouse Valley and enjoy long stretches beside the river before reaching the charming villages of Hemingford Grey and Hemingford Abbots. Along the way are postcard-worthy cottages, medieval churches and waterside views that feel a world away from nearby towns and cities. Those with time to spare can visit Holt Island Nature Reserve in St Ives, explore the town's historic centre or stop by the Norris Museum before continuing through the meadows. The route starts and finishes at Houghton Mill, the National Trust's historic working watermill, where visitors will find a gift shop and a popular riverside tea room. Further refreshments can be found in the nearby villages, including traditional pubs that make ideal stopping points on a warm afternoon. What makes this walk so special is its sense of tranquillity. Even during the summer months, there are stretches where the only sounds are birdsong, rustling reeds and the gentle flow of the river. For anyone seeking a hidden riverside route packed with scenery, wildlife and heritage, this walk is certainly a rewarding day out. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The best woodland walks in Cambridgeshire to discover this autumn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From ancient woodlands and National Trust estates to wildlife-rich nature reserves, Cambridgeshire offers far more woodland scenery than many people realise. Showcasing some of the county's most attractive forest and woodland walks, here are six beauty spots to discover this autumn. While best known for its wetlands, Wicken Fen also contains areas of woodland and scrub that create a wonderfully varied walking experience. The reserve's network of paths passes through reedbeds, grassland and developing woodland, offering visitors the chance to spot everything from dragonflies and marsh harriers to grazing Konik ponies. The ever-changing landscape and huge skies make every walk feel different, whatever the season. One of the county's most important ancient woodlands, Monk's Wood is a haven for wildlife and a favourite among walkers seeking tranquillity. The reserve's oak and ash trees line peaceful trails that weave through centuries-old woodland. During spring, woodland flowers brighten the forest floor, while birdwatchers can enjoy sightings of woodpeckers, nuthatches and other woodland species. The largest country estate in Cambridgeshire offers far more than historic architecture. Its extensive parkland includes pockets of mature woodland, tree-lined avenues and scenic walking routes stretching across the estate. Visitors can wander beneath ancient trees before emerging into open countryside with far-reaching views. Managed by the National Trust, it combines woodland beauty with some of the county's most impressive landscapes. Famous for its gardens, Anglesey Abbey also boasts beautiful woodland walks that are particularly spectacular during autumn. Shaded paths wind through mature trees and carefully designed landscapes, creating a peaceful retreat from nearby Cambridge. Seasonal colour is a major draw, while the estate's varied habitats support a wide range of birds and other wildlife. It is one of the most picturesque places for a gentle woodland stroll in the county. Covering more than 170 acres, Hinchingbrooke Country Park combines mature woodland with lakes, meadows and open countryside. Well-maintained trails guide visitors through shady woodland areas rich in birdlife and seasonal wildflowers. The park's accessibility and variety of routes make it popular with families, dog walkers and runners alike, while its peaceful setting provides a welcome escape from nearby Huntingdon. One of Cambridgeshire's most diverse nature reserves, Paxton Pits features woodland trails alongside lakes, meadows and wetlands. The reserve is particularly popular with wildlife enthusiasts thanks to its rich birdlife and varied habitats. Visitors can enjoy peaceful woodland walks before exploring the waterside paths and observation points. At Paxton Pits, the Heron Trail and Meadow Trail offer opportunities to spot wildlife around the reserve's lakes as the seasons change. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tucked away on the banks of the River Great Ouse, this National Trust site is among Cambridgeshire's underrated attractions. Overshadowed by some of the region's larger historic sites, this riverside retreat combines heritage, wildlife and scenic walking routes. At the heart of the site is Houghton Mill, the last surviving working watermill on the River Great Ouse. Visitors can explore the historic building and discover how grain was transformed into flour using traditional machinery, with volunteer millers helping bring centuries of history to life. During the operating season, the giant waterwheel can still be seen turning, offering a glimpse into a way of life that once powered communities across the country. Beyond the mill lies the beautiful Waterclose Meadows, a landscape of riverside grassland, wildlife-rich habitats and tranquil walking paths. Footpaths lead through the meadows and along the river towards the picturesque villages of The Hemingfords, making it a favourite spot for walkers, photographers and nature lovers. In summer, the meadows buzz with insects and birds, while the river provides a constantly changing backdrop. Despite its rural atmosphere, visitors will find plenty of amenities. The on-site tea room enjoys a picturesque riverside location and serves freshly made cakes, scones, light lunches, hot drinks and seasonal treats. Indoor and outdoor seating allows visitors to relax beside the water after exploring the site. There is also parking, a gift shop, toilet facilities and accessible routes around much of the property. Families are well catered for, with open green spaces, picnic areas and easy riverside walks providing plenty of opportunities to enjoy the outdoors together. The site is also popular with cyclists thanks to nearby links with the wider cycle network. For those looking to discover a quieter side of Cambridgeshire, Houghton Mill and Waterclose Meadows offers history, scenery and relaxation in equal measure.
