summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Local government shakeup in Cambridgeshire slammed as ‘gut punch’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
A planned local government shakeup has been slammed as a “merry-go-round” as the plans face further delays. Local councils in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough were set to be dissolved in government plans for local government reorganisation (LGR). They were set to be replaced with a number of unitary councils which would handle both county and district level responsibilities. An announcement on what form this would take was expected in July, but the Secretary of State for Local Government at the time, Steve Reed, delayed the decision until October. At the time, he said the “shadow elections” planned for May 2027 for the newly-created authorities would still take place. But in September, the government said local elections would go ahead for Peterborough, East Cambridgeshire, Fenland and Cambridge City in 2027. South Cambridgeshire and Huntingdonshire already held their elections in May. All six councils and Cambridgeshire County Council were set to be replaced with two or three bigger councils under the plans, with the shadow elections setting the stage for a transition the next year. Currently, lower-tier district councils look after things like bin collections, leisure facilities and council tax, while the upper-tier county council is responsible for road maintenance, public health and education, including special educational needs and disabilities. Today, it was announced that the transition would face a further delay. Jim McMahon MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth, announced in Parliament that only five of the 14 areas under review would be proceeding. These are East Sussex and Brighton and Hove, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire and Warwickshire and Worcestershire. He said: “To be clear, all options and proposals in these areas will remain under consideration and I will approach all decisions with an open mind. “As such it should not be assumed the same proposal will automatically
  be selected. It is important the process is allowed to run its course and allow full and proper consideration.” To help with the “costs of uncertainty” he said all areas would receive half of transition funding – £450k per new unitary previously announced and £500k for each area in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and West Sussex. He said there would be a further update by Christmas and every area will have outcomes by early next year. Pippa Heylings, Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire, said: “Local Government Reorganisation has become a merry-go-round of changing decisions. “First, we were promised elections in May 2027. Then the decision for Cambridgeshire and West Sussex was delayed, while ministers still insisted elections would go ahead in May 2027. “Just two months later, the whole scheme was put on hold. Now it’s back, with a new date of 2028. Businesses need certainty to invest and plan. “Councils need certainty to set budgets and invest in our communities. the electorate deserve a clear and transparent process and council staff deserve certainty about their jobs and their families’ futures. “Instead, they’ve had shambolic U-turns and no certainty whatsoever. “Business owners across South Cambridgeshire have told me how badly this uncertainty has hurt them, putting their businesses at risk when they could least afford it. “Today’s delay is another gut-punch to Cambridgeshire’s businesses and councils, and it does nothing to solve the uncertainty that has plagued this whole process. “How can businesses and council leaders trust that we won’t be back here in a couple of months facing yet another delay? “I’ll keep pressing the Government until our communities get the certainty they deserve.” Leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, Councillor Lucy Nethsingha, said: “This is a bitter disappointment and once again shows we have a Government incapable of making decisions or following through on its own policies. “Cambridgeshire and Peterborough were already stuck in ‘LGR limbo’ and to simply extend that further beggars believe. “Continued uncertainty simply creates increased risks, prevents us from making long-term plans and all at a time when the demand for and the costs of providing council services are rising. “In particular, the anxiety and uncertainty that this creates for the hard-working staff in the seven councils in this area is intolerable. “We risk being unable to retain and recruit good people, we risk being unable to plan financially over the longer term and we risk being forced into making more short-term procurement and contract decisions, all because this Government can’t get its act together. “Our residents and communities deserve better; our staff deserve better and the democratically elected councillors across this area deserve better. “This Government may have changed Prime Minister, but it remains firmly mired in chaos. “Yes, decisions have consequences, but indecision, dither and delay also has consequences, in this case for local public services, the people we employ and the people who rely on us. “Despite this further indecision, we will remain our focussed upon delivering our services for residents and communities and doing the very best for Cambridgeshire, while once again waiting on the Government.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firms left with ‘more questions than answers’ after Budget
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Business leaders say the latest Budget offers "more questions than answers" for firms across Cambridgeshire. The Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce has welcomed some of the Chancellor’s announcements, including changes to business rates and investment plans, but criticised the lack of support on employer National Insurance contributions, energy costs, and export provision. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "The Budget leaves many businesses in Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Stamford with more questions than answers. "The business-rates threshold increase is a step in the right direction but falls short of what the British Chambers of Commerce called for. "The absence of employer NIC relief, business energy support and export provision means the short-term pressures most businesses are facing remain largely unaddressed." Charlotte said the real impact of the Budget will depend on how quickly the measures translate into tangible benefits. She said: "There are encouraging signals on place-based growth and devolution, but the practical test is simple: how quickly will these measures translate into lower operating costs, stronger investment and real opportunities for businesses on the ground?" The Budget includes a rise in the small business rate relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000, removing rates for 70,000 more businesses and freezing business rates for two years. Other measures include a 3.9 per cent increase in the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage, a tripled trading allowance, and a new entrepreneur’s allowance intended to cover a year of living costs. The Chancellor also announced a scale-up programme for female founders, new founders’ Capital Gains Tax relief, and a fiscal devolution roadmap to expand local powers for mayoral authorities, and referenced the Cambridge Development Corporation. Funding for a local apprenticeship service was also included, alongside a plan that fully funds the defence investment plan and a new defence spending taskforce.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambs councillor and cadet leader guilty of rape and child sexual offences
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A former Cambridgeshire councillor and Army Cadet Force leader has been found guilty of rape and multiple child sexual offences. Rylan Ray, 26, from Westgate, Peterborough, was convicted of 23 offences following a 24-day trial at Ipswich Crown Court. The former Peterborough City Councillor had already pleaded guilty to three other offences before the trial began. Ray used his role as a detachment commander in the Army Cadet Force (ACF) to contact young people on WhatsApp under the guise of discussing cadet duties. He then encouraged them to move conversations to Snapchat, where the messaging became sexual. Ray created a fake Snapchat account posing as a teenage girl named Chelsie to obtain intimate images from his victims. He was linked to the account after a phone call from one victim to Chelsie was answered by Ray. Another fake account was traced to his flat through its IP address. Photos of Chelsie, including the Snapchat icon, were found on Ray’s phone, along with intimate images from six victims that had only been sent to the fake accounts. He also told a 16-year-old cadet that he could get him into clubs without ID because he was a Peterborough licensing officer. Rylan Ray was a former Peterborough City Councillor (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) The offences, involving 11 victims, came to light in 2025 after two 16th birthday parties were held at Ray’s home. The parties were attended mostly by cadets or people connected to the ACF. Parents raised concerns about drinking and behaviour at the parties, prompting complaints to the ACF. When officers spoke to children who attended the parties, several disclosed sexual messaging with Ray. He was also involved with the Combined Cadet Force (CCF) at Stanground Academy and Nene Park Academy in Peterborough. Police were notified in May 2025 and launched an investigation, where some children reported not only sexual messages but also sexual assault. Ray was arrested that same month. In a prepared statement during his police interview, he admitted he "may have" engaged in inappropriate conversations but denied any sexual motivation. He said he was "truly shocked and disgusted" by the allegations and claimed they had "ruined his career." He then gave no further comment. In later interviews, Ray admitted receiving topless images from one child and acknowledged that some messages were sexual in nature. He also admitted sending a photo of his genitals and pornography to the same boy. Ray was charged with 25 offences. Following media coverage of the charges, another victim came forward and reported that Ray had raped him after a night out in Peterborough in 2019. Before the trial, Ray pleaded guilty to two counts of causing or inciting a boy aged 13 to 15 to engage in sexual activity and one count of causing a child aged 13 to 15 to look at an image of sexual activity. During the trial, he admitted two further offences of making indecent images of children. He was found guilty of 23 additional offences, including rape, sexual assault, and sexual communication with a child. Ray will be sentenced at Ipswich Crown Court on January 8. Detective Constable Gordon Logan, who investigated, said: "The roles Ray held allowed him trusted access to young people, and he seized these opportunities to abuse them sexually. "We would like to praise the bravery of the children involved in confiding in others what had happened to them. "Doing so takes a lot of courage but it was so important that they did, because we then began investigating. "Many of the victims involved felt they had no choice but to engage in the chats with Ray. "In an increasingly digital world, mobile phones and social media mean children can be vulnerable to those who prey on their innocence and exploit their trust. "We encourage all members of the public to be aware of adults who pay an unusual amount of attention to a child – no matter their profession. "Sharing any concerns, no matter how small, can make all the difference."

A historic former school is set to get a new lease of life after fears it would be lost forever. The Old Day School in Bluntisham High Street will now be turned into a three-bed house after lying empty for around five years. Huntingdonshire District Council’s planning officers recommended the proposal be refused as it would cause “substantial” harm to the Grade II listed building. This was due to the dividing of the school hall to allow for a third bedroom, but residents submitted 17 letters in support of the plans. Philippa Hope, of Bluntisham Parish Council, told the council’s development management committee the building “needs to be preserved”. She said: “It has a resonance for the people of Bluntisham – and is integral to the spirit of place. “However, it is no longer a school and could never be used as a school again. “To convert any building into a home internal changes are inevitable – the school building is the same and any changes are justifiable in securing the long-term future of this vacant listed building.” A previous proposal was refused in 2025 despite concerns that the building hasn’t been properly maintained since it stopped being used as a school in 1968. Councillors had concerns with the proposed rear extension which was reduced in size in the resubmission, with the hall division the last remaining concern for officers. Simon Claridge, the applicant, told the committee he cares “deeply about the building” which had continued to “deteriorate through vandalism, broken windows, water ingress, roof damage and even attempted arson”. He said: “We’ve listened, compromised and repeatedly amended our proposals. Given the resources already invested though – this really is our last attempt to save this building. “Every year that passes more of the very heritage we’re trying to protect is lost. “I understand the conservation’s desire to retain the school hall as one open space – however, a completely open hall simply does not provide a practical family home.” He added that the partition would be “reversible” as a “further compromise” and the proposal was the “only way of ensuring that this building will continue to stand”. Cllr Paul Hodgson-Jones, speaking as ward councillor for Holywell-cum-Needingworth, said the school hall would “not be open to the public to see”. The Conservative councillor said: “They will still be able to see that it’s an old school hall from the outside because it’s evident from the architecture.” Cllr Julie Kerr agreed that the hall would be too big for a room in a home of that size and couldn’t be maintained “as a viable room”. The independent councillor said: “The person who owns it is clearly passionate about the building, he lives next door, he cares about it, he cares about the village. “I couldn’t think of a more suitable person to renovate it.” Cllr Peter Gammons said it was a “very emotionally challenging thing” being faced with the possibility “it could collapse and be lost forever”. But, the Reform UK councillor, said this should “perhaps have been considered before buying it”. He said: “I don’t know that we can vote against the conservation officer on things which are regarded as being of historical importance. “But the other side of it is, we want to see this building preserved – we don’t want to see it lost.” The committee voted to approve the plans.

The Rothbury Estate in Northumberland, acquired by The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust following a two-year fundraising campaign and priced at £30 million, marks the largest land purchase in England in decades. Sir David, president emeritus of The Wildlife Trusts, said: "The Wildlife Trusts called for your support and you answered in your thousands. "The appeal to secure the future of the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland has been successful and now the opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality. "This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special for generations to come. "Thank you very much." The project will focus on nature-friendly farming, restoring bogs, and enhancing wildlife across the estate. Sir David’s early backing generated more than £1 million in donations within a week. The scheme received around £1.9 million from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, as well as £5 million from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. Public donations totalled £17 million, with contributions from more than 25,000 people across 50 countries. Eilish McGuinness, chief executive at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: "By working with local communities to develop new approaches to land management, this transformational project has the potential to deliver nature recovery at a grand scale, helping to reconnect people to the unique natural and cultural heritage of this remarkable and nationally significant landscape." A post shared by A Life On Our Planet (@davidattenborough) Mike Pratt, chief executive of Northumberland Wildlife Trust, described it as a "remarkable achievement." Mr Pratt said: "The completion of the Rothbury Estate purchase is a defining moment for Northumberland and the North East. "Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare. "By securing this extraordinary landscape, we’ve the potential to create a flagship for nature recovery supported by sustainable farming, whilst delivering lasting benefits for wildlife, local people and the rural economy for generations to come." Portions of the estate have already been secured, and initial work is under way to survey wildlife, landscapes, and historical features. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fake beauty products found to contain mercury, lead, nicotine and methanol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Counterfeit beauty products containing mercury, lead and methanol are putting consumers at risk, following testing of hauls seized by Trading Standards. The toxic chemicals were found in fake cosmetics, skincare and perfumes seized during recent investigations, with four in 10 seized cosmetics found to contain potentially harmful substances. Among the most alarming discoveries was a skincare product containing 13,200 parts per million of mercury, as well as high levels of lead in lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products. Nicotine was also found in some counterfeit perfumes, and one fake fragrance was made up of approximately 80 per cent methanol. The Intellectual Property Office has issued warnings. (Image: IPO/Press Association) Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: "When you hear that mercury has been found in face cream, lead in make-up or nicotine in perfume, it raises serious questions about what is going into these products and how they are being made. "Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. "But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. "Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally, and those effects may not be immediately obvious. "Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. "You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made, or what risk it might pose. "That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters." The Intellectual Property Office’s (IPO) latest Counterfeit Goods Tracker revealed that one in five 18 to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly bought counterfeits, up from six per cent in 2023. In July, the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products, including extensions, shampoos and conditioners, from a warehouse in Manchester. A separate raid in Bolton uncovered £2 million worth of fake goods. This included perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes. The IPO’s Face the Fakes campaign is working with content creators and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential harms of counterfeit beauty products. Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: "These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. "Products can look remarkably convincing, but behind the packaging they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions. Counterfeit manufacturing equipment. (Image: IPO/Press Association) "Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet. "With our latest research showing a sharp rise in counterfeit beauty buying among young adults, we want to make sure people understand the potential risks and know how to protect themselves. "Our Face the Fakes campaign is giving consumers practical advice to shop more safely, including checking who is actually selling a product and choosing trusted sources." Dr Emma Meredith, director-general of the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association, said: "There is a rigorous safety framework behind every legitimate cosmetic product sold in the UK. "Ingredients are carefully controlled, products have to be made in clean and hygienic conditions, and they must undergo a safety assessment. "Companies have clear legal responsibilities for the products they place on the market."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New DWP bank checks begin for people claiming three benefits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: New bank checks targeting people claiming three benefits have begun as part of a major Department for Work and Pensions crackdown on fraud and error. The DWP has issued its first Eligibility Verification Notice, requiring banks and other financial institutions to check information relating to some benefit-receiving accounts. The new system can be used in relation to Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance (ESA). It is designed to identify cases where someone may have savings which affect their entitlement or has remained abroad for longer than benefit rules allow. However, the DWP has stressed that the powers do not give officials access to people's bank accounts, transactions or information about their spending habits. Instead, financial institutions will be asked to check relevant benefit-receiving accounts against specified eligibility rules and flag cases where further investigation could be required. A flag will not itself mean somebody has committed benefit fraud or done anything wrong. The Government also says no decision about a person's benefit entitlement can be made solely using information provided through the new system. Undeclared savings and the amount of time claimants spend outside the country are two of the areas the Government hopes the checks will help identify. The DWP estimates fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad in relation to Universal Credit and Pension Credit cost taxpayers £1.5 billion in 2025-26. The Eligibility Verification Measure is expected to generate £1.2 billion in savings by 2030-31. Minister for Innovation, Fraud and Debt Lilian Greenwood said: “Benefit fraudsters should be looking over their shoulder. These new powers will help us crack down on those who deliberately abuse the system, while ensuring people receive the right support at the right time. “We are not interested in where people do their weekly shop or how much they’re spending on new clothes. Banks will simply be asked to identify if somebody may no longer meet the rules for the benefits they receive, allowing us to investigate further where necessary. “With £1.2 billion in savings expected by 2030/31, this is a major step forward in tackling fraud and error, protecting public money and ensuring support goes to those who genuinely need it.” Being flagged through the system will not automatically result in someone's benefits being stopped. The DWP says a flag does not establish fraud or wrongdoing and further enquiries would have to be made. The measure is initially being introduced through a "test-and-learn" phase and will be subject to independent oversight before any wider rollout. The powers were introduced through the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025 and form part of the Government's wider efforts to reduce fraud and incorrect benefit payments. Further measures are also planned, including 2,000 additional anti-fraud specialists being deployed to Jobcentres and tougher checks involving Universal Credit claims from people who have gone abroad. The Government says its broader package of measures is intended to save taxpayers £14.6 billion over the next five years.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 12 ways John Healey’s Budget 2026 plans could affect your money
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Chancellor John Healey has unveiled a series of measures aimed at easing the cost of living, supporting pensioners and helping households manage their finances. From £100 energy payments and changes to pension tax to a freeze on the cash ISA allowance and new help for first-time buyers, the Budget contains several announcements that could affect what people pay, save and receive. Here are 12 key changes and what they could mean for your money. Around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will receive a £100 payment directly into their bank accounts this winter to help with rising energy bills. The Government said the scheme would cost £2.6billion and provide support during the coldest months. The Chancellor also extended the cut to VAT on electricity until July, which he said would take £50 off the annual price cap. Pensioners whose income is no higher than the value of the full new State Pension will not pay income tax under the Government’s new pension tax allowance during this Parliament. The measure is intended to protect pensioners receiving the full new State Pension from income tax as payments rise. However, pensioners with additional private pensions, earnings or savings interest could still need to consider their total taxable income. More than 13 million State Pension recipients are set to receive a 3.9% increase from April next year under the triple lock. The increase will provide a boost to pensioners’ regular income, although the amount each person receives will depend on their entitlement and whether they receive the new or old State Pension. The Chancellor also promised that every penny of the pension fund surplus for ex-mineworkers would go to miners, alongside a commitment to continue working towards the full transfer of the guarantor’s fund. Martin Lewis said the Chancellor had told him that gas standing charges would be scrapped in 2027. The MoneySavingExpert founder said the charge currently costs around £108 a year, but warned that the cost would be shifted to unit rates. That means households would pay more for each unit of gas they use instead. Mr Lewis estimated that around 60% of people could pay less, while 40% could pay more, depending on their consumption. The Chancellor is also expected to discuss removing electricity standing charges with Ofgem, although this is considered more complicated. Motorists will continue to benefit from the 5p-a-litre fuel duty cut until July 2027. The Chancellor said the extension would help households, hauliers and farmers amid continued pressure on fuel prices. He also announced that the higher mileage allowance for people using their cars for work would increase from 25p to 35p per mile. The increase to the standard mileage rate introduced earlier this year will also become permanent. Savers will be able to continue putting up to £20,000 a year into a cash ISA without paying tax on the interest. The Chancellor abandoned a planned reduction to the tax-free cash ISA limit, saying the allowance would remain unchanged for people of all ages. He also announced plans to work with the sector to create a new Starter ISA aimed at rewarding first-time investors. The decision will be welcome news for savers who want to keep their money in cash while protecting the interest they earn from tax. The Chancellor announced £4.7billion in Government-backed lending for a new Your First Home equity loan scheme, due to launch next spring. The scheme is intended to help first-time buyers who do not have financial support from family. He also announced plans for a new First Time Buyer ISA to replace the Lifetime ISA. In addition, the Government will end the Lifetime ISA penalty for people buying homes costing more than £450,000. Those affected will get back at least what they paid in, according to the Chancellor. The changes could be significant for aspiring homeowners struggling to save a deposit or facing property prices above the existing Lifetime ISA limit. The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will increase by 3.9%, benefiting 2.3 million of the lowest-paid workers. The Chancellor said the increase was intended to help people manage everyday costs, including the weekly shop. The actual benefit will depend on the rate each worker currently receives, their age and the number of hours they work. The Government will change Carer’s Allowance rules so people no longer lose their entire benefit because they earn just a penny above the earnings limit. The Chancellor said the cliff edge would be removed, allowing carers to keep some support as their earnings rise. The change is intended to make it easier for people to combine paid work with caring responsibilities without risking the loss of their entire allowance over a small increase in income. The Government is suspending tariffs on more than 100 supermarket products in an attempt to keep prices down. The Chancellor said the move was intended to help households with the cost of the weekly shop. The impact on individual shoppers will depend on how retailers pass on any savings, so it does not guarantee that every affected product will become cheaper. The Chancellor announced changes to how self-assessed income tax is collected, with affected taxpayers expected to make smaller, more regular payments rather than facing large bills that can be harder to pay. The changes could help people manage their cash flow and budget for tax more consistently. However, the announcement concerns the timing of payments rather than an automatic reduction in the amount of tax owed. The Chancellor also announced that the tax-free trading allowance for people earning money from a new venture would rise from £1,000 to £3,000. Self-employed fathers and partners will become eligible for paid parental leave for the first time. The Chancellor described the announcement as a first step towards wider change, saying he had listened to calls from MPs about paternity leave. The measure could provide additional financial support to eligible self-employed parents following the arrival of a child. The announcement did not set out all the detailed eligibility rules or payment arrangements, so further information will be needed to establish exactly who qualifies and how much they will receive. Recommended reading: The biggest immediate help announced by the Chancellor includes the £100 energy payment for eligible households, the extension of the electricity VAT cut and the continued fuel duty reduction. Pensioners will also be watching the new pension tax allowance and the 3.9% State Pension increase, while savers have been given certainty that the cash ISA allowance will remain at £20,000. Other measures, including the gas standing charge changes and new first-time buyer support, will take longer to come into effect.

He said: "For 2.3 million of our lowest paid workers, I am increasing both the national minimum wage and the national living wage by 3.9%.” Mr Healey opened his Budget statement by saying it is for “the working people of Britain, for British businesses, big and small”, built on “fiscal discipline”. He said: “First, by giving Britain some breathing space on the cost of living and the cost of business, “Second, backing the enterprise of British business to unleash innovation and growth in every postcode “And third, by tackling the big challenges on energy, on national security, on public service transformation and on housing.” The real Living Wage and the Government’s National Living Wage are often confused, but they are different pay rates with different purposes. The National Living Wage is the legal minimum employers must pay eligible workers aged 21 and over. The real Living Wage is a voluntary rate calculated independently to reflect the cost of living, with a separate, higher rate for London. The real Living Wage currently stands at £14.10 an hour across the UK and £15.45 in London. The key difference is that the Government’s rates are legal minimums, while the real Living Wage is a voluntary benchmark based on the cost of living. Recommended reading: The real Living Wage is a voluntary employer commitment that covers workers aged 18 and over. Nearly 17,000 employers, including IKEA, KPMG and LUSH, have signed up to pay it, according to the Living Wage campaign. The movement says almost half a million workers receive a pay increase each year as a result. However, workers do not automatically have a legal right to the real Living Wage. They are entitled to the statutory minimum that applies to them unless their employer has committed to a higher rate or their contract provides for one.

This was higher than September's Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rate of 3.5% and the Triple Lock's minimum increase of 2.5%. The Triple Lock means the State Pension rises each April by whichever is highest out of average earnings growth, inflation or 2.5%. The figures point to a weekly increase of £9.40 for people receiving the full new State Pension, taking payments from £241.30 to around £250.70. That would mean an extra £488.80 over a full year, with the annual payment rising from £12,547.60 to approximately £13,036.40. The full new State Pension would therefore pass £13,000 a year for the first time. But, it's important to say that pensioners aged 75 and over are on the older basic system of pension, which is still lower. The expected 3.9% increase would also apply to the full basic State Pension, paid to people who reached State Pension age before April 2016. The projected rates for the 2027/28 financial year are: Full new State Pension Full basic State Pension These figures are projections based on a 3.9% rise. The actual amounts will depend on the Government's formal uprating decision and rounding. It is important to remember that not everyone receives the full State Pension. The amount paid depends on an individual's National Insurance record and other entitlement rules. People are able to claim the new State Pension when they reach State Pension age if they are: Older pensioners get the basic State Pension, and some also get Additional State Pension. Recommended reading: Labour has pledged to maintain the Triple Lock for the duration of the current Parliament. Changes to the State Pension uprating system are scheduled to take effect from April 2030. The latest earnings figures mean the 2027 increase is expected to be driven by wage growth rather than inflation. September's CPI inflation rate was 3.5%, up from 3.1% in August. ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said increased fuel prices were again the main driver, with diesel prices reaching their highest level since July 2022.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire cat crisis worsens as RSPCA urges public to adopt or foster

Sally Jones, animal centre manager at RSPCA Block Fen, said: "We’ve seen a huge influx of cats and kittens at Block Fen. The animal welfare charity has warned of a “cat crisis” (Image: RSPCA) "Sadly it just isn’t slowing down – and it’s having a massive impact not just on us in Cambridgeshire but across England and Wales." So far this year, the Block Fen centre in Wimblington has taken in 53 cats, and the charity says cats are arriving faster than they can be rehomed. With hundreds of cats in national centres and thousands more housed in branches and private boarding facilities, space is running out. Sweet Matilda came to the RSPCA from a multi-cat household (Image: RSPCA) Ms Jones said: "We’re desperate for adopters and fosterers to come forward to help free up space in our centres. "This means we can help more cats rescued from cruelty and neglect, but also a cattery is not the ideal environment for cats and kittens and they can find it stressful, so getting them into a loving home as soon as we can is so much better for their overall welfare." Eight-year-old Spyhnx Charlie (Image: RSPCA) The RSPCA has named October 'Adoptober' and is appealing for members of the public to consider giving a rescue cat a second chance. The campaign comes as part of a wider effort to ease pressure on centres and improve animal welfare through rehoming. Turkey is around two years old (Image: RSPCA) Richard Hooker, Country Medical Director for inspiring vet care, said: "The number of unwanted and stray cats has reached unprecedented levels, making it even more important to ensure cats are neutered to prevent unwanted litters of kittens putting even more pressure on charities." To rehome a cat from Block Fen, visit the RSPCA website and complete an online application form.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Court shown CCTV that ‘captures knife attacker on LNER train’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: CCTV footage shows a knifeman on an LNER train that made an emergency stop in Huntingdon where he stabbed 10 people, a court heard. Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told Cambridge Crown Court that Anthony Williams "brought terror" to the Doncaster to London LNER service, stabbing 10 people during a "rampage" on November 1 last year. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. His trial opened at Cambridge Crown Court on October 28. In footage played to jurors on Wednesday, a knifeman, dressed in a black hoodie, trousers and cap, is seen walking down the aisle of the LNER train before producing the knife. Jurors also saw footage of passenger Stephen Crean attempting to wrestle the knife from Williams. Another passenger, Jonathan Gjoshe, boarded the London-bound train at Doncaster before he saw a man dressed all in black pull out a knife, prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told jurors. Mr Gjoshe believed Williams was following him and told other passengers: “Please make sure he's not following me”, the court heard. Jurors heard that Mr Gjoshe screamed at other passengers: “Just run, just run, there’s a guy with a knife. I’ve been stabbed. I’ve been stabbed”. Mr Paxton told the court that Mr Gjoshe asked medics: “Am I going to die today or not?” when he was taken to hospital after the attack. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Budget 2026 5 changes that could affect your money before Christmas
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ahead of the Budget 2026 tomorrow Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey have announced five “everyday fixes” covering work-related travel, food prices, parental pay and support for unpaid carers, alongside plans to make sending and returning parcels easier. The measures are expected to feature in Wednesday’s Budget, with Mr Burnham promising further action to help families and businesses. Millions of employees and self-employed people who drive for work are set to benefit from changes to the tax-free mileage allowance. The Government will make the existing 55p-a-mile rate permanent for the first 10,000 business miles. For mileage above that threshold, the rate will increase from 25p to 35p per mile. The Government expects the overall package to help around three million workers. Shoppers could save money on their food bills after ministers announced plans to remove tariffs on more than 100 products. Popular items including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins are among the goods covered by the changes. The Treasury estimates the tariff cuts will save households around £21 on food shopping over the course of a year. The changes are also intended to reduce costs for farmers by cutting tariffs on fertilisers, while households that use kerosene for heating could benefit from a separate tariff reduction. More than 150,000 parents a year are expected to benefit from an extension to parental pay. The changes will include self-employed fathers who have previously missed out on the support. The measure is intended to give more parents financial support during the early weeks of their child's life. Further details are expected as the Budget measures are set out. The Government has promised to end the controversial Carers’ Allowance earnings cliff edge. Under the current system, unpaid carers can lose their entire benefit if they earn even a few pence above the weekly earnings limit. The Government plans to introduce a taper instead, reducing the benefit by £1 for every £1 earned above the limit. The change is intended to prevent carers from suddenly losing all their support when they take on extra paid work. The Government is also rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes. The aim is to reduce the number of people who have to queue at counters to send or return parcels. The extra facilities are expected to be particularly useful in the run-up to Christmas, when parcel volumes typically rise. The Prime Minister said the Government wanted to address everyday financial pressures alongside its wider economic plans. He said: “We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair. “If you’re a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket. “And at Wednesday’s Budget, we’ll go further to give families and businesses the breathing space they need today, while we build a stronger economy, transform our country and bring down cost for people long-term.” Chancellor John Healey said the measures were only a small part of the Government's plans to ease pressure on household budgets. He said: “Today’s everyday fixes are just a small part of what we are doing to give families a bit of breathing space. “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting families here at home through higher everyday costs. “We can’t control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference.” Recommended reading: The Budget is also expected to deliver a £432million boost to help get homeless people off the streets by Christmas. Mr Burnham said he wanted to ensure “every single person” sleeping on the streets received an offer of help by the end of the year. The Prime Minister has indicated that further measures to support families and businesses will be announced in Wednesday’s Budget.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP calls to protect kidney care amid Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire MP is calling for the government to protect kidney care during a major hospital redevelopment. Ben Obese-Jecty, MP for Huntingdon, wants a long-term guarantee that dialysis services will continue at Hinchingbrooke Hospital throughout its redevelopment. He visited the renal unit, spoke to staff and patients, and raised concerns about dialysis under the New Hospital Programme. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "Visiting the unit and speaking directly with patients and staff brought home just how vital this service is to our community. "Haemodialysis is physically exhausting and emotionally demanding; local patients should never have to carry the additional anxiety of travelling miles out of our area simply to access life-sustaining treatment." Mr Obese-Jecty has submitted written parliamentary questions to the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), requesting transparent funding commitments and clear confirmation that constituents will not be forced to travel outside Huntingdonshire for regular treatment. He said: "While the rebuild of Hinchingbrooke Hospital is an essential milestone to modernise our health estate and removing reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC), facility improvements must protect core clinical specialities. "I have taken our community's case to Westminster to secure binding commitments from ministers that renal dialysis will stay right here in Huntingdon for the long term." Patients with end-stage kidney conditions often attend dialysis sessions several times a week. If the service were moved, patients would face lengthy journeys to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge or Peterborough City Hospital. Hinchingbrooke Hospital was added to the New Hospital Programme in May 2023. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust invited the public to have their say on site accessibility and navigation; the desired patient and visitor experience, including digital technology and single rooms; and how the hospital can better support community health and wellbeing. The redevelopment programme is designed to address the challenges associated with ageing hospital infrastructure. A new hospital is expected to be delivered on the existing site, due to open by the end of 2032.

By notifying the watchdog, the nursery met its legal responsibility under the 'statutory framework for the early years foundation stage'. However, after a regulatory telephone call, Ofsted "found the provider was not meeting one of the requirements". This related to safeguarding policies and procedures not being implemented in line with the guidance and procedures of the relevant local safeguarding partners. At the time, Ofsted confirmed the nursery took "immediate action to strengthen their safeguarding policies and procedures". Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: What will Budget mean for pensioners as State Pension set to hit £13,036?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are waiting to see whether Chancellor John Healey will announce a major change to the tax-free personal allowance in the Budget 2026. The Government is expected to set out how it will protect people whose only income is the State Pension from paying Income Tax, after next April’s increase is set to push the full new State Pension above the existing £12,570 personal allowance. According to some reports, ministers are considering raising the tax-free threshold for low-income pensioners to £13,036, matching the projected annual value of the full new State Pension from April 2027. This could shield almost one million pensioners from Income Tax and cost around £200million a year by the end of the decade. However, the reported plan would not mean every pensioner becomes exempt from tax. People with private pensions, savings income or other sources of taxable income could still face an Income Tax bill. The full new State Pension is on course to increase by 3.9% from April 2027 under the triple lock. This would take the weekly payment from £241.30 to £250.70, an annual increase of around £489, bringing the yearly total to approximately £13,036. The increase reflects earnings growth, which is one of three measures used to determine the annual State Pension rise. A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) Under the triple lock, payments increase each April by whichever is highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The projected increase would take the full new State Pension above the current £12,570 Income Tax personal allowance for the first time. The personal allowance is the amount someone can earn in a tax year before they start paying Income Tax. Without a change to the rules, pensioners whose only income is the full new State Pension could technically have a small amount of income above the standard tax-free threshold. The Government has previously promised that people whose only income is the State Pension will be protected from paying Income Tax, with further details expected in the Budget. The Times reports that ministers intend to achieve this by increasing the personal allowance for low-income pensioners to £13,036. If introduced as reported, the measure could mean almost one million pensioners avoid paying Income Tax on their State Pension. The proposed threshold would also rise in line with increases to the State Pension during the current Parliament, according to the newspaper. However, the details of how eligibility would work have not yet been confirmed. Steve Webb, a partner at pension consultants LCP, warned that the policy could create difficulties if the higher allowance is restricted to people on low incomes. He said: “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off. “But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow. And if the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing.” The concern is that someone with a small private pension could lose access to the additional allowance and end up paying more tax than someone whose only income is the State Pension. Pensioners receiving the basic State Pension under the old system will also see their payments increase next April. Under the projected 3.9% rise, the full basic State Pension would increase from £184.90 to £192.10 a week. That would amount to around £9,989 a year, leaving it below the existing £12,570 personal allowance. However, many people who reached State Pension age under the old system receive additional payments on top of the basic pension. These can include additional State Pension entitlements, such as the State Earnings-Related Pension Scheme (SERPS), meaning their total income may be higher. The amount someone receives depends on their National Insurance record and individual circumstances. People with gaps in their contributions may receive less than the full new State Pension. The tax proposal comes as the Government has also announced plans to adjust how the triple lock operates from April 2030. Under the proposals outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the State Pension would continue to rise by at least inflation or 2.5%, while still tracking average earnings over time. The Government says the overhaul would help fund a new National Care Service in England. Any change to the triple lock could have implications for pensioners' future income, particularly as the State Pension continues to rise alongside wages and inflation. Recommended reading: The Budget is also expected to settle questions about whether the Government will change the amount people can withdraw from their private pensions tax-free. There had been speculation that ministers were considering cutting the maximum tax-free lump sum from £268,275 to £100,000. People can normally withdraw up to 25% of their pension pot tax-free, subject to the relevant limits and protections. The normal minimum pension age is 55, rising to 57 from April 2028 for most people.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Home Bargains hot water bottle warning after customer's horror burns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman needed surgery after a hot water bottle spilled on her. Megan Shannon said she suffered first- and second-degree burns when the long bottle she bought from Home Bargains leaked in June 2025. She said she had wrapped the £7.99 Home Collections bottle around her waist to ease period pains and heard a pop after about 10 minutes. She said: "I just heard a pop, and felt the hot water trickle down my stomach, my legs, my thighs, my pelvis." Megan said the water was boiling hot and ran down her legs when she stood up. Megan was rushed to Whiston Hospital in Prescot, Merseyside (Image: Kennedy News/@meg.shann) Her boyfriend called an ambulance while she used cold water in the shower to cool her burns. She said: "It's the worst physical pain I've ever been in, it's like having my skin unpeeled multiple times in the same area." Megan, from Liverpool, was taken to Whiston Hospital in Prescot, where she said a team of plastic surgeons, doctors and nurses assessed her injuries. Megan said her groin, upper thighs and lower abdomen had first- and second-degree burns. Three days after the incident, she underwent a treatment called Recell, which she described as a skin graft treatment. She said: "It was petrifying. I had to have surgery, a treatment called Recell, it's a skin graft treatment. They take skin from somewhere in my body and spray it back on to me." Megan said doctors treated blisters and it took weeks before she could walk comfortably. She said: "To be comfortable walking it took weeks and because of the area I wasn't even able to wear underwear. My mental health went so down after that." She said the burns had mostly healed but marks remained and had left her feeling self-conscious. Megan said she would not use a hot water bottle again, adding that doctors had recommended a microwaveable wheat bag to her. Home Bargains said it was sorry to hear about her experience and encouraged her to get in touch so it could look into the incident. A spokesperson said: "We take the safety of our customers extremely seriously, which is why all our hot water bottles are stringently tested to ensure they meet the relevant safety standards and are labelled with appropriate safety warnings." The spokesperson added: "Hot water bottles can pose a risk of burns if they are not cared for or used correctly, which is why it is important that customers follow the safety instructions provided." NHS Scotland advises people not to use boiling water when filling a hot water bottle, and to let the water cool for a few minutes first. It also recommends filling the bottle no more than two-thirds full, carefully squeezing out the air and using a cover to protect the skin. The NHS says burns and scalds should be held under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible, within three hours of the injury. It advises calling 999 or going to A&E for a very large or deep burn, or one affecting the face, genitals or bottom.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: JD Wetherspoon customers banned from wearing this item in all 800 UK pubs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Meta Glasses are now banned at all JD Wetherspoon venues across the UK. Customers can no longer wear Meta glasses, or any other smart glasses, at any of its more than 800 pubs. The devices, which can record video, photos and audio, have raised privacy concerns due to their ability to film without drawing attention. The ban, announced in August, follows growing reports of people secretly recording strangers and sharing footage online. A JD Wetherspoon spokesperson, explaining the ban, said: "Like many hospitality companies, Wetherspoon has CCTV cameras for security reasons, but their use is strictly controlled by data legislation. "Apart from that, the general code that applies in our pubs, and most pubs, is that you can’t film customers or employees without their permission. "Meta glasses seem to breach this code, and common sense, by enabling surreptitious surveillance, so our instinct is to say turn off the cameras. "This is akin to our efforts to stop audible playing of videos in our pubs, which also invades people’s space." Meta reassured people that their glasses have a light that turns on to let people know when a photo or video is being taken. A spokesperson for the company added: "People use our glasses because they're helpful and help them stay in the moment, from listening to music to live translation or hands-free calls. "They also provide critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards. "Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently." Around 88% of Wetherspoon customers agree with the Meta Glasses ban. (Image: Patrick Glover) We asked readers whether they agreed with the Meta Glasses ban in Wetherspoon pubs, with 88% (4243 people) saying 'yes'. Around 9% (441) of people didn't agree with the ban, while 3% (141) said they weren't sure. Wetherspoon also recently banned customers from playing music out loud or taking calls on speaker at its UK pubs. While Meta Glasses, playing music out loud, and taking calls on speaker are all banned at Wetherspoon venues across the UK, poppies are not. The confirmation comes after customers at The Star, a JD Wetherspoon pub in Gosport, were denied entry on Sunday (October 25) for wearing poppies. The incident occurred during a day of demonstrations in the town, and among those turned away were veterans and members of the public, including Reform UK councillor George Madgwick. Cllr Madgwick said they were denied entry after door staff told them wearing poppies breached company policy. JD Wetherspoon has confirmed that poppies are not banned in its UK pubs. (Image: Getty Images) JD Wetherspoon has since insisted there is "no ban on poppies" in its pubs and apologised for the incident. A Wetherspoon spokesperson said: "Wetherspoon has been a long-standing supporter of the Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal, with poppies for sale in our pubs, including the Star. "There is no ban on poppies in Wetherspoon pubs. "However, there were some standard security measures in place today, as a result of demonstrations in the town. "Unfortunately, some members of the public, including some wearing poppies, did not gain entry to the pub. "The pub closed to all customers, on advice of the police, at 5pm and remains closed today. "We apologise to any regular customers who have been inconvenienced by today’s events and look to forward to welcoming everyone back tomorrow." Do you agree with the new Meta Glasses ban at Wetherspoon pubs? Let us know in the poll above or in the comments below.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Budget 2026 what to expect from John Healey as Chancellor prepares major announcement
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: John Healey will deliver his first Budget as Chancellor today, October 28, with households and businesses waiting to see whether he will announce further help with the cost of living. Andy Burnham's Chancellor faces a difficult economic backdrop, with pressure on public finances compounded by higher borrowing costs linked to turmoil in international markets following the Iran war. Ministers have already unveiled a series of measures aimed at easing everyday costs, including changes to Carers’ Allowance, mileage payments and food tariffs. Further announcements are expected on energy bills, fuel duty, wages and public spending. But with the Government facing tight financial constraints, the Chancellor will also have to balance support for households against his commitment to meeting the fiscal rules. Here is what to expect from the Budget 2026, including the measures already announced and the policies reportedly under consideration. There's been much debate about how the state pension and personal allowance issue will be resolved, and given that the state pension is tipped to rise above the income tax threshold in April, today is likely to be the day that's finally sorted. In a post on social media, Martin Lewis highlighted that the full new State Pension is expected to rise to around £13,040 a year from April 2027, while the Income Tax personal allowance remains frozen at £12,570. Martin pointed out that John Healey has said the Government will honour former Chancellor Rachel Reeves' promise that pensioners whose only income is the State Pension will not pay Income Tax. He questioned whether that protection could create a cliff edge for those with even a small amount of extra income. “An important question for @JohnHealey_MP,” Martin wrote. He continued: “So the full new State Pension would normally attract tax. Yet you've said you'll honour former Chancellor Rachel Reeves' promise that those whose ONLY income is the State Pension won't pay tax. But will that be a cliff edge?” Of course, many would like to see the HMRC Personal Allowance increase for everyone. As Alex Beavis, Interim Director of Banking at LHV Bank, says, it's particularly key for savers. He's calling on the Chancellor to raise the allowance: "The biggest tax rise facing savers won't make the Budget headlines. It's already happening to your hard-earned cash, year after year. "The Personal Savings Allowance hasn't moved since 2016. With savings tax rates due to rise by two percentage points from April, more people will be taxed twice on the same money." Measures to ease pressure on household budgets are expected to feature prominently in the Budget. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked the Chancellor and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to examine whether standing charges on gas bills could be scrapped. Ministers are also looking at whether to break the link between wholesale gas prices and electricity bills, despite gas accounting for only a proportion of total electricity generation. Fuel duty is another key issue for motorists. Mr Healey is expected to cancel a planned January increase, keeping fuel duty frozen at 52p per litre for a 16th consecutive year. The reported move follows concerns about rising petrol and diesel prices and the impact of the Iran war. Ministers have unveiled five “everyday fixes” ahead of the Budget. These include: The Prime Minister has said further measures will be announced on Wednesday to give families and businesses more “breathing space”. The Chancellor is expected to announce an increase in the minimum wage. The national living wage is set to rise by nearly 4%, from £12.71 to £13.20 an hour. The reported plans would also end the trend of increasing the minimum wage for workers aged 18 to 20 by a larger percentage than the rate for older workers. Instead, the younger age group's minimum wage would rise at roughly the same rate as the national living wage, according to the report. The details remain subject to confirmation in the Budget. The Treasury estimates that reducing paperwork and other administrative requirements could save businesses around £800million. The proposals form part of efforts to reduce the burden on firms and support economic growth. Mr Healey has ruled out increasing capital gains tax in the Budget. The tax is charged on profits made when people sell certain assets, such as shares or second homes. Some Labour figures have called for capital gains tax rates to be brought closer to those applied to earnings, but the Chancellor has rejected a rise. A potential increase in the tax surcharge on banks is reportedly under consideration. The surcharge, currently set at 3%, could rise to 8%, reversing a reduction introduced by former chancellor Jeremy Hunt. The Trades Union Congress, which supports the proposal, said the increase could raise £2.25billion a year from banks' “bumper profits”. However, representatives of the financial sector have warned that a higher tax could discourage investment in Britain. It remains to be seen whether the Chancellor will include the proposal in his Budget. Mr Healey has promised to fill a £4.7billion shortfall in Britain's defence investment plan. The plan, one of Sir Keir Starmer's final major announcements as prime minister, promised an additional £15billion for the UK defence sector but allocated only £10.3billion, leaving the Chancellor to find the remaining funding. The additional spending would help raise defence expenditure to 2.7% of the economy by 2027. The Government's longer-term path towards NATO's target of 3.5% of gross domestic product by 2035 is due to be set out at next year's spending review. Mr Healey previously resigned as defence secretary in a dispute over funding, arguing that the Government needed a plan to reach 3% of GDP in 2030. The OBR estimates that reaching that level would cost an additional £17.3billion in 2029/30. More than £600million is set to be committed to projects supporting the development and safe use of artificial intelligence. The planned funding includes: The investment is intended to support the development of AI while strengthening safeguards against potential threats. A £7million fund will be used to examine the feasibility of a potential future bid to host the Olympic and Paralympic Games in northern England. The funding would support a study into whether such a bid could be viable. It does not mean a bid to host the Games has been confirmed. An initial £285million is set to be allocated as part of plans to give mayors and regional leaders in England greater funding and powers. The aim is to allow local leaders to invest in projects in their areas and have more control over regional priorities. More than £1billion is set to be allocated to social and affordable housing. The funding forms part of the Government's wider plans to address housing needs and increase the availability of affordable homes. The Budget is also expected to include an additional £432million for the rough sleeping programme in England. The aim is to help get people off the streets by Christmas. Mr Burnham has said he wants “every single person” sleeping rough to receive an offer of help by the end of the year. The funding was disclosed ahead of the Budget, with the Government expected to set out further details as part of its spending plans. The state of the public finances will be a central issue in Mr Healey’s first Budget. The Chancellor has retained the fiscal rules established by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves. These require day-to-day spending to be funded by tax receipts rather than borrowing by 2029/30, while public debt as a share of the economy must also be falling in the same year. In March, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecast that the Government had around £24billion of headroom against its fiscal rules. However, higher borrowing costs could significantly reduce that buffer. The Resolution Foundation estimates that headroom may have fallen to around £12billion, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) believes it could still stand at approximately £20billion. The figures highlight the uncertainty facing the Chancellor as he considers how much additional support he can afford to offer households and businesses. A post shared by Dan T | The Manc Investor (@dantinvests) The Chancellor say not, but some experts advise that it should. Antonia Medlicott, Founder and Managing Director of financial education specialists Investing Insiders, says: “I wouldn’t like to pay more income tax, and I’m sure nobody else would. But a transparent income tax rise is much better than a dozen smaller, stealthy tax grabs that sneak up on ordinary people and increase financial pressure on them. “The chancellor doesn’t have much headroom, and he has made a mistake by ruling out rises in income tax, employee national insurance, and VAT for working people. All three raise serious money. “The easiest of those to raise is the basic rate of income tax. A rise from 20 per cent to 21 per cent would raise about £8bn a year from 2027-28, according to HMRC. That’s about £224 a year for someone earning £35,000, or about £74 for a pensioner on £20,000. “Raising VAT would feed straight into inflation in the middle of an energy shock, while employee national insurance falls only on earnings, so the whole burden lands on workers. Income tax reaches pension income and rental income too, which spreads the load across a much wider base.” Recommended reading: John Healey will deliver the Budget on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Households will be watching for announcements affecting wages, fuel costs, energy bills and benefits, while businesses will be looking for details on tax, regulation and investment. Although several measures have already been announced, other proposals remain based on reports ahead of the Chancellor's statement and should not be treated as confirmed until the Budget is delivered.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis celebrates end of 'energy poll tax' as £108 Standing Charge axed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis is celebrating the Government's decision to scrap the £108 gas standing charge, declaring an end to what he has branded an “energy poll tax”. The Money Saving Expert founder said he was “very pleased” after meeting Chancellor John Healey, who confirmed the fixed charge will be removed in 2027. The move marks a major victory for Mr Lewis, who said he had campaigned against standing charges for around six years. Standing charges are added to gas bills regardless of how much energy a household uses, meaning customers can face costs even when they make efforts to cut consumption. Mr Lewis has long argued that the system unfairly penalises people who use less gas, including those trying to keep their bills down. Announcing the news, he said: “I have confirmation that the standing charge on gas bills is to be scrapped in 2027. I've been campaigning on this for about six years, so I am very pleased to hear it.” He added: “It is a moral hazard. It disincentivizes people from cutting their bills. It's a poll tax on energy, if you like.” The typical gas standing charge costs around £108 a year, according to Mr Lewis. Under the planned changes, the charge will be removed and the costs shifted into the unit rate customers pay for each kilowatt hour of gas they use. Mr Lewis said he did not yet know the final increase to unit rates, but estimated it could be just under 1p per kilowatt hour. The changes could come into effect with the October 2027 energy price cap, although January 2028 is another possibility. The exact timing has yet to be confirmed. For households that use very little gas, scrapping the fixed fee could mean no longer paying the same daily charge as a much heavier user simply for having a gas supply. The reform is expected to benefit around 60% of households, with the Treasury estimating an average annual saving of £45 for those who gain. Although Mr Lewis welcomed the announcement, he warned that the change would not mean every household pays less. Because the costs will be transferred to unit rates, people who use more gas could end up paying more. He estimated the dividing line could be around 12,500 kilowatt hours of gas a year, although the final figure will depend on the rates eventually set. Around 40% of households could pay more under the new structure, according to his estimate. Mr Lewis also cited research by Nesta suggesting the majority of people in income groups below £100,000 would be better off following the change. He said vulnerable households with high energy use may need additional support if energy prices remain elevated when the reform comes into force. The gas announcement could also be the first step towards a wider shake-up of energy bills. Mr Lewis said Mr Healey would speak to Ofgem about how electricity standing charges could be removed, too. However, he said the Chancellor had described this as “trickier” and indicated it would take longer. For now, the confirmed plan relates to gas standing charges, with no timetable announced for electricity. The reform will primarily affect standing charges under the energy price cap. Suppliers will still be able to offer different pricing structures on other tariffs. Recommended reading: Mr Lewis also reassured people who already have a fixed energy tariff, saying the planned changes should not alter the rates they have agreed to pay. He said: “As for those on fixes: if you get a fix now, the rate of your fix is fixed, so this should not affect it. You will pay what you pay and if it has standing charges they will continue.” For millions of households, the end of the fixed gas fee will be a welcome move away from paying a charge that stays the same regardless of how much gas they use.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Gas standing charges to be scrapped in major Budget energy bill shake-up

The change is expected to affect around 23 million homes, with the Treasury saying the move could save 60% of households an average of £45 a year. However, the charges will not simply disappear from the energy system. Instead, the fixed costs will be transferred to the unit rate customers pay for each unit of gas they use. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “Abolishing gas standing charges is about basic fairness and giving people more control over their bills. “I am determined to reform our broken energy market, so it better serves the public interest.” Simon Francis, coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "Removing the gas standing charge will bring real relief to many low-income households who use very little energy and for prepayment customers it could stop debt building up in the summer months. Mr Healey added: “Gas standing charges are unfair and outdated so I am scrapping them to give millions of households a bit of breathing space. “My Budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.” Recommended reading: The announcement comes as Mr Healey prepares to deliver his first Budget in the Commons on Wednesday afternoon. The Chancellor said the change would give families “breathing space” while making the energy system fairer. The precise timing of the change will depend on Ofgem, which has been asked to implement the reform from 2027 or as soon as possible afterwards.

The man denies all allegations, according to the BBC, including suggestions that he abused his position to contact and form relationships with teenagers and young women for sexual purposes. ‘Well-known individual’ suing two news outlets to halt publication of claims linked to 'inappropriate sexual activities' https://t.co/phZU4JS2oE — LBC (@LBC) October 28, 2026 Sara Mansoori KC, representing the celebrity, told the court that publication would carry a "potentially fatal impact," citing evidence of severe mental health risk.
