"This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur. "The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple – now more than 10 – doctors." She told the court that the man had already made one suicide attempt after receiving letters from the news organisations seeking his response to the allegations, and later attempted to take his own life a second time after absconding from hospital. The claimant, who is referred to in court as PPT, "has no intention of returning to public life," Ms Mansoori said. A medical report submitted to the court stated that inpatient treatment could offer "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk," and that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk". Mr Justice Nicklin, who is presiding over the case, emphasised the public interest in the proceedings but warned against speculation or attempts to identify the individual. He said: "The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings. "Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact." The judge clarified that the case is not about determining the truth or accuracy of the allegations, but rather whether they can be lawfully published. Gavin Millar KC, representing the news organisations, argued that there was a strong public interest in publishing the allegations, which he said formed a "pattern of behaviour." Mr Millar said "numerous allegations" had been gathered during a "wide-ranging and rigorous investigation", with reporters having spoken to more than 100 people. He told the court that "many of the women have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result". Mr Millar acknowledged the seriousness of the suicide risk but argued that "the state may have a responsibility to protect life," but doing so in this case would require the state to "intervene in lawful journalistic activities to prevent an autonomous act by the claimant himself." He suggested that the risk could be mitigated and that there was "no proper basis to restrain the publication of public interest journalism." Justice Nicklin described the matter as "a difficult and important case" and said the court would determine the outcome "fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions." He confirmed that his decision would focus solely on whether the allegations can be published, not on their truth or accuracy.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nine Cambs council workers sacked in one year after disciplinary hearings
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nine county council employees were sacked last year following disciplinary hearings, data has revealed. A Freedom of Information Act request to Cambridgeshire County Council found that there were a total of 57 disciplinary hearings over the last three years. In the 2024/25 financial year, there were 22 disciplinary hearings with nine resulting in the employee’s contract being terminated. This was higher than the year before, 2023/24, when there were just seven hearings and less than five dismissals. To protect privacy, exact figures for numbers under five have not been provided. In 2025/26, there were 28 disciplinary hearings but less than five of these resulted in the employee being sacked. The most common reasons for disciplinary action were breach of policy and procedure and safeguarding, with 13 cases of each across the three years. This was followed by inappropriate communication or behaviour, with 11 cases, and health and safety with ten cases. There were less than five cases each of hearings for absence, bullying, harassment or discrimination, fraud, financial or theft, gross misconduct and negligence. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire County Council said they pride themselves “on being a compassionate and inclusive employer”. They said: “That does not mean that we avoid dealing with inappropriate or unacceptable conduct by our employees – the council is equally committed to achieving high standards across our workforce of more than 4,500 people. “Disciplinary hearings, where necessary, occur following robust and fair investigation processes. “Importantly, disciplinary processes do not and should not always result in the dismissal of employees. “Other sanctions, such as warnings, are available to the council and are applied where appropriate. “The FOI request did not ask for details of these outcomes, it only asked about dismissals.” In 2025, a council worker was sacked after the county council was scammed out of more than £90,000 in a bank mandate fraud. A fraudster had submitted falsified documents to change the bank details of a contracted home-to-school transport supplier and four payments totalling £93,000 were sent to the fraudster’s account. By the time it was discovered, Cambridgeshire Police found that the “suspected fraudster had left the country,” according to council documents. The officer in charge of verifying changes of bank details said they called the supplier and spoke to the owner to verify the change, but the council found they had not done this. They were dismissed for gross misconduct after falsifying a document to say they had conducted these checks, which the council said could have prevented the fraud.

The dessert is usually a small cake served in a cup, pot or ramekin, layered with sponge and buttercream, then topped with a thick layer of tiny round sprinkles. The cakes have since attracted millions of fans globally online, with many creating their own DIY versions at home. A spokesperson for Co-op said: "Staying true to the original flavours social media users love, Co-op’s Raspberry & Vanilla Dot Cake (166g, £2.50) combines vanilla flavour sponge, layered with raspberry jam and vanilla flavour frosting, topped with multi-coloured sugar decorations. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disqualified driver who fled from officers and was sniffed out by a police dog has been handed a suspended prison sentence and a driving ban. Fabio Sanches-Kuiper, 19, of Dovecote Avenue, Great Cambourne, was spotted by officers getting into a BMW at Brampton Hut Services at 11.20pm on September 23. Police had intelligence that he was driving again despite court-imposed bans. Road Policing Unit officers deployed a stinger on the A141, but Sanches-Kuiper refused to stop, drove towards Brampton, then abandoned the BMW and fled into nearby bushes. He was arrested with the help of police dog Ghost. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Monday, October 19, Sanches-Kuiper admitted two counts of driving without insurance, two counts of driving while disqualified and failing to stop. He was jailed for 20 weeks, suspended for 18 months, and given a six-month curfew from 11pm to 6am. He was also banned from driving for four years. PC Colin Dyer, of the Road Policing Unit, said: "Despite being disqualified from driving and previously serving a prison sentence for the offence, Sanches-Kuiper made the decision to get behind the wheel yet again and on one occasion attempted to evade officers. “Driving bans are imposed to protect the public and reduce the risk posed by dangerous drivers. "His repeated offending showed a complete disregard for those restrictions.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 locations to enjoy autumn walks in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From misty fenland and colourful woodland to tranquil lakeside trails, Cambridgeshire offers plenty of opportunities to enjoy the best of autumn. Whether you're looking for wildlife or a peaceful countryside escape, here are five places to enjoy a picturesque walk. Autumn is one of the most atmospheric times to visit Wicken Fen National Nature Reserve, one of Britain's oldest nature reserves. Walkers can follow the Four Lodes Trail or Adventurers' Trail through reedbeds, wetlands and open fenland, where grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies can often be spotted. The Adventurer's Trail is a three-mile circular route, with grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies among the wildlife visitors may see. As temperatures cool, migratory birds arrive and morning mists frequently hang over the landscape, creating stunning views across the reserve's unique habitat. Few places in Cambridgeshire rival Anglesey Abbey for autumn colour. The National Trust estate is famous for its tree-lined avenues, which transform into spectacular tunnels of gold, orange and red during October and November. Several walking routes wind through the grounds, passing formal gardens, woodland and open parkland. The changing leaves, seasonal flower displays and peaceful atmosphere make it one of the county's most photogenic autumn destinations. Part of Nene Park, Ferry Meadows combines lakes, woodland, riverside paths and open meadows across one of eastern England's largest country parks. Autumn brings vibrant colours to the woodland trails while the park's lakes provide beautiful reflections of the surrounding foliage. With a variety of circular routes available, visitors can enjoy anything from a gentle stroll to a longer waterside walk while taking in the seasonal scenery and wildlife. Located in the Great Ouse Valley, Paxton Pits Nature Reserve offers a mix of lakes, woodland, meadows and riverside footpaths. The reserve is particularly appealing in autumn, when trees around the former gravel pits turn rich shades of amber and bronze. The Heron Trail and Meadow Trail provide excellent opportunities for spotting wildlife, with water birds regularly gathering on the reserve's lakes as the seasons change. Tucked away beside the River Great Ouse in the heart of St Ives, Holt Island Nature Reserve is a hidden gem that feels a world away from the town centre. The reserve's raised boardwalk takes visitors through rare wet woodland, where autumn colours are reflected in the surrounding waterways. Wildlife is abundant throughout the season, and the tranquil setting makes this one of the county's most peaceful walks for anyone looking to escape the bustle of everyday life. Vast skies, peaceful waterways and abundant wildlife make it one of the county's most memorable beauty spots. The circular trail around the reservoir attracts walkers, runners and cyclists throughout the year. Meanwhile, expansive views across the water create a sense of tranquillity rarely found in the east of England. The site is also popular with birdwatchers, who regularly spot ospreys, grebes and other water birds against the backdrop of one of the county's largest open spaces. Nestled on the banks of the River Great Ouse, Houghton Mill combines beautiful countryside with fascinating history. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new set of stamps honouring the service of the nation’s armed forces has been revealed. Royal Mail will release six stamps on Armistice Day, November 11, marking 110 years since the Battle of the Somme, which began on July 1, 1916, and became one of the defining battles of the First World War. The stamps feature specially commissioned artworks by British artist Matthew Cook, who has served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and was deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. David Gold of Royal Mail, said: "Remembrance holds a profound place in our national life. "Through these stamps, we pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of those who have served our country through two world wars and many other conflicts. Six new stamps have been released. (Image: Royal Mail/Press Association) "Matthew Cook’s poignant artworks provide a fitting and powerful way to reflect on the sacrifices made by so many courageous men and women across the generations." Cook said: “Remembrance has a very special place in my life, having served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and been deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. “I was delighted to be asked to illustrate these stamps and to take on the challenge of such a sensitive and significant subject. “It is always a privilege to illustrate stamps for Royal Mail, and this project felt particularly special.” If stamps are placed in the wrong place, it could mean the parcel or letter will be delayed because Royal Mail’s sorting machines are programmed to scan that specific area. The automatic machines might also mark the item as having no postage paid, which could mean the person receiving the item will have to pay a fee for it. The recipient can visit the sorting office and look at the envelope but if they do not know who the parcel is from or do not want to pay the fee, the item will be kept for 18 days before it is returned to the sender or destroyed. There are a few other rules that Royal Mail says people should follow to avoid any delays or fees for their items. The stamp should also be placed completely flat and visible with the Queen or King’s head facing the right way up. The area around the stamp must also be kept clear, as Royal Mail uses the space for tracking codes and digital postmarks. Writing over the stamp will make it difficult for Royal Mail machines to read the tracking code. Royal Mail says: "The days of licking stamps are over. Read More "Just peel your stamp and stick it in the top right-hand corner of your letter. "You’ll need your stamp to be clearly visible, not bent over an edge and on the same face of your parcel as the address. With firework season approaching and schools breaking up for half-term, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is reminding the public of the dangers posed by home fireworks and bonfires. Station Commander Scott Fretwell, community risk manager, said: "Bonfire Night is a very popular fixture in the calendar and can be plenty of fun for all of the family to enjoy. "There are, however, potential hazards to avoid, to help keep you and your family safe. "We urge anyone wanting to enjoy fireworks to attend an organised fireworks display rather than hosting your own. "There are many across the county that people can enjoy safely, which can be found on an interactive map on our website." While organised events are safest, the fire service acknowledges that many people will still choose to hold celebrations at home. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is urging residents to stay safe and attend an organised fireworks display (Image: Supplied) Scott said: "While most people enjoy fireworks responsibly, in the wrong hands they can cause injury and damage to property. "Fireworks are explosives and as such should be treated with respect and only used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and the firework safety code. "Lighting a bonfire in a garden presents significant risks to residents if they get out of hand. "Not only this, but the smoke can also aggravate neighbours with respiratory problems. "They can also get out of control very quickly, causing damage to property and sometimes serious injury." The fire service advises only buying fireworks with a CE mark, lighting them at arm’s length with a taper, and never returning to a lit firework. They also warn against giving sparklers to children under five and recommend keeping pets indoors throughout the evening. For those who do decide to light a bonfire, the service urges residents to build it well clear of buildings and fences, avoid burning hazardous items, and never leave it unattended.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the state pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone has passed 100,000 signatures, triggering consideration for a debate in Parliament. The campaign argues that lowering the state pension age could allow older people to retire with dignity, avoid financial hardship and free up jobs for younger workers entering the labour market. The petition, created by Michelle Gill, has attracted 100,769 signatures and remains open until March 16, 2027. It calls for the current state pension age to be reduced to 65, arguing that people aged 65 to 67 can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited employment opportunities while waiting to qualify for their state pension. The campaign argues that forcing people to work longer can be unfair for those who are struggling with their health or unable to find suitable employment. It also suggests that allowing older workers to retire earlier could create more opportunities for younger people trying to get into work. The petition passed the 100,000-signature threshold, meaning the Petitions Committee will consider it for debate in Parliament. An update published on October 24, 2026, confirmed the milestone. However, reaching the threshold does not guarantee that a debate will take place, nor does it mean the Government has agreed to change the state pension age. In fact, earlier this month they made a statement, saying: "The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age." They added: "State Pension age is now gradually rising from 66 to 67. "This increase began in April 2026 and will complete in March 2028. "Increases to State Pension age have been in legislation since the Pensions Act 1995. "As longevity has increased and our society aged, State Pension age rises have maintained fairness between generations and protected the public finances." The petition remains open for people to sign until March 16, 2027. Do you think the state pension age should be reduced to 65 for everyone? Tell us in the comments below...

So, here are seven popular stores across the county that we have loved and lost. The Peterborough branch of Beales occupied the prominent Westgate department store building and became a major city-centre retailer. The original Beales store traded there for around nine years before the chain entered administration in 2020. A revived Beales reopened in the building in May 2021, employing around 30 staff, but the store announced its closure in October 2022 and finally shut in January 2023. The building has since been earmarked for redevelopment. For years, BHS was one of Peterborough's best-known department stores, selling clothing, homeware and electrical goods. The retailer itself was founded in 1928 and became a staple of high streets nationwide. The Peterborough branch was among hundreds affected when the company collapsed into administration in 2016. The store closed during the national shutdown of the chain, bringing an end to a familiar shopping destination for local residents. The Huntingdon branch of Woolworths was a favourite for everything from toys and music to stationery and the famous pick-and-mix sweets. Founded nationally in 1909, Woolworths became one of Britain's most recognisable high-street chains. Like all UK branches, the Huntingdon store closed during the company's collapse in late 2008 and early 2009. For many residents, its closure marked the end of an era on the town's high street. Founded in 1904 by Frank Brittain, Brittains Furnishers was one of St Neots' oldest surviving independent retailers. Originally based in Eaton Ford, the business later moved to the High Street in 1924 and became a trusted destination for furniture and home furnishings. After 120 years of trading, the family-run company announced its closure in 2023, citing online competition, rising costs and changing consumer habits. Ely's Woolworths traced its roots back to a purpose-built store opened in 1935 on Fore Street before relocating to Market Place in the early 2000s. The branch became a popular feature of city-centre shopping before closing in December 2008 as part of the chain's nationwide collapse. The prominent Market Place store has since housed other retailers, but many residents still remember it as Woolworths. The Wisbech branch of Bonmarché, located at 9-10 High Street, served shoppers for many years before closing around 2019. The premises subsequently remained vacant for several years before redevelopment plans emerged. The building itself has a long retail history dating back more than a century, having previously housed drapers and the former Bainbridges Department Store. The Peterborough branch of Debenhams was a cornerstone of the city centre for decades, attracting shoppers looking for fashion, beauty products and homewares. The retailer itself was founded in 1778, and the Peterborough store became one of the city's best-known department stores. Following the chain's collapse, Debenhams began winding down its UK operations in 2021, with stores closing nationwide as the business left the high street for good. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 hidden gems in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire is packed with hidden gems that rarely make the county's tourism brochures. From ancient wetlands and secret nature reserves to forgotten archaeological sites and historic country estates, here are nine lesser-known attractions to visit. Often described as a hidden gem, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. Visitors can explore boardwalks winding through reedbeds, marshes and wildflower meadows while spotting dragonflies, rare birds and grazing Highland cattle. The reserve offers a glimpse into the ancient Fenland landscape that once dominated the region, making it an excellent destination for walkers, families and wildlife enthusiasts. Hidden away between Peterborough and Huntingdon, Holme Fen feels remarkably wild and remote. The reserve is home to the famous Holme Post, marking Britain's lowest land point at around 2.75 metres below sea level. Visitors can explore peaceful woodland trails, wetlands and bird hides while discovering a fascinating story of how drainage transformed the Fens. One of Britain's last remaining washlands, Nene Washes offers spectacular wildlife viewing throughout the year. Winter floods attract thousands of migratory birds, while spring and summer bring breeding cranes, godwits and marsh harriers. Birdwatchers rate it among the county's finest locations, yet it remains surprisingly under the radar with many local visitors. Covering hundreds of acres beside the River Nene, the park combines lakes, woodland, meadows and cycle routes. Families can enjoy water sports, miniature railways, walking trails and abundant wildlife. Created from former gravel workings, Paxton Pits has become one of Cambridgeshire's most important wildlife sites. Its lakes, reedbeds and woodland attract kingfishers, otters and hundreds of bird species throughout the year. Well-maintained trails and viewing hides make it accessible for families, photographers and nature lovers alike. Many visitors compare the reserve favourably with much larger national wildlife attractions while enjoying a quieter atmosphere. One of the most significant Bronze Age archaeological sites in Britain, Flag Fen remains surprisingly little known outside the region. The attraction centres on a 3,500-year-old causeway preserved beneath the peat and waterlogged soils of the Fens. Interactive exhibits, reconstructed roundhouses and fascinating artefacts help bring prehistoric Cambridgeshire to life. One of the largest habitat restoration projects in the country, Ouse Fen offers expansive wetland scenery and exceptional birdwatching opportunities. Visitors can enjoy peaceful walking trails through reedbeds and lakes while looking out for cranes, bitterns and marsh harriers. The sheer scale of the reserve creates an extraordinary sense of isolation, despite being only a short distance from Ely and nearby villages. Tucked inside Huntingdon's former grammar school, the Cromwell Museum tells the story of Oliver Cromwell and the English Civil War through a collection of nationally important artefacts. Despite its historical significance, it remains relatively overlooked compared with larger museums in Cambridge. Visitors can examine weapons, portraits and personal items linked to one of Britain's most influential and controversial historical figures. Located just outside Peterborough, Sacrewell blends history, countryside and family-friendly attractions. Highlights include a restored 19th-century watermill, rare farm animals, woodland walks and seasonal events. The setting offers a gentler and quieter alternative to larger commercial attractions while still providing plenty to keep children entertained. Its combination of heritage and outdoor space makes it particularly appealing for multi-generational visits. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 40,000 sign petition to save 'essential' BBC show as its 'rested' after 27 years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 40,000 people have signed a petition to save the BBC’s long-running home renovation series DIY SOS. The show, which first aired in 1999 and is currently fronted by Nick Knowles, is set to be “rested” in 2027 as part of the broadcaster’s latest round of cost-cutting measures. DIY SOS has earned a loyal following by transforming the homes of families facing severe illness, disability, bereavement, or building disasters, with the help of volunteers and tradespeople from local communities. The BBC’s decision has prompted a wave of public backlash. A Change.org petition calling for the show to be saved has already surpassed 40,400 signatures. The petition states: "In 2025, I had the extraordinary privilege of contributing to a show on the BBC that has made a profound impact on the lives of countless individuals. "This wasn't just another reality TV series; it was a beacon of hope for those struggling in difficult circumstances. "The show brought together a community of tradespeople who volunteered their time, skills, and resources to make miraculous transformations in people's living situations, changing lives for the better. "This program showcased raw and heartfelt stories of real people, grappling with the hardships of everyday life. "It highlighted the power of compassion and community, bringing viewers not just entertainment, but also a myriad of invaluable life lessons. "For the many families it has helped, the show has been nothing less than life-changing, offering them a chance at a fresh start and an improved future. "Unfortunately, there are discussions underway about cancelling this invaluable show. "Ending it means turning away from those in need and ignoring the good it brings. "At a time when reality often feels overwhelmingly challenging, this show stands as a reminder to all of us of the potential we have to make a difference in our communities. "We urge the BBC to reconsider any plans to cancel this essential program. "By preserving it, we continue to foster a spirit of generosity, empathy, and community support that the show so beautifully encapsulates. "Let us keep telling these important stories and making a tangible difference in people's lives." The BBC has confirmed that DIY SOS will be rested after its current series concludes. The corporation insists the programme has not been permanently cancelled, with a new spin-off show revisiting families and renovation projects from its history set to take its place. A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC’s savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore. "DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show’s past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year." The BBC has also rested the annual DIY SOS Children In Need special, which typically involves a large-scale charitable project supporting young people. These decisions form part of wider efforts to save £500 million over the next three years, which have already resulted in the cancellation of other popular programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, and Live At The Apollo. DIY SOS presenter Nick Knowles said he was "disappointed" by the decision but acknowledged the financial pressures facing the broadcaster. A post shared by Nick Knowles (@nickknowles) Knowles said: "You may have already seen the news that DIY SOS is being put on 'pause.' "Of course, I’m disappointed not to be filming the show next year or again in the same format we know and love. "But I do understand there’s no endless pot of money at the BBC and sometimes they have to make difficult decisions. "For 26 years it’s been an honour and a privilege to be part of DIY SOS and I’ve loved nothing more than making it. "What I always come back to is that it’s the people who are the beating heart of SOS. "It really is the best of Britain and we need to see more of it on telly." He also thanked the families, volunteers, production team, and viewers who have supported the show over the years. Knowles continued: "To the volunteers, production team, purple shirts, commissioners and everyone watching at home, we couldn’t have done this without you. "And to everyone who hasn’t seen the series yet, give it a watch. "I promise your heart will be warmed." Are you upset by the BBC's decision to "rest" DIY SOS in 2027? Let us know in the poll above or in the comments below.

"However, subsequent testing has identified that it may contain phthalates at levels exceeding the permitted regulatory limit. "Certain phthalates, including Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP), are subject to regulatory restrictions because prolonged exposure above specified limits may pose potential health risks and possibly cause damage to the reproductive system. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Senior doctors in England to strike for 2 days - what does it mean for patients?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Senior doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and pensions. The walkout will begin on Wednesday, November 25 at 6.59am, with consultants providing emergency cover only. The strike follows a British Medical Association (BMA) ballot in which 76% of participating consultants voted in favour of industrial action. Talks had taken place with the government over the past month. Consultants don’t want to strike, but after 18 months without formal negotiations, they cannot wait any longer. These strikes are planned to take place on 25 and 26 November, with Christmas Day levels of cover provided. There is still time for the Government to make progress. https://t.co/tco6pyInD8 — The BMA (@TheBMA) October 26, 2026 In a statement, the BMA said: "Our intended industrial action will take the form of ‘Christmas Day’ cover as in previous industrial action. "Consultants provide safe emergency and immediately life-saving care on Christmas day and out of hours 365 days a year, so no patients will be harmed but the Government will hear our message loud and clear. "If the Government chooses to act, by formally negotiating with us with a mandate that can lead to a credible offer across our range of demands, then industrial action can and will be stood down." Consultants – the most senior doctors in the NHS – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year. Basic pay for consultants starts at £113,500 with the most experienced paid £150,500. However, they can earn thousands of pounds in extra payments, which means average earnings are more than £150,000 a year. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA, so it was "disappointing" that the strike dates had been announced. She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure". In previous strike actions by resident doctors, patients have been warned that procedures could be cancelled, but urgent appointments should continue as normal. Patients will be contacted if their planned procedures cannot go ahead. NHS England has said in previous strike actions that hospitals should only cancel non-urgent care, such as hip and knee operations, in exceptional circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hardest primary schools to get your child a place in
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The hardest primary schools in Cambridgeshire to get your child a place in have been revealed in new data. Most schools are able to offer a place to every student who picked them as their top preference, but some don’t have enough for everyone. In 2026, the most oversubscribed primary school was Milton Road Primary School in Cambridge with 62.5 per cent of students who picked it as their first choice given a place. This was followed by Ridgefield Primary School in Cambridge which had enough places for 69.8 per cent of first preferences and Abbots Ripton Primary School near Huntingdon which had 70.8 per cent. Ridgefield had 43 first preferences for 30 places and Abbots Ripton had 24 students put it as their first preference – but only 17 places on offer. The school with the most first preferences was Milton Road Primary School, which had 60 places but 96 students picking it as their top choice. Milton Road was also the most oversubscribed school in 2025, when 113 students chose it as their first choice and only 53 per cent were successful. It was followed by Newnham Croft Primary School in Cambridge, with 56.6 per cent of students successful, and St Alban’s Catholic Primary School in Cambridge at 60 per cent. Meldreth Primary School was the most oversubscribed in 2024, when 65 per cent of 46 first preferences were offered one of the school’s 30 places. It was followed by Holywell Primary School in Needingworth, near St Ives, at 69.8 per cent and Houghton Primary School in Wyton, near Huntingdon, at 71.4 per cent. This year, 94.7 per cent of Cambridgeshire children were given a place at their first preference school – and 98.9 per cent at one of their top three preferred schools. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said that, with just over one per cent allocated a place outside their preferences, it was the “second lowest proportion recorded in the last five years”. They said: “We’re committed to providing the best possible start in life for young people in our county and access to high quality education close to home is key. “With population centres changing over time around our growing county, the council’s Education team work hard, in partnership with schools and with careful reference to pupil forecasting figures, to try and ensure we can offer the right numbers of school places, in the right areas, when they are needed.” If your child was born between September 1, 2022, and August 31, 2023, and you live in Cambridgeshire, you will need to apply for a place in Reception for September 2027. This can be done on the county council’s website here, and the deadline for applications is January 15, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We braved the UK's longest scare maze as Horror Mania returns to Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Blood-curdling screams filled the air as we pulled up at the Horror Mania event in Cambridgeshire on Sunday evening, as hundreds of people queued for a night of fright. Staged at Skylark Garden Centre in Wimblington, the event boasts it is the longest continuous scare maze in the UK. The popular horror attraction was cancelled earlier this year after its previous venue, Hinchingbrooke House in Huntingdon, decided to no longer host it. Robert Gough, director of Horror Mania, said they had been worried the event, which attracts thousands of horror fans, would not come back following the cancellation as it needed the right venue to continue. There are plenty of moments to get the adrenaline pumping in the Horror Mania maze - the longest one in the UK. (Image: Sarah Cliss/Horror Mania) Happily, Robert and his team have found that at Skylark. The immersive scare maze has taken two months to build, and the effort was certainly worthwhile, with a variety of marquees with various horror themes delivering plenty of jumps, screams and frights guaranteed to get the adrenaline pumping, and the imagination racing. With more than 100 actors bringing the horror to life, the event is a whole lot of fun for those brave enough to venture into the maze. Loud music, flashing strobe lights, fog and lots of twists and turns with unexpected jumps around every corner; it is certainly not for the faint-hearted. Even knowing it is just a laugh, and that you are not really being confronted by an Egyptian mummy, or a zombie Taylor Swift, the scares are still realistic enough to put your nerves on edge. There were a few visitors nervous about entering some of the marquees, most notably the Clown City one, which was littered with terrifying clowns - as if they were not already scary enough for some people. The Stinkyface World was particularly gut-wrenching, mainly because it smelled just like poo - not for those with a delicate stomach. I won't go into too much detail on what you might find, as I don't want to spoil the surprise/horror/shock for visitors. But suffice to say if you love a bit of horror and are looking for a night of fun this Halloween, then Horror Mania at Skylark is the place to be. Tickets are on sale - although there may be limited availability for some time slots - from £29.95 to £52.95 per person. There are no age restrictions; however, Horror Mania is frightening and is not really suitable for children under 16. Under-16s must be accompanied by an adult.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fire service has given a major update about the cause of a fire at a proposed asylum seeker site in Cambridgeshire. Firefighters were called to the blaze at Roman Court, Leverington, near Wisbech, at 7.26pm on Wednesday (October 21). Firefighters from Wisbech, March and Dogsthorpe attended, alongside the turntable ladder from Stanground and crews from Outwell and West Walton in Norfolk. They found a blaze in a single-storey building which was unoccupied and worked to stop the fire spreading. No injuries were reported but the building has been "severely damaged", police said. Firefighters were called to Roman Court in Leverington (Image: Supplied) Crews left the scene at about 10.30pm after extinguishing the fire. Firefighters inspected the scene the following morning to check it was safe and that there had been no further spread or hot spots. Police said on Thursday, October 22, that they were treating the fire as arson and investigating it. In an update on October 23, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed that a "complex fire investigation" had been carried out. However, due to the significant damage to the building and firefighting operations, a precise cause could not be determined. Roman Court has been at the centre of an asylum row since the government announced plans to house 26 mothers and babies at the site. The site has attracted protests over its potential use as asylum seeker accommodation (Image: Supplied/Chris Tirrell) In September, Fenland District Council revealed it had been told by the Home Office the site could "provide 26 bed spaces for mothers and babies". The proposal is part of a national plan to move asylum seekers from hotels into longer-term accommodation. A Home Office spokesperson said: "Any form of criminal damage is completely unacceptable. "The safety of local communities will always be our highest priority, and the police have our full support in their investigation." The department declined to comment on Roman Court, citing its longstanding policy of not discussing individual accommodation sites.

Plans for a new eight-home development in Warboys have been approved despite objections from residents and the parish council. The proposal, from applicants Mr and Mrs Robinson, involves constructing eight detached homes on land between Heath Farm and Heath Pond, north of Heath Road in Warboys. The land is currently classed as agricultural. Plans include three three-bedroom and five four-bedroom homes, 16 parking spaces, landscaping and a footpath linking the site to the village. It was granted Permission in Principle in July 2025 for between four and nine homes, establishing that the site could be developed for housing. The plans include three-bedroom and four-bedroom homes, 16 parking spaces and landscaping (Image: Huntingdonshire Planning Portal) Despite the formal submission of these plans, the proposal has faced objections from Warboys Parish Council and residents. The parish council objected because the site is located near a former sheep dip, raising concerns over land contamination and risk to human health and the environment. The council added: "In addition, concerns are raised regarding highway safety, as the proposed access is located close to the junction with the A141, a heavily trafficked route, which is considered likely to result in a substandard and potentially hazardous access arrangement." Five residents lodged complaints, with concerns ranging from highway safety due to the proximity of the site to the A141 junction, to the loss of agricultural land and countryside. Residents also fear the homes will put more pressure on the local GP surgery and primary school. However, planning officers have recommended the approval of the application, arguing that the benefits of the development outweigh these concerns. They pointed out that the district has only a 3.68-year supply of housing land, against the required five-year supply, indicating an unmet housing need. The development is subject to several planning conditions, comprising requirements for landscaping, drainage measures, noise mitigation, cycle storage, archaeological investigation, and off-site highway improvements.

Atijus Elertaite was rushed to hospital in a life-threatening condition after officers were called to St John's Chase, March, at just after 11am on January 3. Prior to his death, a 25-year-old woman and 22-year-old man, both from March, were arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm. They were also arrested on suspicion of possessing class B and class C drugs and were released on bail. Atijus tragically died in hospital on January 8 and a post-mortem examination gave a preliminary cause of death as a head injury. The pair were re-arrested on suspicion of murder on January 22 and were released on bail until April 2. They were then re-bailed until April 22 before this was extended to July 22 and then until October 22. In July, Cambridgeshire Constabulary revealed it had taken no further action against against the pair for the grievous bodily harm offence. In an update on Thursday, the force confirmed the man and woman have had their bail extended for a fourth time until March 22, 2027. An inquest on March 12 at Vantage House, in Huntingdon, revealed the circumstances surrounding the baby's death. Area coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Elizabeth Gray revealed Atijus had been found not breathing by his parents. Paramedics attended an address on St John's Chase and managed to revive the toddler after 90 minutes of resuscitation, the court heard. Atijus was transferred to Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, where tests revealed he had a "bleed on the brain." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 cinemas in Cambridgeshire we have loved and lost
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From grand art deco picture houses to busy town-centre screens, cinemas were once at the heart of communities across Cambridgeshire. While modern multiplexes have taken their place, many former venues are still remembered by residents who spent countless evenings watching films there. Here's five cinemas we have loved and lost. The Grand Cinema began life in Huntingdon's former Corn Exchange and officially opened as a cinema on 1 January 1913. It survived a devastating fire in 1954 and reopened later that same year with modern facilities and a new screen. For decades it served as a popular entertainment venue in the town. The cinema eventually closed in August 1964, after which the building was used for bingo before redevelopment. The Princess Cinema was another venue that once played a prominent role in Peterborough's recreation and leisure scene. The single floor cinema opened in 1929 and welcomed countless visitors during a time when a night at the cinema was among the most popular forms of entertainment. Odeon Theatres Ltd eventually bought the Princess Cinema in 1936 before it was leased to J.F. Emery Circuit of Manchester in 1937. It closed in March 1958 with “Son of the Hunchback” and Charlie Chaplin in “The Kid”. The Playhouse Cinema served Cambridge residents during the heyday of traditional picture houses. It became the second cinema on Mill Road in 1913 when a brand new building was created. Like many cinemas of its era, it provided affordable entertainment and a shared community experience before television became widespread. Although little remains of the building today, the Playhouse occupies a notable place in Cambridge's cultural and entertainment heritage. The Hippodrome Cinema was arguably Huntingdon's most fondly remembered picture house. Opening in 1933 with more than 800 seats and a then state-of-the-art Western Electric sound system, it became a popular destination for generations of local cinemagoers. Located close to the town centre, it remained a prominent entertainment venue for decades. Films were dropped in favour of bingo in 1971 before briefly returning, but the cinema ultimately closed and was demolished around 1977 to make way for retail development. The Exchange Cinema was once among several cinemas serving Ely residents during the peak years of cinema-going. Situated in the cathedral city, it provided local audiences with access to the latest film releases at a time when trips to the pictures were a major social event. It closed in 1963 before being demolished in 1964 and remains part of Ely's rich cultural and entertainment heritage. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Only one in five people can pass this three-question IQ test
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Less than one in five people pass this IQ test, thought to be the shortest in the world only three questions long. The Cognitive Reflection Test has a pass rate of just 17 per cent, leaving the majority who attempt it boggled. It was originally part of a research paper published in 2005 by MIT Professor Shane Frederick, and has recently resurfaced online with many people giving it a go. As part of his research, Professor Frederick had more than 3,000 participants from a range of educational backgrounds complete the test, but even those attending top American universities such as Yale and Harvard struggled to work out all the answers. Professor Frederick said: "The three items on the CRT are ‘easy’ in the sense that their solution is easily understood when explained, yet reaching the correct answer often requires the suppression of an erroneous answer that springs ‘impulsively’ to mind." So how will you get on? 1. A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets? 3. In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake? These are the three most common answers that people guess, but they are actually incorrect: 1. 10 cents 2. 100 minutes 3. 24 days Professor Frederick said: "Anyone who reflects upon it for even a moment would recognise that the difference between $1 and 10 cents is only 90 cents, not $1 as the problem stipulates. "In this case, catching that error is tantamount to solving the problem, since nearly everyone who does not respond ‘10 cents’ does, in fact, give the correct response." The correct answers are: 1. Five cents 2. Five minutes 3. 47 days Presh Talwalkar, the author of The Hoy of Game Theory: An Introduction to Strategic Thinking, explained how to work out the correct answers for each of the three questions on his blog, Mind Your Decisions. 1. Say the ball costs X. Then the bat costs $1 more, so it is X + 1. So we have bat + ball = X + (X + 1) = 1.1 because together they cost $1.10. This means 2X + 1 = 1.1, then 2X = 0.1, so X = 0.05. This means the ball costs five cents and the bat costs $1.05 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, then it takes one machine five minutes to make one widget (each machine is making a widget in five minutes). If we have 100 machines working together, then each can make a widget in five minutes. So there will be 100 widgets in five minutes. 3. Every day FORWARD the patch doubles in size. So every day BACKWARDS means the patch halves in size. So on day 47 the lake is half full.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Stormy weather can leave homeowners facing unexpected repair bills, particularly when strong winds damage roofs, fences and other parts of a property. While home insurance can provide protection against some types of storm damage, not everything is necessarily covered. The exact level of protection will depend on your policy and what has been damaged. Here’s what homeowners should know before making a claim. Storm Boelo will bring wet and windy weather across the UK this weekend 🍃🌧️ Here are the details to help you make your plans 👇 https://t.co/Yx3CYaUr3I — Met Office (@metoffice) October 23, 2026 Buildings and contents insurance policies often cover against storm damage. Following a storm, your policy should cover any significant damage that your house suffers as a result of high winds from the storm. However, policies often exclude anything outdoors, such as garden furniture, garden sheds, fences, gates or hedges, so specific cover would need to be found for them. Matthew Harwood, Home & Lifestyle insurance expert at Confused.com , said: "Having home insurance in place helps protect your building and contents from potential storm damage, particularly if you live in an area at high risk of flooding. "It's also important to buy home insurance if your home has features like a thatched roof, timber frames or is made of wattle and daub. These kinds of homes are typically made from old-fashioned construction methods, which makes them more likely to suffer storm damage. "It's also worth checking how much home insurance cover you need to avoid missing key features that help cover your home from storm damage." With high winds still prevalent across much of the UK, many garden fences will be looking a little worse for wear, and may even have blown away. However, fences aren’t normally covered for storm damage under standard home insurance policies, but it would still be worth checking your specific insurance policy to make sure. As wear and tear is rarely covered by most insurers, any fences that were already old and unstable prior to a storm will likely not be covered by your police. You may end up having to prove to your insurer that your fence was well-maintained prior to the high winds which caused the damage.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Binman tells all UK households to make food bin change urgently
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Households risk losing food waste caddies in autumn winds unless lids are clearly numbered. A refuse collector has urged residents across the UK to mark outdoor containers now before seasonal autumn gales arrive in force. Ashley, known on TikTok as The No1 Binman to his 214,600 followers, shared the advice as temperatures drop across the country. He said: "It's that time of year where the wind starts picking up and if you have a food waste bin and don't have your number on it, it could end up a million miles down the road." Householders often blame council collection crews when kerbside bins vanish, but collectors explain that empty food caddies weigh very little once emptied into lorries on collection rounds. Ashley said: "It's not the bin men's fault, it's because they don't weigh a lot." "So once you take the food out, they get put down and if they're not taken in straight away, they could end up down the road." Numbers marked clearly on the top lid allow waste collection crews to return containers directly outside the correct property after emptying. Ashley pointed out that identification stickers can be applied to food waste containers and standard general rubbish wheelie bins alike. He added: "The bin men will make sure it goes right back outside your house and then it's up to you to go and get it." The bin worker previously shared advice on marking bin lids to prevent bins from wandering across streets on collection day. In addition to outdoor containers, guidance outlines steps to maintain hygiene in kitchen caddies as central heating turns on. Kitchen containers should be emptied every two to three days during autumn to stop dampness, fruit flies and odours from developing. Caddies should always be lined with official council-approved compostable or biodegradable liners to keep bins clean and stop liquids from leaking. Hot scraps such as soup or leftover portions must also be allowed to cool completely before disposal, preventing condensation from building up inside the caddy. Households should tie a tight knot in compostable liners before dropping them into outdoor kerbside bins to keep larger containers clean. Retrieving emptied caddies as quickly as possible on collection mornings ensures containers will not blow away down the street.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Chest infection or cold? Boots pharmacist shares key signs and when to see a GP
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: As coughs, colds and flu become more common during the colder months, it can sometimes be difficult to know whether you're dealing with a common seasonal illness or a chest infection. Chest infections can develop after a cold or flu and share some of the same symptoms. However, there are certain signs people can look out for, according to a pharmacist. Boots has shared advice on spotting a possible chest infection as the retailer launches a private Chest Infection Service in more than 90 stores across the UK. Claire Nevinson, Superintendent Pharmacist at Boots, said symptoms of a chest infection can include a chesty cough producing coloured mucus, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest discomfort. Other possible symptoms include a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness. She explained: "A chest infection is an infection of the lungs or large airways and they often follow a cold or flu, therefore symptoms can be similar. "Symptoms of a chest infection may include a chesty cough with coloured mucus, wheezing and shortness of breath, chest discomfort, a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness." According to the Boots pharmacist, symptoms will often get better without treatment within seven to 10 days, although a cough can remain for as long as three weeks. People should seek medical advice from a GP if a cough lasts for longer than three weeks or they are coughing up blood. There are several things people can do at home to help ease symptoms. Nevinson recommends getting plenty of rest, drinking enough fluids and eating a healthy, balanced diet. Sleeping with your head raised or using extra pillows may also make breathing easier. Anyone whose symptoms persist, has had a cough for more than three weeks or is coughing up blood should seek medical attention from a GP, according to the pharmacist's advice. Some people are at greater risk of developing a serious chest infection. Nevinson said this includes babies and young children, older people, pregnant women, people who smoke, those with long-term respiratory conditions such as asthma and people with weakened immune systems. The advice comes as Boots launches a private Chest Infection Service for people aged 16 and over at more than 90 stores. Appointments last 20 minutes and involve an assessment by an independent prescribing pharmacist, who can offer advice and discuss treatment options. These could include over-the-counter medicines or, where considered appropriate, a course of antibiotics. Recommended Reading Nevinson said: "Chest infections are particularly common during the colder months and can leave people feeling unwell and unsure about the best course of action. "Our new Chest Infection Service provides customers with convenient access to advice, support and treatment right on the high street." The consultation costs £25, with prescribed medicines or over-the-counter treatments charged separately. Customers can book online through Boots and pay in store.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 long lost railway stations in Cambridgeshire you may not have heard of
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire's railway network was once far larger than it is today, with long-lost stations serving market towns, villages and growing industrial centres across the county. While many have since disappeared, their stories remain woven into the landscape, offering fascinating reminders of a very different age of travel. Before Peterborough became synonymous with the East Coast Main Line, the city's first railway station was Peterborough East. Opened in 1845 by the Eastern Counties Railway, it served routes towards Northampton, Rugby, March, Wisbech and Norwich. The station was known simply as Peterborough until being renamed Peterborough East in 1923. Passenger services ended in June 1966 as part of wider railway cutbacks, although the site continued handling parcels traffic until 1970. Today, little remains apart from the historic engine sheds, but the former station played a crucial role in shaping Peterborough's growth into a major railway city. Ramsey was once unusual in having two separate railway stations. Ramsey North opened in 1863 as the terminus of the Ramsey Railway branch from Holme. The line was worked by the Great Northern Railway and connected the market town with the wider national network. Renamed Ramsey North in 1923, the station struggled to attract large passenger numbers, particularly as road transport became more popular during the twentieth century. Passenger services ceased in October 1947, although freight traffic continued for many years afterwards. The station was eventually demolished and the site redeveloped, but for decades it served as a lifeline for local businesses and residents. The second of Ramsey's two stations was originally opened as Ramsey High Street in 1889 on the branch line from Somersham. Later renamed Ramsey East, it operated as the terminus of a route that linked the town with the Great Eastern Railway network. The curious existence of two unconnected railway stations in the same small town became a symbol of Victorian railway rivalry. Despite hopes that the lines would eventually be joined, the connection was never built. Passenger services ended as early as September 1930, making it one of the first stations in the area to succumb to changing travel habits. Freight traffic survived until 1956, after which the station disappeared beneath industrial development and later housing estates. Located just south of Peterborough on the Great Northern Railway main line, Yaxley and Farcet station opened in 1890 before being renamed five years later. The station served both villages and provided residents with direct access to Peterborough and destinations further afield. The station closed to passengers in April 1959, several years before the better-known Beeching cuts transformed Britain's rail network. Freight facilities lingered for a few more years before disappearing altogether. Today, little evidence survives of a station that once formed an important part of everyday life for local commuters, shoppers and travellers. Bluntisham station stood on the former St Ives to Ely branch line and served the riverside village for more than a century. Opening in the nineteenth century, it was one of several small rural stations that connected isolated Fen-edge communities with larger towns and railway junctions. Agricultural produce, livestock and passengers all passed through the station during its busiest years. The line gradually declined after the Second World War as road transport became increasingly dominant. Passenger services eventually ceased and the station was closed along with the rest of the route. Although the buildings have long since disappeared, traces of the railway corridor can still be spotted by keen-eyed walkers and railway history enthusiasts exploring the local countryside. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man accused of attempting to murder 10 people in a mass stabbing on board a train in Huntingdon is due to stand trial. Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of carrying out the attack on a London-bound LNER train near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on November 1 last year. The 6.25pm service from Doncaster to London King's Cross was forced to make an emergency stop at Huntingdon after British Transport Police received reports of a stabbing. Forensic investigators on the platform by the train at Huntingdon station Williams denied 10 counts of attempted murder at a hearing in July. His trial is due to begin on October 26. At a pre-trial hearing at Cambridge Crown Court on Monday, October 21, Williams pleaded guilty to 14 further charges. He pleaded guilty to ten counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train. Williams also pleaded guilty to two further counts of wounding with intent relating to an incident at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1 and an incident involving a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31. He also pleaded guilty to the attempted wounding of two men, aged 22 and 28, in Peterborough on October 31. His other guilty pleas covered affray at a Peterborough barber shop, stealing knives from an Asda store in Stevenage and carrying a bladed article in several public places on October 31. Court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Anthony Williams Williams also admitted possessing a knife at Pontoon Dock and on a train between Peterborough and Huntingdon, plus common assault on a Govia Thameslink train between St Pancras and Biggleswade. He further pleaded guilty to the assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a male police officer in custody on November 2. Williams denies 14 counts of attempted murder, meaning there will be a trial as the indictment is not resolved, prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said. Of these, 10 related to the LNER train incident, three are said to have happened in Peterborough, and one is alleged at Pontoon Dock. The trial is due to begin at Cambridge Crown Court on Monday.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Career burglar' who stole war service medal and training sword jailed again
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A serial burglar has been jailed again after stealing a martial arts training sword and a Great War service medal. Jody Stones, 41, was released from prison in May 2025 but carried out more burglaries in Peterborough this year. On July 28, 2026, he broke into a property in Rivendale, Werrington, and stole a gilet and a martial arts training sword worth about £740. A blood smear on a kitchen cupboard door matched Stones, while CCTV showed him outside with the stolen sword. Two weeks later, Stones and another masked man broke into a home on Eastfield Road while the elderly resident was inside. The victim woke to find Stones standing by his bed. When challenged, Stones jumped from a first-floor balcony and fled with the victim’s wallet, bank cards, passport, cufflinks, coin and stamp collection, gold watch and grandfather’s Great War service medal. CCTV showed one of the men wearing the same clothes as Stones during the Rivendale burglary. Enquiries showed Stones had approached local collectibles dealers to sell the stolen coins. Officers recovered the stolen coins and his grandfather’s medal and returned them to the victim. Stones was arrested on August 17 when he went to Thorpe Wood Police Station to answer bail for an unrelated matter. He pleaded guilty to two burglaries and was jailed for six years and nine months at Peterborough Crown Court on October 16. He also admitted six more burglaries, three car thefts and handling stolen goods. The other man seen on CCTV with Stones has yet to be identified. Detective Constable George Corney said: "Stones is a career burglar who showed a complete disregard for the sentence he was already serving for the exact same offences. “He stole not only valuable items, but items of real sentimental value to the victims and even burgled one address while the homeowner was asleep. "I can only imagine how terrifying it must have been for him to wake up and find a masked man beside his bed. "I am glad Stones is now back behind bars."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke hospital garden becomes living tribute to respected horticulturist
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A hospital garden in Huntingdon is blooming into a living tribute to a lifelong horticulturist. David White, a former president of Anglia in Bloom and a respected plantsman, died last month at Hinchingbrooke Hospital. Now, his daughter Carley and granddaughter Kaia—who both work at the hospital—are continuing his legacy by championing the Education Centre Garden, a space he cherished deeply. Carley White, team leader for Hinchingbrooke Community Midwives, said: "Dad's association with the garden spans over many years. Tribute to volunteer gardener (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) "I spent two long stints in hospital as a teenager, and he would push me in my bed down to the garden every day. "More recently we spent many hours in the garden in the weeks before he sadly passed." The garden is supported by a dedicated team of hospital volunteers and was recognised last year with a Royal Horticultural Society Outstanding Award for 'Gardening for Health and Wellbeing'—an honour it received thanks to a nomination from Mr White. Kaia White, a paediatrics medical secretary, said: "Grandpa loved the Hinchingbrooke garden, and the volunteers do such a fantastic job. Certificate for RHS (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) "It held a very special place in his heart—as it does in mine and Mum's." The family has donated plants from Mr White's nursery to the hospital garden and other community green spaces. Kaia added: "It's lovely to be able to give back to Hinchingbrooke Hospital when it has given so much to us." David White (Image: Hinchingbrooke Hospital) Mr White’s horticultural career included work at Kew Gardens and Buckingham Palace. He also contributed to planting schemes along major road networks during his time with the Department of Transport. His family hopes the garden will continue to serve as a place of peace and healing for patients, staff, and visitors—a lasting reminder of his passion for horticulture and community.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hinchingbrooke English department shortlisted for national teaching award
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Hinchingbrooke School’s English department has been shortlisted for a national education award. The team in Huntingdon is in the running for The PTI’s Bernice McCabe Award, which celebrates excellence in subject leadership and teaching. The PTI, formerly known as the Prince’s Teaching Institute, is a national education charity that supports teachers and school leaders through high-quality professional development. Dr Cat Scutt MBE, chief executive of The PTI, said: "The Bernice McCabe Award celebrates the exceptional teachers and departments who demonstrate the transformative power of great subject teaching. "Their expertise, dedication and passion for their subjects can inspire young people, deepen their understanding and open up new possibilities for their future. "We are delighted to recognise this year’s shortlisted departments and to celebrate the teachers whose commitment to their subjects and their students makes such a lasting difference." Named in memory of Bernice McCabe OBE, the founding co-director of The PTI who died in February 2019, the award honours departments that put inspiring subject teaching at the heart of the classroom. The winning department will receive a £5,000 prize and a trophy. Hinchingbrooke’s English department is one of three nominees for the 2026 award, alongside the PE department at Priory School in Lewes and the English department at Thomas Tallis School in Greenwich. The PTI promotes subject-centred teaching as a sustainable approach to school improvement, helping teachers deepen their expertise and share a love of learning with students. Significant funding from Postcode Lottery players has enabled The PTI to support both nominated and winning schools, giving them the resources and skills needed to deliver outstanding lessons. Since 2018, players have raised more than £1.5 million for The PTI, impacting the educational experiences of hundreds of thousands of young people across England and Wales.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: The Cambridgeshire fire station trying to 'break the taboo of menopause'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire fire station is trying to "break the taboo of menopause" by educating firefighters about women's health. Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson visited Huntingdon Fire and Rescue Station on October 15 to mark Menopause Awareness Month. Ms Phillipson said there was still “quite a lot of ignorance” about the menopause and its effects on women, especially at work. She said: "We know that there is still far too much stigma around this and it's good we are speaking more about the health challenges and women's experiences around the menopause. "Employers leading the way are providing a culture where people can be open about the things they might be experiencing and the impact the menopause can have. "One example we have talked about here is just making sure we have period products available routinely for firefighters who might be out on jobs and can't get back to the site to get what they need." Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson Government figures show that only about one in 10 firefighters nationally are women, far fewer than in the police force. At Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, women make up 24 per cent of firefighters, with about a third aged 40 to 55. Huntingdon Fire Station’s menopause champion Hayley Douglas said supporting women through health challenges could help increase those numbers. Hayley said: "We're doing an awful lot as a sector to try and encourage more women to join the fire and rescue service and I think this is a really important part of that. Menopause Champion Hayley Douglas "Firefighting is a career, so people join in their early twenties for example. "We need to make sure we support them through their life cycle of hormones as well." Huntingdon Fire Station has put period protection packs in every toilet and fire engine, as well as portable toilets and tents on its engines. Huntingdon Fire Station has introduced period protection items in every fire engine The station also delivers mandatory training to everyone in the organisation about the symptoms of the menopause, how it impacts work and its effects on relationships. Hayley said: "We are a male majority organisation and a lot of the engagement during those sessions has been from our male colleagues, understanding what their partners at home are going through. "Increasing that knowledge at work is like throwing a stone and seeing all the rippled effect where people start talking about it outside of work as well. "In the service, it's given women the confidence to be able to go and speak to their line manager knowing they have had a level of input in menopause awareness. "It just makes it easier to have that conversation. "Ultimately what we are trying to do is break the taboo of menopause and make people feel like it is a safe environment to openly talk about what they are going through." October marks Menopause Awareness Month Ms Phillipson added: "Often, quite small practical changes around uniform and kit and making sure you have good toilet facilities can just make the world of difference. "From next spring, bigger employers will have to publish plans on how they are taking action to support women including in areas like the menopause. "But already we have employers like Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service who are showing what can be done." Employers with 250 or more staff can currently publish a voluntary action plan on their gender pay gap and support for employees experiencing the menopause. Subject to legislation, the plans will become mandatory from spring 2027.
